item.title: Sales for Biden memoir fall far short of books by Obama and Clinton
item.description:
Promise Me, America, which has lukewarm reviews from critics, sold about 21,000 copies during its first week on sale

Joe Biden’s memoir Promise Me, America debuted with modest sales and lackluster reviews, selling about 21,000 copies during its first week on sale, according to Circana.

It sold well enough to top the New York Times nonfiction bestseller list, but didn’t approach the level of memoirs by such predecessors as Barack Obama and Bill Clinton.

item.title: ‘Abusive and insulting to Canadians’: campaign to oust US ambassador presented to parliament
item.description:
Hundreds of thousands of Canadians call for Pete Hoekstra to be declared ‘persona non grata’

A petition signed by nearly 290,000 Canadians calling on Mark Carney’s government to oust Pete Hoekstra as US ambassador to Canada was formally presented to the House of Commons on Thursday, a sign of the strained relations between the neighboring countries.

Elizabeth May, a Canadian Green party member, originally opened the petition for signatures in July 2026 after a woman from Calgary sponsored it. The petition requests that the Canadian government declare Hoekstra “persona non grata” due to his “US” diplomatic interference in Canadian domestic affairs”.

item.title: The explosion of extreme wealth is the major problem of our time | Bernie Sanders
item.description:
At this pivotal moment in American history, let us move forward together to take on and defeat a powerful, greedy and corrupt ruling class

We are at a pivotal moment in history. Never before in human history have so few people held so much wealth and so much power. And never before have we seen such an unprecedented level of greed, arrogance and irresponsibility on the part of the world’s ruling class.

Here is the good news: leaders from around the world are finally starting to wake up. This week, elected officials and economists from around the world – including four Nobel prize winners – came together in Paris for a “Summit Against International Oligarchy”. As the summit’s proclamation stated, “The explosion of extreme wealth is the major social fact of our time … We are sounding the alarm: billionaires are a threat to our democracies.”

Bernie Sanders is a US senator, and ranking member of the health, education, labor and pensions committee. He represents the state of Vermont and is the longest-serving independent in the history of Congress

item.title: OpenAI countersues Apple for allegedly stealing trade secrets
item.description:
Lawsuit also alleging pressure on hardware suppliers comes after Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly poaching employees

OpenAI sued Apple on Friday, accusing the company of ⁠stealing its trade secrets ​and discouraging hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices.

The suit, filed in northern California federal court, comes after Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly poaching its employees to gain access to its technology.

item.title: Schools in England must set aside time for pupils to read for pleasure
item.description:
Education secretary expected to announce measures as part of proposed reforms to national curriculum

Schools in England will have to allocate time for children to read for pleasure as part of Labour’s proposed reforms of the national curriculum.

The education secretary, Lucy Powell, is expected to announce to parliament on Monday that primary schools must earmark time each day for children to read.

Continue reading...

item.title: Purse found of woman, 24, swept from California beach three weeks ago
item.description:
Se Nah Park was overwhelmed by a wave at the notorious Panther Beach

The purse of a 24-year-old who was swept into the ocean at a notorious California beach three weeks ago was found on Wednesday, as the west coast saw record high king tides.

The Santa Cruz county sheriff’s office confirmed that Se Nah Park’s purse was found by a beachgoer at 4 Mile Beach, south of Panther Beach, where she was swept away into the ocean on 8 November.

item.title: Men dominate this Japanese game. One woman broke a 100-year-old barrier to rise to the top
item.description:
Tomoka Nishiyama will soon compete against men in professional shogi, often known as Japanese chess, but women remain marginalised in the popular game

Encouragement was in short supply when, in the 1960s, Akiko Takojima set her sights on becoming an elite shogi player. Women were too “stupid” to excel at the Japanese board game, a male instructor told her, before suggesting she find something else to occupy her time.

Decades after Takojima and five others became the first female professionals, a 100-year-old barrier in the game is about to be broken. From April, Tomoka Nishiyama will turn shogi’s gender bias on its head when she becomes the first woman to compete against men at the highest level of the game.

Continue reading...

item.title: Could New Zealand head back to the polls? The new centrist party on the block holds the power| Lara Greaves
item.description:
With a hung parliament, newcomer Opportunity now needs to choose between backing right-leaning bloc or returning country to another election

After a 20-day wait for the results, New Zealand’s election doesn’t have a clear winner. Several unprecedented events, including the success of a new centrist party and the looming threat of an election re-run, mean a definitive outcome could still be months away.

Election night revealed that parliament would have a substantial overhang: extra seats added to the house when a party wins more electorate seats than its party vote is entitled to.

Lara Greaves is an associate professor of political science at Victoria University of Wellington

item.title: Thanksgiving meal in Florida leads to mass food poisoning incident
item.description:
Local media reported that 18 people fell ill after attending a Thanksgiving lunch at a medical center headquarters

A Thanksgiving meal in Florida triggered a bout of food poisoning so bad that local emergency officials said it was a “mass casualty” event as numerous stricken diners were sent to hospital.

Local media reported that 18 people at the Leon medical center headquarters in Doral fell ill due to possible food poisoning after attending the center’s annual Thanksgiving lunch on Wednesday.

item.title: ‘I felt a zap race through my body’: what happens when someone is hit by lightning?
item.description:
Tens of thousands of people experience strikes each year. What are the effects of a current five times hotter than the sun – and how can you keep safe?

Caitlin Thomas recalls knowing that something terrible had happened but not fully understanding what.

She and her partner had arrived at a music festival some 270km north of Melbourne in the early afternoon and began setting up their tents and a gazebo for shade when the sky suddenly turned dark and the rain became incredibly heavy. A huge gust of wind picked up and Thomas asked her partner to hold on to the gazebo so it wouldn’t fly away. “He then asked me to hold on to it also so he could crack open his beer.”

item.title: Sunrise on the Reaping: The new Hunger Games film is a gen Z call to action – critics have missed the point | Rafqa Touma
item.description:
We’ve been brought up on literature about underdogs who fight – and triumph – against an unjust status quo

I first read The Hunger Games trilogy in early high school. Set in the post-apocalyptic nation of Panem, society is ruled by the Capitol – they are fascistic, surveil everything, and keep the middle and upper classes quiet with annual reality war games in which lower-class teenagers must fight to the death.

Ten years later, in 2020, I was about to enter a newsroom for the first time, at the tail end of Donald Trump’s first presidency. That same year, Suzanne Collins returned to her dystopian world with a prequel. The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes is set decades before the original trilogy, revealing the origin story of both the games and their architect, President Snow, through his young, possessive perspective.

Continue reading...

item.title: ‘Mass-casualty event’ in Europe possible amid rise in Russian sabotage, says thinktank
item.description:
Report warns attacks on critical infrastructure could lead to demand for retaliation and expose EU divisions

Russian sabotage attacks on Europe are increasing and a “mass-casualty event” is now possible as increasingly skilled operatives target critical infrastructure with ever more complex methods, a leading strategic thinktank has said.

The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) said in a report that Russian intelligence services and their proxies were targeting European railways, energy networks and defence industries in an attempt to weaken support for Ukraine.

item.title: Hackers reportedly breach US air force’s flagship cloud computing platform
item.description:
Intrusion into Cloud One platform could jeopardize security of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data

Hackers are reported to have breached the US air force’s flagship cloud computing platform, a break-in that comes days after reports that a CIA database was accessed.

Reuters reported on Friday that the intrusion into the USAF’s Cloud One platform could jeopardize the security of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data.

item.title: ‘Punched in the guts’: Poundland staff left reeling as it goes into administration
item.description:
Workers are sad but unsurprised as closures and job losses loom, while 2,000 suppliers will take a big hit

  • Poundland staff fear they’ll be left out in the cold for Christmas. When will workers have a say in their future?

“I feel Gordon Brothers punched us in the guts and took us down,” says Kelvin Blake, one of thousands of Poundland workers at risk of redundancy after the budget retailer’s US-based owners rejected at least two solvent bids for it.

While administrators at AlixPartners, who were appointed on Wednesday, continue to consider bids for the whole group, which has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland including the Dealz chain, more than 10,000 staff and thousands of suppliers face a grim Christmas of uncertainty.

item.title: Three studies link glyphosate to cancer, contradicting claims of Trump EPA
item.description:
Experts say NIH research raises concerns about chemical companies’ influence on US agency’s pesticide division

The US government’s top medical research agency has released three new studies linking glyphosate, the world’s most widely used pesticide and an active ingredient in Roundup, to cancer. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) findings contradict a controversial recent Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) conclusion that the weedkiller is not a carcinogen, and deals a blow to the White House, which has been closely allied with Roundup’s producer, Bayer.

The NIH’s three papers could have significant political and legal fallout. The EPA is in the process of a court-ordered re-evaluation of glyphosate’s cancer risks. The NIH findings generate new pressure for the EPA to find that the substance is linked to cancer, which would subject it to a modest increase in regulations.

item.title: Newly released documents suggest CIA did more post-9/11 waterboarding than previously acknowledged
item.description:
Declassified documents appear to support belief that waterboarding was more common and may have occurred beyond two acknowledged sites

Newly released documents suggest that the CIA waterboarded more detainees during the post-9/11 “war on terror” than previously acknowledged, utilizing a site north of Kabul, Afghanistan, for the practice of simulated drowning.

The agency has acknowledged waterboarding three men: Abu Zubaydah, believed to be a high-ranking member of al-Qaida; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, suspected architect of the 11 September 2001 attacks; and Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, accused of planning the 2000 bombing of a navy destroyer.

item.title: They crossed the doom loop of Groundhog Day with Nightmare on Elm Street. Voilà – it’s Peter Mandelson | Robert Hutton
item.description:
He’s perennially disgraced and yet he just won’t go away – now he’s joined the latest Brexit debate. Isn’t there a mute button, or an exile plan that really works?

What a week it has been for Indispensable Men. In the old days, if someone were forced to resign, whether as ambassador to Washington or boss of a trillion-dollar company, they would become what we quaintly used to call “disgraced”. Perhaps they would spend the rest of their days volunteering with a charity. Certainly, for a good decade afterwards, they would acquire the journalistic epithet “shamed” on first mention. Later – much later – they might be allowed back into public life, in some lesser role where they could be discreetly supervised, to check exactly how many emails they were sending to which people arranging what holidays.

But what’s this we find over on news website UnHerd? Why, it’s a 2,000-word essay from one Peter Mandelson on the difficulties of rejoining the European Union. Mandelson … Mandelson. That name definitely rings a bell. Let’s see if there’s a clue at the bottom of the piece. Ah, yes: “Peter Mandelson is a former cabinet minister and EU Trade Commissioner.” That’s the chap: Gordon Brown’s former business secretary. Though I feel as if I’ve seen his name in the news a bit more recently than 2010. Might he be a “former” anything else?

Continue reading...

item.title: Norse Atlantic Airways files for bankruptcy and cancels all future flights

Norwegian airline tells customers not to come to airports after surging fuel costs caused by Iran war ruin finances

Norse Atlantic Airways has filed for bankruptcy and cancelled all future flights after surging fuel costs caused by the Iran war ruined its finances.

The Norwegian airline said it was entering insolvency and posted a message on its website telling customers not to come to airports – including passengers stranded away from home. Its collapse came a day after it put flights on hold with a warning that its finances were critical.

Chris O’Shea, the chief executive of Centrica, reportedly told staff at the Rough gas storage facility off the east Yorkshire that the government had rebuffed the company’s plea for short-term support to run the store over the winter.

item.title: Canada’s top court upholds Quebec law barring public sector workers from wearing religious symbols
item.description:
Closely watched decision exposes tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights

Canada’s top court has largely upheld a controversial secularism law in the province of Quebec barring public sector workers from wearing conspicuous religious symbols, in a closely watched decision that exposes the tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights.

In a 6-1 ruling released on Friday morning, the supreme court found Quebec was permitted to shield the law, Bill 21, from most court challenges on the grounds that it violated charter rights.

item.title: Honey, we’ve shrunk the country! But at least the Brexiters got their wish | Gaby Hinsliff

Immigration has plummeted so we’ll probably have to work until we drop – yet many still obsess about people arriving in small boats

Will the last person to leave Britain, please turn out the lights?

It was way back in 1992 that the Sun ran that headline, predicting a national exodus if its readers dared vote for that dastardly Neil Kinnock. And to be fair, it was only out by 10 prime ministers and 34 years, for now we really are a nation heading for the exits.

item.title: Jared Kushner’s 70-minute interview reveals naive bias in handling of Putin’s aggression
item.description:
Trump’s son-in-law and senior negotiator paints Russian invasion of Ukraine as a misunderstanding to be resolved

In the space of a 70-minute interview, Jared Kushner – Donald Trump’s son-in-law and a prominent US negotiator in Russia, Gaza and Iran – probably did more to reveal why the world is mired in entrenched conflicts than a thousand geopolitical tomes or seminars.

During the conversation this week with Mathias Döpfner, the chief executive of the Axel Springer media publisher, Kushner gave a rare insight into his diplomatic technique, offering a string of homilies that veered close to banalities: “You have nothing until you have something”, “diplomacy is like untying knots on a fishing line for his son”, and “you play the ball from where it lands”.

item.title: Google told to halt Belgium datacentre construction over lack of planning permit
item.description:
Greenpeace publishes report showing tech firm is continuing to build despite planning appeal still unresolved

Belgian authorities have ordered Google to halt construction work on a large datacentre in the south of the country because the US tech firm’s requests to modify the original terms of the planning permission did not have approval.

“Inspectors visited the site and observed that the building was almost finished, with the structural work completed, even though the permit had been refused,” Raphaël Stokis, a Wallonia regional official, told the public broadcaster RTBF.

item.title: The Com: the global cybercrime network posing a ‘chilling threat’ to children
item.description:
FBI estimates thousands of people identify as members, or recent members, of group linked to indecent images of girls and blackmail

It sounds benign: the Com, short for the Community. But crime agencies around the world warn that it is far from that and the young cybercriminals involved are causing havoc and putting children at chilling, sickening risk.

Beau-Jack Mensforth was jailed by a UK judge on Friday for his activities as part of the Com. He was one individual operating from his bedroom in north-east England, but there are probably thousands more like him and parents are being urged by police to be aware and to check their children’s devices.

item.title: The Guardian view on the Children’s Booker prize: everyone is a winner | Editorial
item.description:
In a landscape dominated by the same names and celebrity authors, this new award shines a spotlight on great titles that might have been overlooked

“Why shouldn’t a great children’s book have the same status as a great adult book?” asked Frank Cottrell-Boyce, the former children’s laureate and chair of the inaugural Children’s Booker prize, as the shortlist was announced this week. In nearly 60 years of the adult prize, the only children’s book to have made the longlist is Philip Pullman’s The Amber Spyglass in 2001. Now children’s fiction has its own Booker, with four of the seven judges aged between eight and 12. Crucially, the kids get the casting vote.

The shortlist, “the great eight”, includes five novels, two graphic novels and an illustrated collection of short stories. Big names such as Eoin Colfer, Liz Hyder and Shaun Tan appear alongside less established writers. There is time travel, humour and sci-fi fantasy, in novels dealing with war, grief and identity.

item.title: The Guardian view on AI and the Riemann hypothesis: a triumph of intelligence, a test of democracy | Editorial
item.description:
Machines are solving problems that have been beyond the reach of human ingenuity. Their growing power must not become the sole preserve of billionaires

For the average person, the news that AI has helped crack a problem that has defied mathematicians since 1859 might elicit momentary awe. What ought to worry everyone is not the discovery per se, but what it says about the power of the machines making it. The pace of scientific discovery looks like it is outrunning the ability of humanity – and its institutions – to understand, let alone regulate, AI’s advances.

Last Friday Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said that he, with the assistance of an unreleased version of the company’s Claude chatbot, had produced what many mathematicians see as the holy grail: a proof for the Riemann hypothesis. Mathematicians like Cornell University’s Steven Strogatz had already cried on podcasts, lamenting that students were asking: “What’s the point if the AI can do math better than any human being?” Computers can validate the Alpöge-Claude proof. But Prof Strogatz fears AI’s discoveries may soon defy human understanding. Asking AI to explain them, he said, would be like him trying to teach calculus to his own dog.

item.title: Trump is destroying the rule of law in the US – to protect himself and the tech titans he worships as new gods | Jonathan Freedland
item.description:
To get Jensen Huang back at Nvidia, the president trampled on the justice system, national security and the trust America needs to do business in the global economy

Don’t let the sex distract you. Or the lies or the boardroom intrigue or even the AI-generated bra, all of which could have come from an especially wild episode of Succession. Don’t let that lure you into thinking that the Jensen Huang affair is, as Donald Trump would have it, little more than a sex scandal involving a corporate maestro. It is much more serious than that. The events of the past week tell instead a story of legal immunity and indeed impunity – revealing how Trump is putting himself, the tech bros and even artificial intelligence above the law.

It can be hard to see that through the thicket of questions that surround this episode, each one of which, don’t get me wrong, merits attention. Consider the personal profit Trump made thanks to his re-installation of Huang as the CEO of Nvidia, the world’s leading maker of advanced AI chips. Breaking the norm observed by previous presidents who, keen to avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest, either divested themselves of stock holdings or placed them in a blind trust, Trump cheerfully buys and sells stocks in companies whose fates he can influence. He saw the value of his shares in Nvidia plunge when Huang was forced out, following revelations that the CEO had had an affair with Alice Huang, reportedly an asset of Chinese intelligence. Last weekend Trump urged the board to reconsider; Huang was reinstated on Monday and Nvidia’s value promptly soared – putting $15m in Trump’s pocket. Not for the first time, he had used the power of his office to enrich himself.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

item.title: The US army just detonated a poison bomb over Iowa | Steven Donziger
item.description:
The shocking situation in Iowa is a metaphor for much of what is wrong with the United States

There’s no way to hide it: the US government just deliberately detonated a poison bomb of lead azide over the state of Iowa when a totally safe alternative was available.

The problem in Iowa was relatively simple to solve. The army for decades had stored lead underground at a munitions facility. As far back as 2009, the government knew the lead was deteriorating and might blow up on its own. But it procrastinated. Finally, in March, the army hired a Georgia-based company to use a chemical spray to neutralize the lead, creating a non-hazardous byproduct that can be disposed of in landfills.

Steven Donziger is a US-based human rights and environmental lawyer and the author of Donziger On Justice on Substack

item.title: The religious beliefs of a hospital operator should not determine the healthcare available to Australians | Nisha Khot
item.description:
Women suffer the consequences when Catholic healthcare providers acquire hospitals and create geographic deserts for abortion, contraception and IVF

In 2012 in Ireland, Dr Savita Halappanavar, who was then 17 weeks pregnant, attended a hospital with back pain. An examination found the pregnancy sac protruding through her womb. Her medical team refused to perform a procedure to end her pregnancy, because in Ireland the law prohibited abortion if a fetal heartbeat was still present. The 31-year-old developed sepsis and subsequently died of a cardiac arrest. During an inquest into her death, a midwife admitted to have said, “We don’t do that [abortion] here. Ireland is a Catholic country.” Halappanavar’s death became a catalyst for the campaign that ultimately led to the legalisation of abortion in Ireland.

This would never happen in Australia in 2026, I hear you say. Except, in Australia, Catholic hospitals provide healthcare based on the same Catholic beliefs as Irish hospitals did in 2012. And this scenario could very easily occur in Australia. In 2022, an ABC journalist interviewed an obstetrician working in an Australian Catholic hospital who described admitting a woman at 17 or 18 weeks whose waters had broken and a fetal heartbeat was still present. As the woman’s condition steadily deteriorated, the doctor was unable to recommend the care she required.

Continue reading...

item.title: Thousands of girls and women report bleeding and miscarriages after French police use of teargas
item.description:
Almost 10,000 women and girls who took part in nationwide protests in October give testimony about disrupted menstrual cycles

For three years, Naïma Di Piero says she barely had a period. The 46-year-old charity worker, who suffers from endometriosis, takes the contraceptive pill to suppress her menstrual cycle. But two days after being exposed to police teargas during France’s nationwide protests on 17 October, she began bleeding heavily.

French police fired about 22,000 teargas grenades at protesters on 17 October at the height of the protests – equivalent to two grenades every three seconds (over 10 hours of maintaining order).

item.title: Race hate exploded in this Spanish town last year. Now its residents are bracing for more
item.description:
Torre-Pacheco’s diverse communities are fearful that the far-right Vox party will enter government after Sunday’s election

Sitting on a park bench, taking in the sunny day, Naima reflected on all that had seemingly changed since she moved to Spain three decades earlier.

Back then, the Moroccan national had felt warmly welcomed by Spaniards. “I had never, at any point in my life, felt like there was racism,” she said. “But now things are changing. And the blame lies with rightwing politics.”

item.title: Why all of Europe should be watching as Spain’s far-right Vox closes in on power | Eoghan Gilmartin
item.description:
Santiago Abascal’s party has adopted radical ideas from France and beyond. If it joins a PP coalition, it would be a morale boost for allies across the continent

It was a scene few would have imagined possible in Spanish politics until recently. Flanked on stage by Catalan flags, the far-right Vox leader, Santiago Abascal, addressed a packed campaign rally in Girona, where he promised “to defend Catalan identity” against supposed “Islamisation”. He urged his audience to confront what he claimed was “the primary challenge” of a new “caliphate” across Spain. For a fringe party that made its breakthrough in 2018 by demonising Catalonia’s independence movement, it was a striking change of emphasis, reflecting a strategic shift that has brought Vox to the brink of power. When the results of this Sunday’s snap general election become clear, there is a strong likelihood that centre-left PM Pedro Sánchez will be forced out, with Vox as kingmakers and junior coalition partners to the traditionally dominant rightwing People’s party (PP).

The perpetually dour Abascal may lack the charisma of Trump or Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, but Vox is projected to increase its vote share from 12.4% in 2023 to close to 20%. It has achieved this surge not by moderating its rhetoric as it draws closer to power, but by embracing some of the most radical positions on immigration from across the European far right. A place in government for the party could, in turn, embolden its allies across Europe, as France, Italy and Poland prepare to go to the polls next year.

Continue reading...

item.title: Mad about mara: the DIY dance movement helping young Nigerians escape the daily grind
item.description:
What started as one artist’s response to being cut out of a music video has exploded, becoming a driving force in Nigeria’s cultural landscape

As a student in the central Nigerian city of Ilorin, Lawal Habeeb Kola loved staying in his hostel room to produce beats rather than returning to his family house in Lagos, the more frenetic city of his birth.

In 2022, one of his beats became popular on TikTok, and a version featuring ad-libbed vocals from a hypeman sent it viral. He was invited to the music video shoot in Lagos and thought his big break had finally come, but when the video was released, he was absent.

item.title: The most surprising thing about Burnham’s slow politics is this: it could be working | Andy Beckett
item.description:
‘Andy time’ may frustrate the media and voters impatient for change – but after years of short premierships and rushed policies, isn’t this the reset Westminster needs?

Andy Burnham is making a lot of people impatient. Political journalists, pro-EU activists, climate campaigners, fossil-fuel lobbyists, recipients of welfare benefits, advocates of welfare cuts, enemies of neoliberalism, enthusiasts for renationalisation, members of the armed forces and even cabinet colleagues: all are waiting for the prime minister to make big decisions, and thus reveal the true nature of his administration, four months after its beginning.

Since his Manchester mayoralty, some of Burnham’s co-workers have had a phrase for his tendency to take things at his own tempo: “Andy time”. He lets interesting conversations overrun, likes to ponder issues without being rushed, and pushes back crucial announcements. The unveiling of his 10-year plan – a typically ambitious but loose Burnham timespan, and one of his government’s pivotal moments – has been repeatedly delayed. According to the website Politico, it has been pencilled in for 17 December, the final day of the parliamentary calendar.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

Human rights groups report increasing attacks on Palestinian healthcare workers

Less than an hour earlier, armed Israeli settlers had attacked the village of Qusra, killing three Palestinians and wounding several more. They were now shooting at the paramedics who had come to help.

item.title: Natural England objected to a datacentre. Weeks later ministers threatened to abolish the agency
item.description:
Body urged Bristol city council to reject plan because of risk to nearby protected wildlife and habitats

Natural England objected to the building of a large AI datacentre near Bristol weeks before the government threatened to abolish the independent environmental adviser.

The nature adviser made a significant intervention to urge Bristol city council not to grant planning permission for a 40MW datacentre at Avonmouth, because of the threat to protected wildlife and habitats at one of the UK’s most important sites for migratory birds, which is within 600 metres of the site.

item.title: Never mind EU student fees – it’s time to rethink the entire UK higher education system | Simon Jenkins
item.description:
The last shake-up, in the 1960s, was based on pure anti-technological snobbery. Let’s put vocational learning back in the heart of our cities

What is it about the EU student fees debate that means it has almost derailed Andy Burnham’s Brexit reset? Can the issue be that important? The answer is simple – and, I am sure, personal. Before Brexit, the EU’s citizens, among them its diplomats, were paying the same as UK citizens to have their children’s English perfected at a UK university. Now, some pay up to three times that figure. To put it mildly, they have an interest in persuading the UK government to slash fees. As of now, the issue is still deadlocked.

The total cost of meeting the EU’s demand and reducing EU student fees to the new British rate of £9,790 a year has been put at an astronomical £570m a year for Russell group universities alone. Burnham has declined to answer the question of who would foot the bill. Indeed, it is difficult to understand why British taxpayers should subsidise the education of wealthy Europeans. But the cost would then fall on individual universities. The University of St Andrews estimates it would lose a devastating £12m annually.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

item.title: Heavy rain, wind and flooding hit much of US on Thanksgiving
item.description:
Homes without power, travel disrupted and Macy’s Thanksgiving parade postponed for first time in New York

Storms have flooded communities on the US east coast, knocking out power to nearly a million customers and prompting the first-ever postponement of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade in New York City.

High winds and flooding hammered both coasts, disrupting holiday travel. More than 900,000 homes and businesses were without electricity on Thursday evening, with the majority in east coast states, according to the outage tracking website PowerOutage.us. More than 2,200 flights to or from US destinations were delayed and more than 400 were cancelled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware.

item.title: At critical juncture, Friedrich Merz finds Germans’ support for Ukraine wavering
item.description:
German chancellor is on difficult terrain, at home and abroad, as he fights to maintain European backing for Kyiv

The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, is navigating choppy waters both at home and abroad over his insistence that Europe must keep up support – both military and financial – for Ukraine.

At a Brussels summit on Thursday, Merz reiterated his view that all EU member states – pointedly, “not 23 or 24” – should support a €45bn (£38bn) loan for Ukraine for 2027. He has threatened to veto the bloc’s budget unless all countries sign up to the loan, a stance that saw him accused of “classic blackmail” by Robert Fico, the populist prime minister of Slovakia. Czechia, Hungary and Bulgaria have also voiced their misgivings, to varying degrees, over Berlin’s dogged position.

Continue reading...

item.title: Pizza history: AI agent’s cardless purchase is a first for UK
item.description:
Papa John’s order was made without sharing bank security details – tech that could revolutionise shopping

  • Retailers enter the unknown with AI shopping assistants on Black Friday

An order of Papa John’s margherita pizzas has become the first purchase in the UK to be made using an AI agent using cardless payment technology.

The order of nine mini pizzas was made as part of the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) regulated sandbox trials to test the technology, using Lloyds Bank and payment specialist TrueLayer.

item.title: ‘It’s not helping’: calls for guardrails and regulations as AI use rises at US retailers
item.description:
Labor leaders and advocates urge protections for workers and consumers as AI use becomes more commonplace

As millions of Americans begin holiday shopping this Black Friday, consumers and workers alike are already seeing how artificial intelligence is reshaping the retail landscape.

Anna, a cashier in a southern Oregon Walmart and leader with United for Respect, who requested to remain anonymous for fear of retaliation, criticized the implementation of AI at Walmart and its effects on workers.

item.title: Banks may pass on £1.5bn tax rise to customers, warns Bank of England chief
item.description:
Big lenders will aim to ‘protect their earnings’ from temporary increase in corporation tax surcharge, says Andrew Bailey

  • Business live – latest updates

The governor of the Bank of England has said he fears banks could attempt to pass on the £1.5bn cost of Labour’s tax increase on their profits.

The chancellor, John Healey, used his first budget last month to temporarily increase the bank corporation tax surcharge from 3% to 6% for a 15-month period from January, with the proceeds funding “breathing space” to relieve pressure on household finances.

item.title: For whom the bells troll: French town divided over church’s night-time chimes
item.description:
Long-time residents of La Garnache defeat newer neighbours in latest rural culture clash over ‘sensory heritage’

A ding-dong has divided the town of La Garnache in western France over attempts to silence the bells of the local church, which strike all night.

Since 1942, the clock tower of Notre Dame de l’Assomption has chimed an 8th-century hymn every 15 minutes … day and night. Between 10pm and 7am, the bells ring 37 times, adding up to more than 700 individual chimes.

item.title: Israeli justice system at tipping point as judges call for end to Netanyahu trial
item.description:
Dropping of corruption charges against PM after highly unusual intervention could set damaging precedent

The Israeli judges presiding over Benjamin Netanyahu’s corruption trial have called on prosecutors to end proceedings, a highly unusual intervention that leaves the attorney general facing a momentous political decision.

The prime minister has been charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three complex and overlapping criminal cases that hinge on his relationship with telecoms magnates and other wealthy businessmen. Ending the trial without a ruling could set damaging precedents for media independence and how politicians are held to account.

item.title: King tides batter US coasts as storms threaten Thanksgiving celebrations
item.description:
Heavy rain, strong winds and coastal flooding creating hazardous conditions for millions travelling for holiday

King tides and huge waves have been battering both coasts of the US during a turbulent Thanksgiving period, with severe weather threatening millions across the country. Along the California coast, king tides caused considerable damage. In Pacifica, south of San Francisco, large waves battered the coastline on Wednesday, destroying part of a pier and sending debris into the ocean.

The National Weather Service issued coastal flood warnings covering parts of the Pacific coastline and shorelines around San Francisco Bay and San Pablo Bay. Several beachfront properties in Pacifica have already experienced flooding, while authorities in Marin County temporarily issued an evacuation warning for residents of beachfront homes at Stinson Beach.

Continue reading...

item.description:
Ukraine’s president labels US counterpart’s comments ‘strange’ and urges Washington to increase pressure on Moscow

in Madrid

Last night’s debate between the leaders of Spain’s four biggest political parties was a rambling, ratty and revealing spectacle in which Ada Colau, the leader of the leftwing Broad Front, is generally agreed to have come out on top.

item.description:
The days of coming to blows over a Furby before dawn are over. It was scary, but at least it was real

Congratulations. You’re alive. And for that, I applaud you.

You didn’t choke on a particularly large piece of pie or fall into a ditch on your post-Thanksgiving-meal walk. Thanksgiving is one of the more hazardous holidays on the American calendar, with all the binge eating, binge drinking and binge shopping.

item.title: Europe joins global stock market rally as AI trade rebounds - business live
item.description:
Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news

France’s economic output shrank by -0.2% in the third quarter, compared with a previous estimate of -0.1%.

The French statistics agency found that its economy was hit by a drop in investment in the construction sector and a fall in exports.

Following this revision, the annual growth carry-over for 2026 stands at only 0.1%. It is very difficult to see domestic demand rebounding strongly enough in the fourth quarter to improve this result.

Business and consumer confidence both deteriorated in October and November. A weakening labour market and growing fears of unemployment will keep households cautious. At the same time, weak demand and a lack of visibility will continue to weigh on business investment.

This would leave average GDP growth at just 0.1% in 2026, well below the 1.0% we expect for the eurozone.

The outlook for 2027 remains very gloomy. Salaried employment fell by 94,400 jobs over the past year, a decline of 0.3%. The situation is even worse in the private sector, where 109,000 jobs were lost over the same period, a fall of 0.5%.

We completed this payment transaction with Papa John’s with no account numbers, no password [and] handled with the highest possible security profile.

We talked with the AI agent, described the occasion and dietary requirements. Of course the agent suggested different flavours and quantities. We confirmed the order and the pizza arrived later.”

Continue reading...

item.title: Trump alleges ‘fake’ economic figures released before US midterms but doesn’t provide evidence
item.description:
In a Thanksgiving post, the US president seeks investigation after blue wave of Democrats unseat Republicans

Donald Trump has alleged without evidence that economic figures published by the US federal government before this month’s midterm elections were “fake” and demanded an investigation after voters roundly rejected his Republican party.

In a holiday message on social media tinged with bitterness, the US president wished a happy thanksgiving “to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%”.

item.title: Southern and central Australia face summer of heightened bushfire risk and heatwaves
item.description:
Fire chiefs say large swathes of the country are at risk from fires driven by high fuel loads, dry soil and hot weather

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Large parts of southern and central Australia face elevated fire risk this summer, authorities say, while heatwaves and extreme temperatures are likely nationwide.

Most of Victoria, eastern Tasmania and large parts of South Australia, Western Australia, New South Wales and the Northern Territory face heightened bushfire risk – driven by high fuel loads, low soil moisture and forecast hot and dry conditions – according to the seasonal outlook from the Australian and New Zealand Council for Fire and Emergency Services (AFAC), released on Friday.

Continue reading...

item.title: Strobe Talbott, Time magazine reporter and deputy US secretary of state, dies aged 80
item.description:
After 21 years at Time, Talbott joined the Clinton administration and later headed the Brookings Institution

Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.

His son, Devin Talbott, confirmed he died peacefully after a long illness in his East Hampton, New York, home.

Continue reading...

item.title: Nearly half of ethnic minority people in UK have faced racism at work in last year, survey finds
item.description:
Figures show impact on mental health, with majority having no confidence HR will take their concerns seriously

Nearly half of people from minority ethnic backgrounds have experienced racism at work and the majority have no confidence that HR would take their concerns seriously, a survey has found.

It also found that 75% of people from the UK’s five largest minority ethnic communities had experienced racism or unfair treatment linked to their race, ethnicity or religion in the previous year, and three-quarters of those who had experienced racism said it had affected their mental health to some degree.

Continue reading...

item.title: Water firms to identify 250,000 vulnerable households in England eligible for discounts
item.description:
Department for Work and Pensions to provide data about households missing out on WaterSure support scheme

Water companies will use government data to identify as many as 250,000 vulnerable households in England eligible for discounts, after criticism that not enough people are aware of the £428 support for their annual bills.

The Department for Work and Pensions will provide information to identify and contact a quarter of a million households who are missing out on support to which they are entitled under the WaterSure scheme.

item.title: Threat from China looms large over Taiwan’s local elections
item.description:
Taiwanese officials raise alarm over interference by China in elections that will shape fortunes of ruling party

Taiwanese voters go to the polls on Saturday in closely watched local elections that will shape the fortunes of the ruling Democratic Progressive party (DPP) as it navigates an increasingly precarious set of relationships on the global stage.

Saturday’s vote will choose mayors, council members and other local leaders across 22 districts. Unlike the presidential elections, in which foreign policy is often a key issue, the local elections, held every four years, are largely focused on bread-and-butter issues such as housing affordability and wealth distribution.

item.title: New Zealand election: final results show ruling coalition needs minor party to govern
item.description:
Incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon loses majority and needs support of Opportunity party to remain in power, or country faces another election

The final results of New Zealand’s general election show the incumbent rightwing coalition will need the support of a centrist newcomer party to form a government, and to avoid sending the country back to the polls.

Preliminary results on 7 November handed the National party and its two coalition partners, the populist New Zealand First and libertarian Act parties, a slim two-seat majority, making the election too close to call until final votes were tallied.

Continue reading...

item.title: Detention of pro-democracy activists in Vietnam amounts to a ‘transboundary abduction’, UN experts say
item.description:
Three men, including an Australian and a Norwegian national, disappeared from Cambodia on 18 September and are now detained on terrorism charges

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The United Nations has intervened in the case of three pro-democracy activists, including an Australian and Norwegian national, who were detained in Vietnam in September, alleging it is a “transboundary abduction” that violates international law.

Eleven UN experts published a statement on Thursday about the alleged abduction and detainment of the three activists: Vietnamese-Australian Tran Hiep, Vietnamese-Norwegian Nguyen Duc Thuan and Vietnamese national Thai Cong Truong Son.

item.title: Employers: do you have concerns about the rollout of Muse and other AI agents?
item.description:
Are you worried about staff connecting their digital assistants to work emails and databases? What steps are you taking to address this?

Meta has rolled out its Muse AI assistant, which can be tasked with shopping, booking tickets and carrying out negotiations on a user’s behalf, across countries including the UK, US, Canada, Australia and Japan.

The AI agent needs the customer’s permission to go out and make purchases, connect to apps, use bank details or send emails autonomously. However, the possibility of employees connecting their Muse assistant to their work emails and databases is a concern for companies and their clients.

item.title: Suit alleges Louisiana land deal between SpaceX and ExxonMobil violates open meetings law
item.description:
Suit says parish board was manipulated to allow deal to go through and settlement agreement hidden from public

After ending a lawsuit over ExxonMobil’s damage to wetlands, Louisiana officials moved quickly to approve a deal giving SpaceX access to 125,000 acres (50,600 hectares) of marsh formerly owned by the oil company. A new lawsuit now alleges they did so in violation of the state’s open meetings law.

The lawsuit, filed by three south-central Louisiana residents, follows state and Vermilion parish officials’ approval of what is estimated to be a record $27.5bn tax incentive package for SpaceX’s Starbase Louisiana project, announced over the summer. The officials violated the state’s open meetings law eight times while facilitating the agreement in attempts to “keep the public in the dark about what they are doing for SpaceX”, the lawsuit alleges.

Continue reading...

item.title: Faulty electrical goods returned to UK supermarkets ending up on Ghana ‘megadump’
item.description:
Mountains of household items are burned and stripped down at the tip by workers without protection such as masks, investigation alleges

Electrical goods that were returned as faulty to leading British stores including Tesco, Argos and Asda have been found dumped on a waste tip in Ghana, an investigation has found.

The faulty electrical appliances, including toasters and slow cookers, had been returned to major UK supermarkets. They were found at Agbogbloshie, one of the world’s largest e-waste sites, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, a joint investigation by Unearthed and Greenpeace Africa has found. The findings raise serious questions about e-waste export rules.

Continue reading...

item.title: ‘I’m no longer a UAE official’: UN hopeful Lana Nusseibeh tries to shake off Sudan record
item.description:
The US and Russia’s candidate for secretary general is on a charm offensive. Can she overcome London’s resistance to her bid?

Lana Nusseibeh is in Britain this week, attempting to present herself as a potential future UN secretary general, and shift the focus from her past as a United Arab Emirates diplomat who denied the country’s role in arming a militia accused of war crimes and genocide in Sudan’s four-year civil war.

It is a high-risk strategy that involves meeting ministers, MPs, academics and holding a public event with the UN Association.

item.title: Rescuers blocked from a fire. A child killed on the way to school. Miles-long trains are upending US lives
item.description:
Communities say big railroad companies won’t act and that lawmakers are moving too slowly to address a major problem

The drive from the Lockland fire station to a house fire on Patterson Avenue should have taken no more than 45 seconds.

But East Wyoming Avenue and Davis Street were both blocked: a Norfolk Southern train was stopped across several streets – the fire engine had to turn around and take a detour via a nearby highway. By the time firefighters snaked through the highway traffic and reached the fire last month, seven minutes after the call came in, 89-year-old Marian Haefner was dead in her own home.

item.title: Ministers have ‘failed to make the case’ for Heathrow third runway, MPs say
item.description:
Transport committee says policy papers show expanding airport would fall short of pledges on economy and climate

Ministers have “failed to make the case” for a third runway at Heathrow, according to a damning report by MPs.

The Commons transport committee said on Thursday that the detailed policy papers laid out by the government showed expansion of the London airport would fall short of pledges on the economy and climate.

Russians once packed their swimming trunks and sunscreen for summer holidays in occupied Crimea, or hiking boots for trips in the colder months to the picturesque Black Sea peninsula annexed by Vladimir Putin in 2014.

Now, travellers swap advice on first-aid kits and how to avoid drones as they drive through a war zone to the peninsula.

item.description:
Saved from the slaughterhouse, the two behemoths are turning heads on opposite sides of the country, having grown to 192cm

Two massive steers, named Frank and Tiny Tim, have sparked headlines in recent days for being, well, big boys.

item.title: I’m an AI leader at a tech giant. Our industry has stopped taking safety seriously | Anonymous
item.description:
We’re developing the most powerful tech in history – but trust, safeguarding and privacy are being sidelined in favour of huge profit

I’m a senior AI leader at one of the world’s biggest tech companies, and the products we put out into the world are increasingly being recklessly rushed, without proper consideration. The tech industry used to take safety and privacy seriously, but lately I have become worried by how rash we have become. In a sector that is obsessed with being first, ethical hesitation is now viewed as a luxury we can’t afford.

If you want to properly understand the actions of big tech, you have to look at the industry’s culture. It moves fast and there is a mindset of constant one-upmanship. Being first matters financially. But just as importantly, competition is believed to bring out the best in people.

The writer is an AI expert working in the tech industry. A version of this piece originally appeared with the Bureau of Investigative Journalism as part of its Secret Source series, a regular column featuring industry whistleblowers

Continue reading...

item.title: Spanish opposition criticised for AI video of Pedro Sánchez in Morocco shirt
item.description:
People’s party alters video of PM putting on Lamine Yamal’s Spain shirt in latest contentious use of AI in election race

Spanning 17 seconds, the campaign video showed the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, speaking to the camera as he put on the jersey of the national football team. “Because this is what Spain is: a pluralistic and diverse country,” he said as he turned to reveal the number 19 on his back – the shirt number of the star player Lamine Yamal.

One day later, the opposition People’s party (PP) came under fire after it used AI to manipulate the same video, making it falsely appear as if Sánchez had put on the shirt of the Moroccan national team.

item.title: I helped organise the letter from Labour MPs urging Andy Burnham to reject Rosebank. This is why | Catherine Fookes
item.description:
Approval would be celebrated by the oil giants, but it wouldn’t help our constituents who worry about the climate crisis, and their bills

  • Catherine Fookes is Labour MP for Monmouthshire

  • Labour split over Rosebank oilfield exposed by letter from nearly 100 MPs


This week it was confirmed that millions of households are facing yet another winter of unaffordable energy bills, just as we learn that this summer’s heatwaves were linked to more than 5,000 deaths in the UK.

The cost of living and climate crises are two sides of the same coin: our continued dependence on fossil fuels is driving up bills, fuelling deadly extreme weather and causing widespread harm to people in this country. It was one year ago that Storm Claudia’s floods swept through Monmouthshire, devastating hundreds of homes, businesses and livelihoods. I know, as flood season is upon us again, how sick residents feel every time it rains.

Catherine Fookes is Labour MP for Monmouthshire

item.description:
The New York governor declares a state of emergency in several parts of the state due to severe weather

Heavy rain, winds, flooding and high tides are hitting the eastern and western US, snarling travel and leading to the cancellations of at least two commercial Thanksgiving parades.

On the East Coast, authorities in Philadelphia ordered the city’s Thanksgiving Day parade in Philadelphia off the streets and will be featured as an “alternative TV event”.

item.title: Politician hosts 400,000 guests at daughter’s wedding in India’s poorest state
item.description:
Six helipads built and feast prepared by 500 cooks for wedding hosted by Anant Singh, an MP charged with murder

It takes a brave soul to try to match the mythic opulence of the wedding arranged by the Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani for his son Anant in 2024. Estimates of the cost for the months-long celebration ran to at least $600m, with world leaders and celebrities among those on the guest list.

Smaller fry though he is, Anant Singh, a legislator in India’s poorest state, Bihar, gave it his best shot on Wednesday, albeit in a rustic rural setting, for the nuptials of his daughter Shivangi Singh, and Rishikesh Kumar, an MBA student from Georgia State University in Atlanta.

Superior court judge Kelly Lee Ellerbe paused the order after county election officials filed a notice of appeal.

item.title: US army calls detonation of bomb chemicals in Iowa a success after fears of toxic plume
item.description:
The army blows up US stockpile of lead azide, a chemical used for explosives, to avoid uncontrollable explosion

The US army blew up the nation’s entire stockpile of lead azide, a chemical used to make explosives, saying the first checks show Wednesday’s controlled detonation in Iowa didn’t spread toxic dust to nearby homes and farms.

Earthen barriers were put up and foam and water were poured onto a pair of bunkers holding the 5 tons (4,500kg) of lead azide, and officials said those measures appear to have absorbed much of the blast.

Shares in UK tobacco company jump by more than 14% on news US rival is looking into making offer

Imperial Brands could become the next UK company to fall to a foreign takeover after its US rival Altria announced a possible bid for the tobacco firm.

Altria, whose Philip Morris division makes Marlboro and Benson & Hedges cigarettes, told the City on Thursday that it was considering an offer. If made it was likely to be solely in cash, it said.

item.title: Poundland staff fear they’ll be left out in the cold for Christmas. When will workers have a say in their future? | Polly Toynbee
item.description:
High streets and ultimately the taxpayer will suffer from the chain’s liquidation. Who will benefit? The company that snapped up this institution for just £1

When the bad news came through on his mobile on Wednesday afternoon, the manager of Poundland’s store in Camden, north London, Aboud, summoned all his staff. “One lad, been here 11 years, was in tears and ran out of the store, he was so upset. This is home and family for many of them.”

They are among 11,000 staff whose jobs are now at risk, but some shops might get bought by other chains. “Do you know,” Aboud asks me, “can we find out if this store might be saved?” I can’t, and the liquidators are only just starting work. He can no longer get through to his senior regional manager: “He doesn’t pick up now.”

item.title: Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos wins race to be next ECB president
item.description:
Former Bank of Spain governor chosen to succeed Christine Lagarde after winning support of EU’s biggest countries

Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos has been chosen as the next president of the European Central Bank, to succeed Christine Lagarde, after winning support from the EU’s biggest countries.

The economist and monetary policymaker will become the first Spaniard to lead the ECB, defeating his rival candidate Klaas Knot, the former head of the Dutch central bank.

item.title: EU leaders wrestle over Ukraine aid as potential Le Pen victory sparks fear
item.description:
Slovakia, Hungary and Czechia want to opt out of €45bn Ukraine loan, as Germany tries to protect funding from possible far-right French presidency

  • Europe live – latest updates

EU leaders were bracing for a clash over long-term financial aid for Ukraine amid an effort to finalise high-stakes budget talks by the end of the year.

Arriving in Brussels on Thursday, the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, reiterated his view that all EU member states should support a €45bn (£38bn) loan for Ukraine for 2027. “When the European Union provides funding, it does so as the European Union – and that union consists of 27 member states, not 23 or 24,” he said.

item.title: Israeli strikes kill 16 schoolchildren so far this month, Gaza ministry says
item.description:
Statement follows death of sisters, aged 15 and 13, in airstrike on residential apartment in Gaza City

Israeli strikes have killed at least 16 schoolchildren in Gaza since the start of November, as young people across the territory face intensifying bombardment and struggle to find food, clean water and shelter.

On Wednesday, Gaza’s ministry of education said: “Palestinian students had been targeted for the third time in less than 24 hours, in an escalation reflecting the continued Israeli violations against children in the Gaza Strip.”

item.title: Ofsted’s pedagogically pinheaded approach to inspections | Letters
item.description:
Ian McCormack and Sid Cumberland respond to a letter from the FDA union

Remarkably, Helen Kenny’s defence of Ofsted (Letters, 18 November) dodges the central criticism of Simon Jenkins’ article. She offers no response to his criticism that inspections are menacing and based on a damagingly reductionistic idea of education. Neither does she address the stress that results from fear of Ofsted, not only for teachers but children, too.

The FDA public service union’s own research finds that only 18% of inspectors believe “educators perceive them ‘positively’”. Why might that be?

item.title: Palantir has created bespoke tech solutions for the NHS | Letter
item.description:
Stephen Childs responds to a letter that said the US software firm was not the right fit for Britain’s health service

Prof Caroline Mitchell is right that US systems designed for an insurance market are rife in the NHS (Letters, 18 November). But Palantir’s software isn’t among them – and should not be confused with a range of other systems, some designed as far back as the 1970s for billing and then exported to the NHS over the following decades.

Our story is different. Each application built on the federated data platform – which connects information across the NHS – is bespoke to the NHS and to the healthcare trust that uses it. The NHS is a highly complex, loose association of healthcare trusts and commissioners, with data that is rich, but often unstructured and frustratingly disconnected.

Continue reading...

item.title: Don’t price EU students out of UK universities | Letter
item.description:
Widening pathways for disadvantaged youngsters from Europe should be top of the agenda in discussions about fees, says Angela McRobbie

It is dispiriting to hear arguments against young people from the EU being able to attend British universities with fees reset to home student level (EU nationals will pay higher tuition fees than UK students, Burnham indicates, 25 November).

Fees for international students are horrendously high at approximately £25,000 a year, and that does not include living costs. This means that only very wealthy families can afford to have their children study for a degree in the UK.

Russia is reportedly preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite into space later this year, in a scenario that could pose a significant threat to global communications.

Regional mayor says cancelling works on A38 at Derby and Newark bypass on A46 ‘disappointing and short-sighted’

Upgrades to roundabouts on the A38 around Derby and to the Newark bypass on the A46 will be shelved.

item.title: The Guardian view on fostering: ceremonies and sibling rights should help care leavers | Editorial
item.description:
Ministers have recognised that young adults need more support. But children’s social care reform must go deeper

The first lifelong guardianship ceremonies, held in Northampton last week with Josh MacAlister, the children’s minister, among the guests, are the latest in a series of measures aimed at boosting support for care leavers. While the decision to register a link between a person who has been looked after as a child and another adult such as a former carer or friend does not carry legal obligations, those involved spoke movingly about what it meant for these relationships to be formally recognised. New rules requiring councils to support contact between siblings in the care system are similarly aimed at strengthening networks that could sustain them beyond childhood into adult life.

Belatedly, the government is acting on a mound of evidence that children who are taken into local authority care are frequently acutely vulnerable when they come out of it as 18-year-olds. Care leavers are over-represented in prisons and homeless shelters, and among those who are not in education, employment or training. In August, the Department for Education published an analysis of 112 deaths of care leavers aged between 18 and 24 in 2025, which made for devastating reading.

item.title: The Guardian view on Russia’s war dead: the toll won’t stop Putin. Resolve in backing Ukraine remains essential | Editorial
item.description:
New data offers shocking details of military fatalities. But without domestic accountability, only external pressure can end this conflict

The toll of Russia’s war on Ukraine is appallingly evident in the devastation of apartment blocks and hospitals, in the suffering of survivors and, above all, in the mourning of the dead, which included an estimated 150,000 soldiers and at least 18,000 civilians.

The toll on Russia’s population has been carefully obscured by Moscow. But a fuller picture has emerged from its own statistics after the hacking group Cyber Partisans, linked to the Belarusian opposition, and the Ukrainian hacker collective Silent Crow obtained 11m death certificates. Analysis by the Guardian offers disturbing insights into the deaths of almost half a million Russians in Ukraine since Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.

Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here.

item.title: Water levels fell sharply in world’s rivers and lakes in two hottest years on record, study finds
item.description:
Researchers say effects particularly felt in South America where levels plunged even as some areas had extreme rain

Extreme global heat caused an unprecedented decline in the water levels of lakes, rivers and reservoirs around the world in 2023 and 2024, an international study has found.

The analysis of global water systems, a collaboration led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, found that the planet’s surface freshwater fell sharply during the two years, which were the hottest on record. Global river flows fell to about 5.7% below normal, while the water stored in lakes and reservoirs dropped by 9.5%. Together, this was the largest synchronised decline in surface water since at least 1991.

item.title: The bleph lady: Britain’s backstreet cosmetic surgeon
item.description:
Luyen Vu’s discount eye surgeries represent the dangers of an unregulated beauty industry. But for her fans, she is a folk hero

Robert Laycock, a facial plastic surgeon at Aintree University Hospital in Liverpool, first knew that something was up when a patient came to him in early 2024. She was a woman in her 40s who had undergone a blepharoplasty, a procedure that involves making an incision just below or above the eyelids and removing small amounts of skin and sometimes fat and muscle. The point of the surgery is to make the patient’s face look more youthful. This woman’s stitches, however, had started coming apart, leaving an open wound right above her eyes.

It is not unusual for botched private cosmetic surgeries to be fixed on the NHS. Laycock estimates that he sees three or four patients a year who need surgical intervention after too much tissue has been removed in a blepharoplasty. But something was different about this woman. “The surgery was done in a very odd way,” Laycock told me. The incision, he explained, had been made just beneath the eyebrow rather than on the crease of the eyelid. “[It’s] not the way that we would generally do a blepharoplasty in the UK.” He asked the woman where she’d had the work done but she was evasive and he dropped the subject.

item.title: I am staunchly pro-choice – but abortion statistics in the latest sexual attitudes survey shocked even me | Zoe Williams
item.description:
Deprivation is behind the sharp rise highlighted in the Natsal study, and that’s an outrage. High energy bills should never be a factor in reproductive choice

The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal) is the crowdpleaser of the data world. Nerds love it because of its extraordinary thoroughness. It’s one of the largest studies of sexual behaviour in the world, surveying nearly 7,000 people in the UK between the ages of 16 and 59, once a decade. Everyone else loves it because they get to talk about sex. Some of the statistics speak for themselves – among 25- to 34-year-old women, the number who say they never want children has gone up fourfold, a sad, completely understandable reflection of the outside world.

Other figures, though, are mysterious: the number of women aged 16 to 24 who are on the pill has dropped precipitously, from nearly half to less than a third. Over the same period, the online space has been flooded with information about hormonal contraception, some of it better than it has ever been – more accessible, more accurate – and some of it plain wrong. Is there strategic, funded disinformation coming from Christian fundamentalists, such as we have already seen in the abortion space, where anti-abortion activists hose money at putatively “grassroots” online influencers? Or is it a quirk of the algorithms that once you go down the rabbit hole of “has the pill made me depressed?”, you will be shown endless influencers who have experienced that very (improbable) thing? It’s hard for a young person to navigate what’s real, and it’s hard to distinguish superstition from preference.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

item.title: We may all be eating too much protein. But that won’t stop the influencers and big business | Devi Sridhar
item.description:
Protein is the food industry’s current nutritional good guy. The fact that it’s often added to ultra-processed food makes it anything but

When I was growing up in the US in the 1980s and 90s, fat in foods was demonised. Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine were all the rage, with the message that fat was bad for our hearts and arteries. By the early 2000s, concern had moved to added sugar and its apparent links to obesity and type 2 diabetes, driving food reformulations.

Sugar was replaced with artificial sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame K, which have their own health impacts. Aspartame is classified by the World Health Organization as possibly carcinogenic in humans, while observational research such as a 2022 study of about 102,000 adults has linked acesulfame K with increased cancer risk. Then carbohydrates came into the spotlight, with pasta, rice and bread becoming the bad guys for our diet and blamed for weight gain. There is a fashion cycle in nutrition, where each food group or ingredient takes its turn being blamed for our poor health.

Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

item.title: The dhow builders crafting giant historic ships in India – in pictures
item.description:

In the 16th century, the port city of Mandvi on India’s west coast was founded by the rulers of the kingdom of Kutch, and quickly established itself as one of the most dynamic ports in the western Indian Ocean. Its strategic geographical position, along the estuary of the Rukmavati River, which flows into the Arabian Sea in the Gulf of Kutch, and mastery of monsoon wind navigation enabled it to become part of vast maritime networks connecting India to the Gulf, the Arabian peninsula and east Africa.

Mandvi prospered through trade, exporting cotton textiles, indigo, cereals and handicrafts, while importing dates, pearls, Arabian horses and luxury goods.

A stemson, a piece of supporting timber in the bow of a boat, is carved from teak in a Mandvi shipyard under supervision by the master shipwright, or mistri, who designs boats without written plans. All photographs: Frédéric Noy

item.title: AI's shock-and-awe raid on maths looks like pride before a fall | Rafael Behr
item.description:
Machines are bulldozing through hard problems to assert the power of their tech bro creators, not to advance human knowledge

In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven.

That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week. Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof.
