item.description:
Plymouth, where Pilgrims settled, accused of breaking 28-year old agreement over National Day of Mourning protest

Nearly 30 years after a violent clash between Native Americans and police, the Massachusetts town of Plymouth is in court accused of “silencing” their National Day of Mourning – again.

A Native American group won a “mixed” victory over the historic Massachusetts town of Plymouth after they sued them for breaking a 30-year-old ‘treaty’ involving their National Day of Mourning.

Continue reading...

item.title: Spain has been hit hard by the climate crisis. Why are politicians saying so little about it before the election?
item.description:
Wildfires and floods can do little to move climate change up voters’ list of priorities, experts say

Beneath the blackened branches of a pine tree that rises high above a landscape of scorched hillsides and the odd charred and ruined house, two older men address the obvious. Four months after one of the summer’s many wildfires threatened to devour the hamlet of El Morro, an hour west of Madrid, local people are still counting the cost and awaiting compensation.

“Look at that house,” said Esteban Pérez, pointing to one of the properties that did not make it through July’s flames. “Everything inside is scorched, completely destroyed. You can still see the windows, but they’re gutted. The entire structure of the house next to mine had to be torn down, too. And they’ve given the owner nothing so far.”

Continue reading...

item.title: BBC lodges urgent appeal against Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit
item.description:
Corporation asks US court of appeals for the 11th circuit to throw out case brought over Panorama documentary

The BBC has lodged an urgent appeal to have Donald Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against it thrown out, after internal surprise at a judge’s decision to allow the case to go to trial.

The corporation is currently heading to court next year over a Panorama documentary that spliced together two parts of Trump’s speech made before the 6 January insurrection at the US Capitol.

Continue reading...

item.title: Australia is inching closer to a recession after one RBA rate rise too many | Greg Jericho
item.description:
It’s not like we couldn’t see the rise in unemployment coming. Pretty much everyone else could feel the stuffing being knocked out of the economy

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Earlier this month, the six members of the Reserve Bank monetary policy board voted to raise the cash rate to 4.85%. Last Thursday, the October labour force figures showed unemployment hit 4.9%. And on Wednesday, the inflation rate jumped to 4.9%, overwhelmingly due to surging fuel costs.

If they weren’t sure they had stuffed up by raising the cash rate on Melbourne Cup day, the market quickly told them.

Continue reading...

item.title: Swiss tourist killed and British and Americans injured by elephants in Cameroon
item.description:
Alain Throo, insurance executive based in London, reportedly gored and later died on hike near Mount Cameroon national park

A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon.

The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports.

Continue reading...

item.title: China sends first foreign astronaut to ISS rival as it globalises space operations
item.description:
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali – the first Pakistani to reach orbit – greeted with Chinese ‘space handshake’ at Tiangong station

China has flown the first foreign astronaut to its Tiangong space station, starting what it says will be the globalisation of its space operations as the US-led International Space Station (ISS) enters its final years of operation.

Floating through a hatch to enter Tiangong, Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali grinned broadly as he was embraced by the onboard crew in what China’s space agency called the country’s first foreign “space handshake”.

Continue reading...

item.title: High prices force many across the US to scale back for Thanksgiving: ‘We can’t afford the food’
item.description:
Americans are opting for smaller gatherings, reconsidering travel or swapping expensive ingredients for cheaper alternatives

Thanksgiving is just one day away, but for some Americans, the holiday may look a little different this year as higher costs for food, drinks, household goods, air travel and gasoline have prompted some families to rethink their plans and spending.

The Guardian recently asked readers across the United States how they were marking the holiday this year and whether higher prices had affected their plans or made them rethink their usual traditions.

Continue reading...

item.title: World has six consecutive days 2C above preindustrial levels for first time
item.description:
Daily global surface temperature hit record 2.24C above baseline levels on Monday and streak is forecast to continue

For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned.

This record hot streak, which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating.

Continue reading...

item.title: Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU
item.description:
Administration is suggesting an added 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total to about 40%

  • US politics live – latest updates

Donald Trump is proposing new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the European Union, that would go into effect early next year, the office of the US trade representative said on Wednesday.

The administration is proposing an additional 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total tax to about 40%. Other countries affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

Continue reading...

item.title: Is grandma asking rude questions at the dinner table again? This Instagram account can help
item.description:
Life100 features the wisdom of two women in their 80s and has gone viral by exploring important life lessons

It is, unfortunately, a familiar scene. At the dinner table, a woman berates her granddaughter with invasive, personal questions – why are you still single? When are you going to have kids? – punctuated by unnerving thrusts of her steak knife. The granddaughter is clearly uncomfortable, but her grandmother pays no attention.

Anyone who has been in this situation likely knows what comes next. The granddaughter may try to deflect, only to invite further questioning, or call out her grandmother’s rudeness, which risks escalation.

Continue reading...

item.title: Brussels on split-screen: where it flexes – and where it bends
item.description:
From a choreographed summit that dominated Westminster but barely registered in Brussels to a climate showdown in Turkey, last week revealed the EU’s priorities – and the limits of its collective power

• Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

Two very different European diplomatic dramas played out almost simultaneously last week. On Friday, a tightly choreographed EU-UK summit transfixed London, while barely registering on the continent. On Sunday, Cop31 collapsed after a united EU forcefully vetoed a watered-down climate pact, even as it relaxed its own green rules at home.

What do these two events reveal about the EU: how it works, what takes up its bandwidth, how it exercises its clout – and where it’s vulnerable?

***

Continue reading...

item.title: Kilmar Ábrego García, target of Trump’s immigration crackdown, lands in Spain after ‘leaving happy’
item.description:
Ábrego García chose to depart from US after previously being deported to El Salvador due to ‘administrative error’

Kilmar Ábrego García, the Salvadoran national whose mistaken deportation turned him into a symbol of Donald Trump’s mass deportation efforts, has landed in Spain.

Ábrego García arrived in Madrid on Wednesday after leaving the United States of his own volition. Prior to his departure, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents met him at the airport and removed his ankle monitor, according to We Are CASA, a Maryland-based advocacy group.

Continue reading...

item.title: ‘Russia wants more than Ukraine,’ Germany’s Merz warns – as it happened
item.description:
German chancellor, in wide-ranging speech, says Moscow is ‘escalating on a massive scale’

If you want to hear more about the new death toll, listen to today’s Today in Focus podcast with our Russia expert, Pjotr Sauer.

“Two groups of hackers accessed Russia’s main statistics database last month and discovered a cache of 11m death certificates that revealed nearly 500,000 Russian losses in Ukraine since 2022. Among these were 1,000 – the equivalent of a whole regiment – who took their own lives.

The documents show how the majority of soldiers come from poorer areas and ethnic minorities, drawn in by high salaries. There are also recruits from abroad and even those lured to Russia by offers of jobs. But for how long can Vladimir Putin keep this shocking death toll from the Russian people?”

Continue reading...

item.title: The bathroom’s wrecked, I’m soaked – but at long last the dog is clean | Adrian Chiles
item.description:
‘It’s the washing he doesn’t like,’ said the dog groomer sagely. Talk about an understatement

He knew what was coming. I don’t hold with the idea of dogs being super-clever. All the bum-sniffing, squirrel-chasing and obsession with balls and sticks suggest otherwise. But on this occasion my dog was on the money. I know this, because he disappeared.

We’d got in, mid-afternoon, and I’d put the bath on. The dog groomer was coming later, you see – though with my dog it’s more about shearing than grooming. What the job really demands is a bare-chested Aussie sheep-shearing champion, but there are none advertised in my area.

Continue reading...

item.title: They belong to Jerusalem’s past and present: meet the African Palestinians
item.description:
Despite militarisation, occupation and marginalisation, African culture prevails in the Old City, something I discovered first-hand when I visited

  • Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

In occupied East Jerusalem, I met an often overlooked community: African Palestinians. This week, I explore their unique history, and how they are, in a classic diaspora fashion, integrated and marginalised in equal measure.

There are about 450 African Palestinian people in occupied East Jerusalem, mostly living in the historical buildings of the Old City, near al-Aqsa mosque. That mosque, the third holiest site in Islam after those in Mecca and Medina, is the reason they are there. While Christians make up a small part of the African Palestinian population, most African Palestinians descended from Muslim pilgrims who came to East Jerusalem in the early 20th century (before Israeli occupation), and stayed either to tend to the mosque, or to continue Islamic practice and devotion within the city’s religious ecosystem.

Continue reading...

item.title: Influencers Behaving Badly at No 10? Burnham could have worse problems | Emma Brockes
item.description:
For all the fuss, it makes perfect sense for the PM to engage young people through TikTokers. He’ll have the last laugh on this one

These are dangerous times to be a prime minister. So it is perhaps reassuring that the trouble into which Andy Burnham barrelled this week is so old school as to be almost soothing. Four months into his premiership, Burnham has arrived early at that rite of passage: the catastrophic attempt to engage with popular culture and subsequent category-5 storm in a teacup. After footage emerged of Influencers Behaving Badly at Downing Street, Burnham, in my view, has come out of the whole thing in surprisingly good shape.

To recap: earlier this month, Burnham held a reception for social media influencers, one of whom, Luke Hamnett, was permitted to film himself doing the Hugh Grant dance from Love Actually before sitting down to interview the prime minister. Meanwhile, self-described “presenter, podcaster, idiot” Max Balegde filmed himself outside the door of No 10 miming what, in the words of the Daily Mail as it geared up to go the full Judge Pickles, “appeared to be a viral meme song”. These words were “bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets”, which, as the Telegraph took a breath from its own meltdown to explain, turns on “a Jamaican profanity popularised online”.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

Continue reading...

item.title: Poundland collapses into administration, putting 12,000 jobs at risk
item.description:
US owner Gordon Brothers rejected at least two last-ditch bids for UK budget retailer

  • Do you work for Poundland? Tell us how you’re affected

Poundland has called in administrators, putting 12,000 jobs at risk in the run-up to Christmas after its owners rejected at least two last-ditch bids for the budget retailer.

Administrators at AlixPartners have been appointed to the retailer, which has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, by Poundland’s directors. The chain is now expected to be broken up with significant job losses and store closures.

Continue reading...

item.title: Nasa knocked an asteroid off course. New closeup photos may shed light on aftermath
item.description:
Images of Dimorphos four years on from crash should give clues for design of potential planetary defence system

Humanity may not yet have a means of fending off a Vogon constructor fleet – the destroyers of Earth in The Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy – but its prospects of surviving an encounter with a rogue asteroid are looking considerably brighter.

Four years after Nasa deliberately slammed a spacecraft into a roughly 160-metre-wide asteroid called Dimorphos to knock it off course, scientists are poised to release the first closeup images of the aftermath.

Continue reading...

item.title: Is Vanity Fair’s takedown of Taylor Swift illuminating – or just a lot of hot air? | Arwa Mahdawi
item.description:
A war correspondent interviewed 100 sources about the pop star, but what does the 4,500-word story reveal?

If you are extremely online you will have known for a while that a big takedown was coming. An exposé of a well-known blond billionaire, a powerful figure that people are terrified to criticise, was in the works at a large publication. A former war correspondent had been assigned the story! A hundred sources had been interviewed! The reporting had taken a year! The truth would finally out!

For everyone else, let me explain in plain English. On Monday Vanity Fair published an eagerly anticipated, 4,500-word piece, about Taylor Swift called The Mastermind. While it was labelled as “commentary”, it was framed as a deeply sourced piece written by May Jeong, a journalism professor at Princeton who has won awards for her reporting from Afghanistan.

Continue reading...

item.title: California beaches close as record-breaking tides and major flooding loom
item.description:
Most of state likely to avoid worst-case scenario of coastal flooding amplified by intense winter rainstorms

Major flooding is expected in California today as a second day of record-breaking high tides hits up and down the west coast.

While forecasts suggest most of the state is on track to avoid the worst-case scenario – coastal flooding amplified by intense winter rainstorms – local officials have been preparing for weeks for the risk that flooding will disrupt travel during Thanksgiving week, one of the busiest times of the year.

Dani Anguiano contributed reporting

Continue reading...

item.title: US Army calls Iowa lead detonation a ‘huge success’ and says threat of spontaneous explosions has been ‘eliminated’ – as it happened
item.description:
This live blog is now closed. For the latest news on this detonation in Iowa, read our full story:

  • Smoke seen from a mile away as army detonates bomb-making chemicals

The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has activated an emergency response to support the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services to “provide accurate public health communication and technical assistance to our state and federal partners.”

In a statement, the CDC said that at the request of the state of Iowa, it will support the state’s health department to develop “recommendations to help protect people from potential exposure to lead and air pollution” and in preparing to support the state with any “any post-event community health assessment needs.”

Continue reading...

item.title: Trump open to pardoning Jensen Huang if needed: ‘It’s always an option’
item.description:
The president’s comments came after pressuring Nvidia’s board to reinstall Huang as CEO despite lawmakers’ concerns over national security

Donald Trump said on Tuesday he would be open to pardoning Jensen Huang, the recently reinstalled Nvidia CEO, for potential crimes but didn’t think it would be necessary.

“It’s always an option, I guess,” the US president told the New York Post in an interview. “But I don’t think it’ll be necessary.”

Continue reading...

item.title: A historic ruling: inside the 27 November Guardian Weekly
item.description:
Justice for the Rohingya. Plus: Burnham’s EU deal

• Get the Guardian Weekly magazine delivered to your home address

History was made in the world’s highest court last week. The international court of justice ruled that Myanmar’s government committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 military campaign.

The landmark judgment was the first time a state had been found responsible for genocide since the passage of the 1948 genocide convention.

Continue reading...

item.title: The Labour party has lost the plot on net zero | Letters
item.description:
Raymond T Pierrehumbert and Dr Lynne Jones respond to an article by the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh

Watching Miatta Fahnbulleh, the secretary of state for energy security and net zero, forced to defend the government’s retreat from net zero (Where do people want to see Britain’s climate action plan working? On their own doorstep, 17 November) was painfully reminiscent of the way in which Colin Powell, a former US secretary of state and an honourable man, was forced to defend George W Bush’s claims justifying the disastrous Iraq war.

Fahnbulleh states that people need to see the benefits of net zero on their doorstep – meaning jobs, cost of living and warm homes. But in fact the policies of this government mark a retreat of all of these “doorstep” benefits. Andy Burnham has slashed heat pump subsidies, which means more vulnerability of homes to heating price shocks from international affairs spiking fossil gas prices; it also means fewer warm homes and jobs in the heat pump manufacturing and installation industry.

Continue reading...

item.title: Cop31 collapse must be a catalyst for genuine climate action | Letters
item.description:
Readers on the failure of the climate talks in Turkey and the lessons we can learn

The failure of Cop31, as commented on by Bill McGuire (A year of deadly floods and fires – and yet Cop31 still collapsed. When will our leaders grasp the scale of this crisis?, 24 November), is the expression of the overwhelming momentum of the value system of a global culture that is wedded to the seemingly unstoppable expansion of our material production and consumption.

The disjunction between peril and necessary action is explained by the impossibility of taming appetites that are insatiable. It is convenient to blame fossil fuel producers, and while they are obviously guilty parties, the ultimate problem is the continuing demand for their products.

Continue reading...

item.title: UN sacked Palestinian staff on back of unproven Israeli allegations, tribunal rules
item.description:
Judgment casts doubt on evidence linking aid workers to Hamas and says humanitarian efforts in Gaza were damaged

A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of Palestinian UN aid workers in 2024, saying it was based “almost entirely” on unproven assertions from the Israeli government and had damaged humanitarian operations in Gaza.

The judgment, seen by the Guardian, raises fresh questions about the decision by the UN Relief and Works Agency (Unrwa), the main humanitarian organisation working in Gaza, to sack members of staff. It was taken on the basis of Israeli allegations of involvement in the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.

Continue reading...

item.title: All hostages rescued after Colombian security forces storm supermarket
item.description:
Operation in which one hostage-taker was killed ends daylong siege in Cartagena shopping centre, where 30 people were initially held

Colombian police have stormed a supermarket in one of the country’s most popular tourist cities, ending a daylong siege in which all the hostages were freed and one hostage-taker was killed.

Abelardo de la Espriella, the far-right president, travelled to the Caribbean port city of Cartagena to follow the final hours of negotiations and the tactical assault, in which special forces officers broke through blocked entrances and detonated stun grenades.

Continue reading...

item.title: Trump administration approves Elon Musk’s plan for datacenters in space
item.description:
The FCC approved 1m Starmind satellites, with the deployment of 100,000 no later than November 2035

US federal regulators approved a constellation of datacenters to process data in space on Wednesday, saying that they would “support America’s booming super intelligence economy”.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said in a statement that regulators had approved 1m Starmind orbital satellites, or compute modules, built by Elon Musk’s SpaceX. It is the first such authorization in US history.

Continue reading...

item.title: ‘I am leaving with my freedom’: Kilmar Ábrego García lands in Spain after choosing to leave US - live
item.description:
Before his departure, Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents met him at the airport and removed his ankle monitor, an advocacy group reported

  • Sign up for the Breaking News US email to get newsletter alerts in your inbox

US trade representative Jamieson Greer claimed this morning that he did not expect the new proposed tariffs to rattle the global economy.

“We’ve talked to our trading partners about this — they know what we’re proposing,” Greer told CNBC. “I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don’t think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now.”

item.title: Smoke seen from a mile away as army detonates US stockpile of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa
item.description:
Controlled blast to dispose of lead azide risks releasing plumes of toxic chemicals in 100-mile radius

The US army detonated the nation’s entire stockpile of the the bomb-making material lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday morning, despite an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.

The controlled blast, which took place at about 10.00am ET, was to dispose of 9,700lb (4,400kg) of the chemical that was stored at the Iowa army ammunition plant in Middletown, a small town in south-eastern Iowa that is home to about 400 people.

item.title: The Guardian view on the next UN secretary general: sacrificing principles will damn the institution, not save it | Editorial
item.description:
The UK must continue to oppose the UAE’s tainted nominee, Lana Nusseibeh. The ethical course is also the pragmatic one

The future of the United Nations has rarely looked more perilous in an age of impunity for atrocities, raging wars, open US hostility, a funding crisis and security council deadlock. It is widely agreed that the choice of its next secretary general is critical – perhaps even existential. Unfortunately, that’s where agreement ends.

Under the opaque selection system, security council members are privately polled on their views of each candidate. A “discourage” vote from one of the five permanent members is diplomacy-speak for a veto. Only when a consensus emerges does the general assembly get a say on the candidate. The next straw poll is due on Monday, with no deal yet in sight. With António Guterres completing his term on 31 December, the seat could fall empty for the first time.

Continue reading...

item.title: The Guardian view on rising energy prices: only bold action can win public confidence | Editorial
item.description:
Andy Burnham needs a radical vision of economic change to move on from policies aimed at giving voters ‘breathing space’

Ask Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this month, he said that the Democratic party’s triumph meant that there was “an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living”.

This wasn’t a non sequitur. The Republicans lost control of Congress in large part because Donald Trump failed to address concerns about the cost of basic goods – a failing aggravated by the US president’s disastrous war against Iran, which caused a spike in commodity prices, exacerbating the affordability problem.

Continue reading...

item.title: Schumer accuses Huang of violating US export control laws amid shipments of chips to China
item.description:
Senate minority leader joins lawmakers from both parties outraged over Nvidia CEO’s reinstatement

Chuck Schumer, the current Senate minority leader vying to lead the Democratic majority in the next Congress, accused Jensen Huang, the newly reinstated Nvidia CEO, of shipping “extremely advanced chips to China” and violating US export control laws.

On Tuesday, Schumer said the move “amounts to the equivalent of selling rocket engines to the Soviets during the space race”.

Continue reading...

item.title: Kilmar Ábrego García, man at center of Trump deportation battle, leaves US
item.description:
Salvadorian man, who was deported in March 2025 and returned to US after supreme court ruling, leaving of own volition for Spain

Kilmar Ábrego García has left the United States of his own volition, his lawyers confirmed on Tuesday, with the Department of Homeland Security confirming that he was travelling to Spain.

The Salvadorian immigrant was at the center of a months-long legal battle since he was deported to El Salvador in March 2025 by the Trump administration, in defiance of a court’s protection. He was held in Cecot, a notorious anti-terrorism mega-prison.

Continue reading...

item.title: Coastal areas in England at risk of erosion to receive £11m in new funding
item.description:
Exclusive: Laser-equipped drone surveys and road relocations among schemes to get government support

Laser-equipped drone surveys, sand dune restoration and moving roads inland are among the projects that will receive government funding to help seaside communities in England adapt to rising seas and coastal erosion accelerated by climate breakdown.

More than £11m will be shared between 12 council-led projects that will test ways to spot coastal change earlier and help communities plan for the effects.

Continue reading...

item.title: US army to detonate 68 barrels of toxic lead in Iowa on day before Thanksgiving
item.description:
Residents warned to stay indoors amid conflicting information about how far the dust plume could travel

The US Army is set to detonate 68 barrels – five tons – of lead azide at an ammunition plant in rural Iowa on Wednesday morning, after delays and conflicting information about how far the toxic lead dust plume could travel after the explosion.

That controlled blast has been scheduled for 10am ET on Wednesday, the day before the Thanksgiving holiday.

Continue reading...

item.title: One lame duck and two turkeys as Trump plays the hits at Thanksgiving ceremony
item.description:
Levity was in short supply as president, reeling from midterms rout, talked up his achievements – and fixated on White House vanity project

For some, it was his pardoning of the January 6 rioters or the deployment of masked ICE agents. For others, it was Elon Musk’s chainsaw or the demolition of the White House East Wing.

Donald Trump’s second term as US president has been full of moments when people exclaim: this is the last straw! But on Tuesday even he went too far.

Continue reading...

item.title: I asked AI if it was OK to use AI to write an obituary. The answer surprised me | Anna Spargo-Ryan
item.description:
Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson’s tribute to Molly Meldrum contained heaps of the right words. But they were written by something that can’t feel

I know how this will sound but when my nanna died the second thought I had, after utter devastation, was: “This is a writer’s dream.” She was 101. That is so many years old. I wrote the eulogy to end all eulogies, breaking my own heart with a bottomless well of memories, anecdotes and in-jokes. It was achingly personal and exquisitely her.

The Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson’s team took a similar approach in this week’s tribute to the music legend Molly Meldrum, by which I mean they generated it with AI. I imagine the conversation went something like: we are 25 years old, who even was she? And then one of them plugged Molly’s name into Claude while the others went downstairs for $11 coffees. Job done.

Continue reading...

item.title: China investigates politburo star in Xi Jinping’s latest purge
item.description:
Chen Jining, regarded as a contender for higher office, becomes the fourth member of China’s elite politburo to be investigated since 2025

China has launched an investigation into Shanghai’s Communist party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s elite politburo, the state-run Xinhua news agency unexpectedly announced on Tuesday, marking the fourth member of the top leadership ⁠body to be probed since ⁠2025.

China’s anti-graft watchdog is investigating ​Chen for “suspected severe violations of discipline and laws”, Xinhua said, using a common euphemism for corruption.

Continue reading...

item.title: Australia’s security pact with Solomon Islands a blow to China’s influence in the Pacific
item.description:
Anthony Albanese and Matthew Wale sign new treaty as Solomon Islands PM states his country no longer ‘a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region’

The Solomon Islands prime minister says the days of his country being an uncertain partner in the Pacific are over as he signed a sweeping agreement to make Australia his country’s primary security partner and limit ties with China.

Matthew Wale signed the new treaty with Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, in Canberra on Wednesday after Solomon Islands earlier this week announced it was terminating a landmark security pact with Beijing.

Continue reading...

item.title: Rescue crews search for six people after plane crash off Mississippi coast
item.description:
US Coast Guard said crews had so far found the cabin of the plane, a life raft and three life jackets

Rescue crews were searching for six people on board a small plane that crashed Tuesday afternoon off the coast of Mississippi.

Crews have so far found three life jackets, a life raft and the cabin of the plane. The plane’s cabin was floating on the water, Juan Ros, a US Coast Guard spokesperson, said.

Continue reading...

item.title: Al Gore buys local, family-owned newspaper in central Tennessee
item.description:
Former vice-president, who started his career as a journalist, purchases Carthage Courier in Smith county

Al Gore, who started his career as a journalist, is returning to the industry as a newspaper owner in his Tennessee town.

The Lake family, which has operated the Carthage Courier for five decades, said Tuesday it will sell the paper to the former vice-president in the coming weeks. The weekly paper serves Smith county in central Tennessee, which has roughly 20,000 residents and sits about 55 miles (88km) east of Nashville.

Continue reading...

item.title: In charts: how power could shift in Europe’s big year of elections
item.description:
More than half of EU voters will go to the polls in the next 12 months, with the far right targeting significant gains. We set out the political landscape and trends

  • Europe is entering a ‘supercycle’ of national elections. Their outcomes could shake the EU’s foundations

Over the coming 12 months, more than half of the EU’s electorate will go to the polls in elections that could change the direction of the continent, with attention focused on voters in four of the bloc’s five biggest states.

In Spain, France and Poland, elections could bring the far right into government. Italy’s far-right prime minister looks likely to remain in power, but is under pressure from a challenger even more to the right.

Continue reading...

item.title: ‘They don’t believe in freedom’: Yemenis plan their escape as Houthis advance on Aden
item.description:
With Iran’s proxy fighters encircling the temporary capital, residents and NGOs prepare to evacuate

Hussein fled his home six years ago after it fell under Houthi control, moving as far south as he could to the port city of Aden, where there was a measure of safety.

The Saudi-backed Yemeni government had made the city its temporary capital; the hundreds of kilometres between it and the Houthis were well fortified.

Continue reading...

item.title: What do Brexit and an Australian cricket scandal have in common? Sometimes it’s right to reopen old wounds | Jonathan Liew
item.description:
Just like the ball-tampering scandal of 2018, the Brexit debate is back. The lesson here is that anything with a dodgy whiff about it will only come back

Just move on. You lost, get on with it. Why rake up the past? And why, for the love of all that is holy, is Theresa May back on my television?

Of all the many regrettable political figures to have surfaced over recent days, perhaps May has been most triggering of all: a bleak reminder of unhappier times. But of course she has been far from the only former prime minister lured from obscurity by the irresistible siren call of Brexit Revisited. David Cameron has been portending a “very long and painful argument”. “Divisive” and “all-consuming”, argued Rishi Sunak. Boris Johnson warned Andy Burnham – with no apparent sense of irony – that reopening the Brexit negotiations would be “wasting his premiership”. Here they come, the cast of the Tory remake of Avengers: Doomsday, presaging of rancour and paralysis from the people who brought us years of rancour and paralysis.

Jonathan Liew is a sportswriter and Opinion columnist for the Guardian

item.title: What’s the most sustainable way to eat fish? Forget it. There isn’t one | George Monbiot
item.description:
Don’t take the bait offered up by ‘conservation’ charities. Fishing is about as good for our ecosystems as tobacco is for our health

Drumroll please. I am about to unveil the species of fish that’s best to eat if you want to protect the living seas. Ta-dah! It’s … I hope that clears things up. Unfortunately, over the past few years, a noisy industry has developed to tell you otherwise. You’re doing the planet a favour if you eat mackerel, sorry, cod, I mean haddock, no coley, make that pollack – oh, whoops! These choices might make you feel better about yourself. But they do nothing but harm to marine wildlife. The fish you should choose is none of the above.

Cause, could I introduce you to effect? In April, the Marine Conservation Society, through its Good Fish Guide, suggested you stop eating cod and eat hake instead. Six months later, it lamented that hake is now overexploited thanks to “increased fishing pressure”, and downgraded its sustainability ratings. How on earth did that happen? Beats me.

item.title: Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia is elite impunity | Moira Donegan
item.description:
After the CEO was reinstated after Trump’s pressure campaign, it is abundantly clear: there are different rules for rich people

There are different rules for rich people. If you or I acted the way that Jensen Huang has been accused of acting – allegedly berating and mistreating employees, sleeping with subordinates, and seeming to carry on a staggering number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman identified by US intelligence as a likely Chinese spy who helped smuggle the company’s product to China – we probably would find ourselves out of work and out of favor for quite some time.

But this is not so for Huang, the tech founder and close ally to Donald Trump who was recently ousted from Nvidia, the chip manufacturer he founded. On Monday, after a pressure campaign from Donald Trump, JD Vance and other members of the Trump administration, Huang was reinstated as CEO by the Nvidia board.

item.title: Mariella Frostrup calls AJ Odudu ‘aggressive’ – and here we go again. We tire of this angry black woman trope | Natalie Morris
item.description:
Microaggressions pile up, and then they are triggering. Amid the latest row on I’m a Celebrity, we’re obliged to explain this hurt all over again

When I heard Mariella Frostrup call AJ Odudu “aggressive” over the weekend on I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!, my heart sank with sick recognition. For her part, AJ’s mother has since said that watching her daughter experience this all-too-familiar dynamic was a “living hell”. I know many Black women tuning in will have felt a collective shudder of disgust and solidarity.

Of course, there is pushback. “Our addiction to offence is tearing us apart,” wrote a Telegraph pundit on Monday. But, this language is not neutral. There is a long history of Black women having their conduct and tone disproportionately scrutinised by white people. And what happened between Odudu and Frostrup is a tale as old as time. A Black woman stands up for herself and, no matter how reasonably she presents her argument, she is accused of aggression. It is an efficient tactic to flip the focus on to the behaviour of the Black woman, and it is rooted in racist stereotypes.

Natalie Morris is the author of Mixed/Other: Explorations of Multiraciality in Modern Britain

item.title: Why white-tailed sea eagles are a danger to Britain’s seabirds | Letters
item.description:
The reintroduction of the birds in England and Wales spells disaster for fragile marine ecosystems, warns Tim Birkhead

Your article on white-tailed sea eagle reintroduction (Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts, 8 November) highlighted the risk that white-tailed sea eagles are likely to pose to Britain’s seabirds. To argue, as Prof Ian Convery and Rebecca Wrigley did in their responses (Letters, 15 November), that the re-establishment of white-tailed sea eagles will somehow restore a lost paradise is fallacious. Where is the evidence that sea eagles will restore that balance? There is no evidence.

Also, suggesting that because in the distant past sea eagles and seabirds coexisted, their reintroduction will pose no problems is naive. By failing to acknowledge that past marine ecosystems were much more robust, and seabird prey more abundant, than they are today, these two authors miss the point that it is precisely because our seabirds are currently short of food that they are so vulnerable to disturbance and predation from white-tailed sea eagles.

item.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham and Wales: a devolution blindspot at No 10 | Editorial
item.description:
The PM has summarily dismissed Welsh demands for further powers similar to those enjoyed in Scotland. The approach seems at odds with his consensual style

As he headed for Downing Street this summer, Andy Burnham said that he aimed to be “as collaborative and pragmatic as possible” in his dealings with the governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. His predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, had notoriously warned ministers against being “overly deferential” in discussions with the devolved administrations. But Mr Burnham’s signature commitment to distributing more power and responsibility out of Westminster, and his consensual style, appeared to augur well for a positive reset in relations.

In Wales, this early optimism has just been brutally quashed by an uncharacteristically peremptory letter from Mr Burnham to the first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth. In it, the prime minister flatly rejected Welsh calls for the devolving of powers in relation to policing and justice, the crown estate and rail infrastructure. In the case of policing, Mr Burnham is in the curious position of denying to Mr ap Iorwerth the type of power that he enjoyed as the mayor of Greater Manchester.

item.title: The Guardian view on disability benefits: Timms’s radical review is rooted in experience | Editorial
item.description:
Ministers have taken on board their MPs’ message about cuts. Now anxious claimants need reassurance

Four million people with disabilities or long‑term health conditions in the UK claim personal independence payment (Pip). A review by Sir Stephen Timms, the social security minister, offers a blueprint for how to overhaul it. Its recommendations pose a difficult question for ministers: are they prepared to meet the needs that a more accurate assessment of the costs of disability might reveal?

Sir Stephen worked as one of three co-chairs with a steering group of 12 people with a range of professional and lived experience. There is broad agreement that Pip needs to be reformed. The announcement on Tuesday that the government would accept the recommendation of a new fast track for claimants whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve, and abolish unnecessary benefit reviews, signalled that ministers are ready for change. The decision, affecting one in 10 claimants in England and Wales, is welcome but long overdue. Ministers should work with the devolved administrations to ensure similar progress elsewhere in the UK.

item.title: Men have used wealth and fame to get away with abuse. No longer | Andy Burnham
item.description:
The NDAs that enforce silence, the behaviour that exploits the age of consent. I'll address both with sweeping changes to keep women and girls safe

  • Burnham opens door to wider NDAs ban at ‘watershed moment’ on abuse

Powerful men using their fame and money to silence anyone who calls out their behaviour. Victims treated as though they’re the ones who’ve done something wrong. And a culture where abuse can hide in plain sight because people in positions of power think they can get away with it. That’s what we’ve seen in the past few weeks. This must be a watershed moment. Not just for the culture of the entertainment industry but for us as a nation.

Things have improved in the past decade or so, but we are still far from being where we need to be for women and girls to feel safe and be safe. Sadly, many women and girls will find the stories of the past few weeks all too close to home, whether it’s casual disrespect in the workplace, undermining “jokes”, or being told they are somehow at fault for something that has happened to them.

item.title: Europe’s big threat is not Trump and Putin redrawing the map. It’s our own learned helplessness | Natalie Tocci
item.description:
The US and Russia lack the power to impose their will on the continent – the Shenzhen summit was no Yalta 2.0

But those – particularly in eastern Europe – who are fretting about another historic betrayal should remember that when it comes to European security today, we are the ones who hold most of the cards. item.title: A year of deadly floods and fires – and yet Cop31 still collapsed. When will our leaders grasp the scale of this crisis? | Bill McGuire
item.description:
Fossil fuel producers are choking off progress while we reap the whirlwind of our inaction. This is what sleepwalking to disaster looks like

It’s sometimes said that we are sleepwalking into climate catastrophe. But the reality is that we are walking into it with our eyes wide open, in the full knowledge that we are dooming the lives of our children, and countless generations down the line, to hell on Earth. In the UK, summer temperatures could hit the mid-40s within decades, making extreme drought and harvest failures the norm, and leaving people camping in the streets as houses become overheated death traps. Across Europe, the fastest-heating continent on the planet, the 50C temperature mark could be broken as soon as next year. Elsewhere, by 2050, humid heatwaves could take many thousands of lives in a single day in parts of China, South Asia and the Gulf region.

We continue to pump out the CO2 weight-equivalent of 800,000 Titanics every year, with no end in sight. Meanwhile the latest climate Cop – the only global initiative with the potential to turn things around – has just collapsed in disarray, unable to get its act together even to agree on a vague form of words about the need to transition away from fossil fuels.

item.title: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee
item.description:
These ancient and often grossly unfair taxes are stifling the economy and young people. It’s long past time for radical reform

When voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first, council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax.

Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan. Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

item.title: After 80 years in Oxford, Naga ancestors are finally going home
item.description:
A campaign securing the landmark return to India of ancestral remains taken during British colonial rule has opened a wider conversation about restitution

The lacerating legacy of colonialism survives in many spaces, particularly in museum collections and private holdings across the western world. And it’s not just limited to inanimate artefacts or cultural objects.

For almost 80 years, human remains were displayed on crowded glass shelves at Pitt Rivers Museum at Oxford University, one of the world’s most celebrated institutions.

item.title: The Ukraine-Russia war is escalating – and it will go global unless Europe speaks with one voice | Simon Tisdall
item.description:
Attacks from the Mediterranean to eastern Europe to the Baltic Sea are a rebuke to western complacency. Trump is a liability, and he must be bypassed to ensure peace

Ukraine’s spectacularly successful weekend drone attack on a spanking new Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi, more than 1,300 miles (2,200km) from Kyiv, is further proof, if it were needed, that the catastrophic full-scale war Vladimir Putin launched in 2022 is escalating and spreading uncontrollably.

The sinking follows a similar incident in the Baltic last week, which crippled a Russian cargo ship, and previous Ukrainian attacks on oil tankers and Russian navy ships and bases in the Black Sea region. Last week, Russia was blamed for a missile and drone strike on Nato member Poland, which Donald Tusk, the Polish prime minister, claimed was intentional, and for deliberately targeting western diplomatic compounds in Kyiv. While Moscow’s murderous winter bombing of Ukrainian civilians and energy infrastructure continues apace, provocative and disruptive Russian hybrid warfare operations across all of Europe, including sabotage, arson and cyber-attacks, are becoming daily occurrences.

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

item.title: Leader of India’s Cockroach movement says he was stopped from boarding flight to UK

Saurav Das, 27, has been at the forefront of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), which has amassed millions of social media followers since its launch in May. Das, who was due to fly out early on Tuesday, said immigration officials told him at the airport that his passport had been flagged.

item.title: ‘The numbers are very stark’: This primary school is the heart of a Welsh village. Can it be saved?
item.description:
Gladestry primary school is predicted to have only 19 pupils within two years, while its county council is forced to make cuts year after year. But residents still believe it’s worth fighting for

The kitchen in the Alman family farmhouse is large, airy and decorated with hundreds of rosettes awarded over the decades for prize-winning dogs, sheep and cows. I grew up just up the hill, so I know this kitchen well. Apart from the video feed in the corner, showing what the cattle are up to in the barn, it hasn’t changed much since the 1980s when we’d pile in here after helping our fathers with the baling.

From the kitchen, Gladestry’s small, slate-roofed primary school, set against the steep green slope of Hergest Ridge, is clearly visible, and – it being playtime when I visited – clearly audible too. That hasn’t changed much either since the days when Joseph Alman and I were pupils at that tiny school, and our own parents looked out of that same window and heard us calling to each other as we played football.

item.title: The case for Chris Van Hollen as US Senate majority leader | Linda Sarsour
item.description:
Electing Van Hollen would show voters that the Democratic party is serious about change. We can’t keep waiting for Chuck Schumer to catch up

Despite some bumps in the road, Hakeem Jeffries, a Democratic congressman from New York, largely cruised to victory last week and will be the next speaker of the House. I don’t expect Senator Chuck Schumer to have the same fast track to majority leader. And he shouldn’t.

On Thursday, Senator Elissa Slotkin threw her support behind Senator Chris Van Hollen for majority leader, citing the need for “a new generation of leadership”. When asked on MS Now why she also supports Van Hollen, the senator-elect Peggy Flanagan cited what Minnesota has been through the past two years and Trump’s appointment of Stephen Miller to the chief of staff role, concluding that we need a majority leader who will fight back. Over the weekend, Senator Cory Booker declined to endorse either Schumer or Van Hollen but emphasized the need for a new generation to lead in Congress.

item.title: Trump must act now to stop a three-way nuclear arms race | Edward J Markey

Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping met last week in southern China, where Trump said they would “talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization”.

It was the first time the leaders of the world’s three largest nuclear powers had come together to discuss the future of nuclear weapons. That discussion was long overdue.

Edward J Markey represents Massachusetts in the US Senate. He is a co-chair of the bicameral congressional nuclear weapons and arms control working group

item.title: You Can See Everything in Elizabeth Holmes’s unblinking eyes. Or can you? | Jason Okundaye
item.description:
The idea that seeing is believing is turned on its head in this documentary about the inscrutable Theranos founder, a world-class liar who may just be completely unreadable

  • Warning: this article contains spoilers for You Can See Everything

Elizabeth Holmes doesn’t believe that she’s ever told a lie. She “knows” that she hasn’t committed any crime. And she has no reason to deceive you. While speaking, she is gazing at her interviewer, Nathan Fielder, with those enormous, blue, vacant, unsettling, unblinking eyes. She doesn’t break eye contact.

This is You Can See Everything, Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary, which, at her invitation, follows Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans, at their home in San Diego in the weeks up to her surrender to custody at federal prison. Holmes is the disgraced tech ex-billionaire whose startup Theranos claimed the ability to run hundreds of comprehensive blood tests from a single pinprick of blood. This false claim posed “immediate jeopardy” to the health of thousands of patients and defrauded investors of more than $700m.

item.title: Their loss changed Appalachian forests for ever. Now the American chestnut is back
item.description:
The trees have been functionally extinct in the US for nearly a century. But new techniques are creating plants resistant to the parasitic blight that almost wiped them out

Jeff White is starstruck by a tree. The farmer and environmentalist from rural Maryland has an affinity with the American chestnut but has never seen one stretch from root to sky like this one. “About how tall is it?” he asks. “Over 70ft [21 metres],” says Cassie Stark, director of science implementation for the American Chestnut Foundation (TACF).

“Just incredible,” White says, his gaze fixed upwards. “I’ve never seen one so tall and so healthy.”

‘Thompson’, above left, is an unusually tall specimen of an American chestnut, a now-rare species once ubiquitous in the US. Jeff White next to ‘Gladys’, a thriving 15-metre-tall pure American Chestnut in Virginia’s Lesesne forest

item.title: Trump appears to make millions from Nvidia intervention over Huang | First Thing
item.description:
US president holds significant stock in AI company whose value soared after Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO. Plus, why GTA shouldn’t, and won’t, be adapted for streaming

  • Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here

Good morning. Donald Trump made up to $15m on his holdings of Nvidia stock after the US chipmaker’s share price soared on the surprise return of Jensen Huang as chief executive. Huang, who was forced to step down briefly over allegations of extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy, returned to the company’s HQ in Santa Clara, California, receiving a hero’s welcome.

The US president’s financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics indicate he might have owned as many as 370,000 shares in Nvidia as of 30 September. Nvidia’s shares rocketed by 31.5% on Monday. Johana Bhuiyan has this useful timeline of how the scandal unfolded.

What has been the political reaction? Republican lawmakers roundly criticized the Nvidia board’s decision, apparently brokered by the US president, to reinstate its chief executive. Senior Democrat, Elizabeth Warren, said the decision was “reckless”. The reinstalled Nvidia CEO will appear before the Senate banking committee on 3 December, and the US commerce department has added the Singapore-based Nvidia partner Megaspeed to a blacklist amid an investigation into whether it diverted AI chips to China.

What other conflicts of interest do Nvidia and Trump appear to have? Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat, pointed to a series of ties between Huang and Trumpworld as evidence of the executive’s influence over administration policy on advanced chips, including Nvidia’s $25m donation to Trump’s White House ballroom project, his personal holdings of Nvidia stock, Huang’s contribution to Trump’s inauguration fund and his attendance at a $1m-a-plate dinner at Mar-a-Lago.

What has the Guardian found out about Russia’s overall casualties? The Guardian identified more than 460,000 deaths in the data linked to the war between the start of the full-scale invasion in February 2022 and September 2026. War became the leading cause of death in Russian men under 65 last year.

item.title: $150 for photos of Melania looking like a waxwork? Will the Trumps ever run out of money-making ideas? | Arwa Mahdawi
item.description:
From the first lady’s Amazon documentary to Barron’s energy drink, the family is raking it in during Donald’s second term. And that includes the president

Melania Trump is not a regular mom. She’s “a very cool mom”. We know this because she says so in her very cool new TV docuseries, which no one asked for, but which Amazon made anyway. I should clarify that Melania: The Series is not to be confused with Melania, the 104-minute-long $75m (£57m) movie Amazon released earlier this year. You know, the one an industry insider called “the most expensive documentary ever made that didn’t involve music licensing”. Various people insinuated nasty things about alleged corruption when that film came out, but I think it’s sweet how patriotic Amazon seems to be.

While our cup may runneth over with Melania content, I have good news for first lady fans. We’ve been graced with even more Melania merch. At the weekend, Melania announced an “exclusive collection of digital photographs by internationally acclaimed photographer Ellen von Unwerth” to complement her new docuseries. For the non-refundable price of $150 (£115) you get one black-and-white digital image of the first lady sitting on a chair and one photo in which she is posing next to a clapperboard. According to Melania’s website, she and “Ms von Unwerth worked collaboratively during a two-day shoot to develop this visual narrative”.

item.title: Why the genocide verdict against Myanmar has big implications for Israel | Geoffrey Robertson
item.description:
Proving the ‘crime of crimes’ against an individual is notoriously difficult, but the ICJ has set a precedent for states to be found liable. Israel could be next

For the first time ever, a state has been found guilty of genocide – that “crime of crimes” – and has been ordered to compensate victims and to prosecute and punish the perpetrators. This judgment came from the international court of justice (ICJ), which has convicted Myanmar of killing and expelling many thousands of Rohingyas in Rakhine state in 2017.

The court did not change “as such” the definition of the crime, settled by the genocide convention in 1948 as requiring proof of an intention to destroy, in whole or part, a racial or religious group. But it made the prospect of proving this against a nation a good deal easier than against an individual. It set a precedent for its next case concerning state liability, namely the case brought by South Africa against Israel.

Geoffrey Robertson KC was a UN appeal judge and is author of World of War Crimes – Eyeless in Gaza and Beyond

item.title: The next fight for democracy is in the states | Stacey Abrams
item.description:
Defend those being targeted, even when the threat has not reached your door

Welcome back to How We Win, a Guardian opinion series with bold ideas for America’s political future. Today’s edition was written by Stacey Abrams, a voting rights activist, author, and former Georgia house minority leader.

On 3 November, from Arizona to Georgia to Pennsylvania to Wisconsin, where a 16-year Republican majority fell, voters flipped at least 12 legislative chambers, the strongest statehouse showing for pro-democracy candidates since 2008. This did not happen by chance.

Our democracy will be measured by what we protect, what we build and whom we refuse to leave behind.

item.title: Was Benjamin Franklin the original wellness bro? I lived like him for a day to find out
item.description:
Before online influencers existed, the founding father published an annual wellness pamphlet. I followed his 13 virtues he found necessary for a good life

Benjamin Franklin doesn’t get enough credit. Yes, he was a founding father of the United States; he invented the lightning rod and his face is printed on $100 bills. But rarely is he celebrated for his contributions to the most meaningful field of human achievement: wellness influencing.

Centuries before GRWM videos and scientifically dubious podcasts were a dollar-sign-shaped glint in their creators’ eyes, Franklin was doling out life advice. Under the pseudonym Poor Richard, Franklin published an annual pamphlet and minted maxims like “Diligence is the mother of good luck” and “Fish and visitors stink after three days.”

item.title: Tech sell-off resumes as Nvidia shares drop 5% and Anthropic tumbles below IPO price – business live
item.description:
Republicans and Democrats object over Trump’s role in Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO, following an affair with an alleged Chinese spy

  • Democrats hit out at Nvidia and Trump over Huang’s return – US politics live

  • Have you downloaded Meta’s AI assistant Muse or do you plan to?

  • The AI doomsday threat: Distinguishing facts from fear

Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, despite concerns over his conduct and the supply of AI chips to China, may show that AI – and Huang himself – are ‘too big to fail’.

That phrase was on everyone’s lips almost 20 years ago when the Global Financial Crisis struck, and several major banks were bailed out.

Given Nvidia’s pivotal role in the AI capex rollout, the implications of Huang’s reinstatement could be profound. Borrowing from the GFC, are some technology CEOs now so systemically important to the future of AI and US leadership in the latest technology revolution that they cannot be fired?

Questions around the scale of financing required and future monetisation remain, and the dependence on Huang for the future success of AI may paradoxically heighten those concerns especially given Anthropic fell despite yesterday’s broad market rally.

“We must investigate these actions. No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions. Congress must come together in swift bipartisan action and demand answers immediately.”

item.title: Natural beauty made this New Zealand tourist village. Now it threatens its existence
item.description:

item.title: From mocked to mainstream: how Spain’s far-right Vox transformed its fortunes
item.description:
Party that won just 0.2% of the vote in 2016 is on course for almost 20% this time and could be part of next government

Almost exactly eight years ago, a video clip of a stocky, bearded man riding a horse through western Andalucía went viral in Spain. The rider was Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, the soundtrack was a bombastic snatch of the Lord of the Rings score, and the caption was an equally unsubtle callback to the 700-year fight to wrest the Iberian peninsula from Islamic rule. “La Reconquista comenzará en tierras andaluzas,” it read – the reconquest will begin on Andalucían soil.

Celebrated by some, jeered by others – and inventively lampooned by those with sufficient skill and time on their hands – the video didn’t seem quite as amusing three weeks later when Vox broke through into the political mainstream by winning 12 seats in Andalucía’s regional parliament.

item.title: Will the Jilly Cooper plagiarism allegations taint our love of Rivals? I doubt it | Nadia Khomami
item.description:
The evidence seems overwhelming, but artists and writers have borrowed from each other for hundreds of years. The line between homage and theft is a thin one

“Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal,” the poet TS Eliot wrote a century ago. No work of art, he argued, exists in a vacuum. Great writers draw on what came before them, transforming their influences into something entirely their own.

Eliot’s words came to mind when I read the revelations about the queen of the country house bonkbuster Jilly Cooper, who has been accused of “extensive and deliberate” plagiarism in her 1978 book Prudence. At least 35 passages appear to have been lifted from The Serial, a satirical novel by American writer Cyra McFadden, alongside remarkable similarities to sections of Josephine Tey’s 1948 novel The Franchise Affair. McFadden’s daughter is threatening legal action, describing the treatment of her mother’s work as “unconscionable”.

Nadia Khomami is arts and culture correspondent at the Guardian

item.title: Words are not enough after the Myanmar genocide ruling. The world can do better – but it must take these steps | Gordon Brown

item.title: You Can See Everything tells us nothing about Elizabeth Holmes. I guess that’s what the courts are for | Zoe Williams
item.description:
The Theranos founder talks in frustrating riddles – but was she lying to us, or to herself? Or could she be a cog in a larger, more sinister, lie-machine?

I went to see You Can See Everything with a friend who had never heard of Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder of blood testing startup Theranos. She knew that she was a convicted fraudster, because as the film opens, Holmes is 34 days from commencing her prison sentence for defrauding investors. But she was completely open-minded as to whether this was definitely fraud or a miscarriage of justice, whether Holmes was the puppeteer or the puppet (of her previous business and romantic partner, Sunny Balwani, who was also convicted of fraud), and whether Holmes’s central claim, of huge diagnostic capabilities from putting a drop of blood into a tiny box, had any scientific foundation. My friend was probably the co-director Nathan Fielder’s perfect viewer, someone who had no preconceptions about what was true: what would she learn, from three hours with a camera so close to the subject’s face that you could count her eyelashes? “Well … She seems nice?” she said after the film had finished.

I veer towards the old-fashioned and deeply held view that the courts, having soberly examined many documents, must have got it right. The whistleblowers and bystanders, giving their testimony not only to lawyers but also to podcasts, which turned into TV documentaries and dramas, as well as investigative print journalism, which begat yet more journalism – that all seemed pretty convincing as well. I definitely did not go into the cinema with my true-crime head on, which is fortunate, because I’m a sucker for a faulty conviction and I’d have probably found her innocent within 15 minutes.

item.title: Sweden’s datacentre politics are more complicated than they appear | Letter
item.description:
There are distinct tensions over who controls, benefits from and gains access to natural and public resources, write James White and Nora Söderberg

Steve Rose’s account of Sweden’s datacentre sector (‘Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?’, 12 November) is a welcome reminder that digital infrastructure can be developed in more environmentally responsible ways. However, his suggestion that datacentres have become politically contentious elsewhere, “but here in Sweden, not so much”, is a misrepresentation.

Consider the proposed Google datacentre development at Torsboda, near Sundsvall, which requires an enormous allocation of electricity and industrial land. The StoppaGoogle campaign, initiated by the regional political party Norrlandspartiet, has been vocal in challenging what this development will mean for electricity prices, employment and regional development.

Controversy over datacentres in Sweden’s north reflect wider debate about resource extraction for the green and technological transitions, and the worry that Sweden is becoming an “electricity colony” of big tech, providing cheap, green energy while the economic benefits are realised elsewhere.

At the same time, Sweden-based researchers, such as Julia Velkova, and Jutta Haider and Malte Rödl, have argued that the sustainability of digital infrastructure cannot be reduced to carbon emissions and technological efficiency. Datacentres place high demands on electricity grids, necessitating government investment and compromising access for other industries, communities and public services. While these direct impacts of datacentres are important, so too are the downstream consequences that they overshadow, including how digital services promote climate disinformation and unsustainable mass consumption.

Sweden’s renewable energy infrastructure does not make datacentre development environmentally or politically unproblematic, but contributes to distinct tensions over who controls, benefits from and gains access to natural and public resources.

Rather than presenting Sweden as an exception to the growing politicisation of datacentres, we should recognise how these conflicts emerge differently in different places, shaped by their histories, infrastructures and political economies.
James White and Nora Söderberg
Department of Technology and Society, Lund University

item.title: If Trump, Xi and Putin are carving up the pudding, who gets the sixpence? | Letters

Rafael Behr (Trump, Xi and Putin have a shared vision of global power – with no place for Europe, 18 November) draws parallels between the Shenzhen summit and Winston Churchill, Joseph Stalin and Franklin D Roosevelt meeting at Yalta. I see it as bringing us a step closer to George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four, in which the world is divided into three superstates: Oceania, Eurasia and Eastasia.

We already have the surveillance in the form of CCTV, facial-recognition technology and email trawling. Daily we witness the rewriting of history. We could be sleepwalking into a situation from which we will be unable to escape.

The scale of bird declines in the UK is impossible to ignore, and songbirds are among the worst affected. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs’ wild bird indicators show that nearly 70% of farmland songbird species have declined since 1970. Woodland songbirds are faring little better, with more than 30% of species in decline. Unfortunately, none of this comes as a surprise. Decades of monitoring by scientists and dedicated volunteers have shown that our wild birds are in trouble. Yet successive governments have failed to act with the urgency needed to halt these declines.

item.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s EU intentions: undogmatic consensus building is a sensible strategy | Editorial
item.description:
On treacherous political terrain, the government is right to want to proceed with caution and at a pace of its own choosing

During the 1980s and 90s, the French president of the European Commission, Jacques Delors, consciously pursued deeper EU integration via a gradualist approach that sought to minimise confrontation. Rather than focusing on ambitious end-goals, risking a showdown with some member states, Delors calculated that taking steps such as the creation of the internal market, in 1993, would eventually generate the momentum to go further. One thing would lead to another, in a logic of deeper union.

Mindful of the unique capacity of the Brexit debate to divide and polarise, Andy Burnham appears, for the time being, to be adopting a version of this strategy. On Friday, the prime minister rightly hailed the signing of a reset deal with the EU on food exports, emissions trading and youth mobility as a “good day” for the UK. He then reiterated that further discussion was needed on finding the right long-term relationship with Brussels.

item.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: a just transition needs more than fine words | Editorial
item.description:
Petrostates blocked ambition while wealthy nations withheld cash support. The climate crisis demands the next UN summit turns promises into action

In a negotiation the maxim is usually that no deal is better than a bad deal. But the failure of Cop31 in Turkey to get a climate pact – the first time this has happened in 17 years – should not be an excuse for leaving the planet with the damaging status quo. A hard bargain needs a credible route to agreement: by making commitments, seeking concessions and getting others to reciprocate. This did not happen at the weekend.

Responsibility for the breakdown lay principally with petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels and wealthy nations that are unwilling to finance it properly. With the US absent, the EU was foremost among the latter. European governments’ objection to fossil-fuel backsliding by a Saudi-Russian coalition was right, but they were wrong to rule out fresh EU funding for developing countries’ climate action. Despite their reservations, others – notably China and the African group – were prepared to accept a flawed package to keep multilateralism alive.

item.title: Connecting with Britain’s unsung carers has allowed me to feel a deep compassion for my younger self | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
item.description:
Looking after my brother when I was a child was challenging and life-affirming. Now we need to give the next generation of carers proper support

As the years have passed, I have often observed that caring for another person is a responsibility that few human beings completely escape. “Hardly anyone gets off scot-free in this life,” I recently said to a friend, as we discussed our various loved ones and their care needs, the worry and the responsibilities. Whether it’s our children, siblings, friends or parents, some sort of care work is usually required of us on our life’s journey. Illness, disability, mental health issues, ageing, accidents and other vulnerabilities inevitably touch our lives.

There are 5.8 million unpaid carers in the UK, but I suspect there are far more who don’t identify as such, yet regularly care for loved ones or neighbours by helping with bills, shopping, appointments or more personal tasks. If you stood in a busy street in any town or city and stopped a passerby to ask them about the care they’ve given, or indeed the care they have received, many people would have a story to tell.

item.title: Monday briefing: What could Andy Burnham’s reset mean for the UK?
item.description:
In today’s newsletter: The prime minister has reopened the debate over a future relationship with a changed EU – as the bloc faces the rise of the far right, a protectionist economic agenda and growing defence ambitions

Good morning. Nobody really wants to think about Brexit any more, save for the original Brexiters, who seem delighted that Andy Burnham’s “reset” with the EU has given them an excuse to get the old gang back together. But arguments about whether the UK should rejoin the EU will reignite in parliament this week, as Burnham briefs MPs on the deal he agreed on Friday.

That deal wasn’t so much a victory as the culmination of Keir Starmer’s incrementalist approach to UK-EU relations. Its core agreements haven’t been ratified by member states yet, and the EU won’t sign them off until Britain resolves a dispute over tuition fees for European students. Burnham is apparently “determined” to take the UK back into the EU, but don’t expect any progress on that before the next general election.

Cop31 | The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal that “failed to meet the moment” in a dramatic finish to the UN talks in Turkey. The proposed deal failed to endorse a away from fossil fuels that more than 130 countries demanded.

The warning came as the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons concluded without an agreement on an instrument for regulating autonomous weapons.

item.title: How can we explain psychosomatic illnesses?
item.description:
Emotions play a significant part in physical symptoms – but not in the way people often imagine

When Diego started seeing bright flashing lights in his field of vision and felt his legs go weak, he thought he knew immediately what was happening. His mother had a stroke in her 60s, and although Diego was active and (unlike his mother) didn’t smoke, he had always expected that the same would happen to him. So it was a huge relief to be told – after seeing a stroke specialist and having a brain scan – that he had not had a stroke at all. Unfortunately the relief was short-lived. The visual disturbances and the weakness were real and debilitating. If this wasn’t a stroke, what was it?

Some illnesses aren’t caused by disease or damage, but arise when the coordinated functioning of the body goes awry. In a percentage of these cases a person’s psychological health is an important element in their symptoms. Intuitively this seems mysterious. We are accustomed to thinking about physical symptoms as being caused by physical events; viruses, inflammation, bleeding. How can something as intangible as a thought have any impact on something as physical as a leg? How can the mind make us ill?

item.title: The life, death and improbable rebirth of LA’s most beloved diner

For decades, it served pancakes, hash browns and steaks to hungry Angelenos. Then came closure, and a city mourned – but now the Original Pantry is back

Sometimes, an old-school American diner is just a diner. And sometimes, like the Original Pantry in downtown Los Angeles, it feels like the heart and soul of a city, a bellwether of good times and bad.

For decades it was famous for never closing. Located in a low-slung shotgun building on a busy corner, it fed politicians, movie stars, students, criminals and street bums around the clock, seven days a week. The doors had no locks, because the place had no need for them. The portions were huge, the prices dirt cheap, and many of the servers, in bow ties and white shirts, looked like extras from a Harold Lloyd two-reeler.
