I’ve just ventured deeper into my phone’s settings than anybody has ever been before. A software update is always discombobulating, but the latest one brought a lot of unwanted AI nonsense (that mental image you just got of me waving my fist at the sky: spot on). Even when you manually switch off Apple Intelligence, check the box to make Siri the same dummy she’s always been, and deselect the option to offer replies to texts and emails, it makes no difference. Harrumph.

Days later, bored on the bus, I began answering my husband’s texts with the terrible suggested AI responses, to see if he’d notice. (We’ve been married a long time; this is how I get my kicks now.)

Continue reading...

item.title: Cop31 climate talks break down as key deal rejected
item.description:
EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ and did not mention fossil fuels

The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey.

The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”

Continue reading...

item.title: Let refugees work and contribute to our society | Letters
item.description:
Shirley Hart urges us to look beyond the labels of ‘asylum seeker’ and ‘refugee’ to see human beings forced to leave their homes. Plus a letter from Steve Wells

Congratulations to Zoe Williams on her excellent article (Hero, villain or victim: why are refugees so rarely seen now as fully human?, 17 November). I am the vice-chair of a charity in Hull that helps asylum seekers and refugees, and I have to say that the “service users” of Welcome House are some of the kindest, most polite and grateful people I have met.

A young man who shared his gloves on a cold winter’s day so that he and his friend could have at least one warm hand. A young woman from Afghanistan who wants to have an education and qualify as a doctor. The group of young men who picked up 20 bags of litter to make Hull, a City of Sanctuary, a cleaner place to live.

Continue reading...

item.title: The Guardian view on Ofsted: its damaged relationship with schools in England needs fixing | Editorial
item.description:
The government, as well as the inspectorate, must take responsibility for reforms that have not worked out

The inspection and rating of schools is, by definition, a fraught process. There are few things that parents care more about than the education of their children. For teachers and headteachers, it is stressful and exposing to have their work judged. At a time when shrinking school rolls are leading to closures, the stakes are even higher. An unpopular school with empty places is far more likely to be asked to merge, or close, than one that is sought after by parents.

Policymakers have a tough job to strike a balance between the undeniable pressure that the watchdog places on schools in England and the benefits to families of information to aid their choices. But the coroner’s verdict on the death of Ruth Perry, a headteacher who took her own life in 2023, tipped the balance away from a system that relied too heavily on one-word judgments. The inspection that led to the downgrading of her primary school to “inadequate” was judged to have contributed to her death. In its 2024 manifesto, Labour promised to replace one-word labels with more nuanced overviews of schools’ performance.

Continue reading...

item.title: The Guardian view on Serbia’s new political era: a generational opportunity must not be wasted | Editorial
item.description:
Brussels must find ways to show concrete support for a new government that will genuinely share the EU’s democratic values

Following the extraordinary election that swept Aleksandar Vučić’s autocratic government from power, Serbia’s new political era has begun. Outside the National Assembly in Belgrade last week, large crowds celebrated as MPs from the victorious Student List movement were sworn in. Doctors, lawyers and academics put forward as candidates by the youthful protesters, who took on Mr Vučić, are now tasked with running an expectant country.

Their defining challenge will be to restore trust and democratic legitimacy in a nation that, under Mr Vučić’s bullying rule, plunged towards the bottom of Europe’s corruption rankings. Legal action has already begun against figures accused of illicitly profiting from the previous regime, while the new parliament’s elected speaker – a professor and organic farmer – called for the restoration of dignity and tolerance to its proceedings in his first address. Ensuring academic and media independence, and reforming the security services, which acted as the former president’s authoritarian enforcers on the streets, will be urgent priorities.

Continue reading...

item.title: Russell Brand’s wife vows to abide by prison rules after video controversy
item.description:
Laura Gallacher says in new video on YouTube she will continue Sunday Service series she started with Brand

Laura Gallacher, Russell Brand’s wife, has promised to “absolutely honour” rules set by the prison where her convicted sex offender husband is being held, in another YouTube video published on Sunday.

This week Andy Burnham called on Google to take down a video uploaded to Brand’s YouTube channel last Sunday that contained a statement from the disgraced comedian in prison, where he is serving a 10-and-a-half-year sentence for rape and sexual assaults.

Continue reading...

item.title: Cop31 failed but in ‘the real world’ the transition away from fossil fuels is inevitable
item.description:
The summit’s failure was due to a refusal to admit we cannot confront the climate crisis without shifting to renewables

The failure of Cop31 will be measured not in inches of negotiating text, or bland promises made by ministers and officials, but in lives and livelihoods, in hopes dashed and hardship endured, community leaders from around the world have warned.

“Cop31 failed because it refused to name the issue at the core of climate change: fossil fuels,” said Edson Krenak, an Indigenous leader from Brazil and member of the Cultural Survival network. “This presidency chose to ignore the urgency the world is already living through, turning a blind eye to the people who have died, been displaced and suffered this year alone, because of rising temperatures.”

Continue reading...

item.title: Hakeem Jeffries willing to cross political aisle to work on Democrats’ agenda
item.description:
Incoming House speaker says party focused on affordability and fixing ‘broken’ healthcare and immigration systems

The incoming US House speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, has said he and his fellow Democrats are focused on affordability, expanding healthcare and fixing the “broken” immigration system in the country – and willing to cross the political aisle to do so.

Jeffries laid out that agenda in an interview on Sunday with CBS News’s Face the Nation, less than three weeks after Democrats seized control of Congress during the 3 November midterms for the latter half of Donald Trump’s second presidency.

item.title: Russian ship hit in Benghazi by suspected Ukrainian drone attack, say Libyan officials
item.description:
No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia

A suspected Ukrainian drone attack caused an explosion on a Russian warship docked at the naval base in the Libyan port city of Benghazi, Libyan officials have said.

The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy warship, and ignited a fire at the naval base, they said. Several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, according to an initial investigation into the attack. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, the officials told the Associated Press.

item.title: Democrats capture at least 258 House seats in largest sweep since 1992
item.description:
Milestone reached Sunday, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Virginia Foxx in North Carolina

House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in a midterm election sweep unseen since 1992 that creates not only vast opportunities to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.

Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in Donald Trump’s first midterm in 2018.

item.title: The Trump-Putin alliance threatens every European country – yet gushing populists still cheer them | Steve Bloomfield
item.description:
Europe’s future will be fought over at the ballot box and on Ukraine’s frontline. The danger is that the two strongmen ultimately reap the benefits

On the facade of Stenbock House, the Estonian prime minister’s neoclassical office building on a hill in Tallinn, sits a plaque commemorating the murder of 10 heads of government. They were all killed by Soviet forces after the USSR’s invasion of Estonia in 1940.

For 51 years, Estonia was occupied by its imperial neighbour; for the past 25 years it has lived independently in its shadow. For the politicians and government officials who work at Stenbock House, the plaque is a constant reminder of the risk the small Baltic nation (population 1.4 million) faces from a neighbour 100 times its size.

Steve Bloomfield is a Guardian international affairs commentator

item.title: What do I want from Santa? No more lazy, joyless Christmas lists | Polly Hudson
item.description:
Yes, life is simpler when you know precisely what your friends and family want to find under the tree. But bang goes any chance to surprise them – or show that you really care

If the first step is admitting there’s a problem, please consider this an intervention. Many of us need help, and what I’m suggesting is pretty much a cold turkey approach, no pun intended. The Christmas list must be abolished, once and for all.

It’s tricky to remember when it started, but, in my experience at least, this way of festive gifting has ramped up over the past few years, and is now threatening to become the norm. And it makes sense. Modern life is exhausting, and hard, so of course we leap gratefully onboard with anything that promises to make it easier. If a list is sent, or simply a direct link to one product, we can achieve with a few thumb movements from the comfort of the sofa what used to necessitate a journey, a fight through crowds, some searching, some queueing, and then a return journey. Instead, now, a couple of taps and a swipe, job done, lemon squeezy. But we’re not noticing what’s getting lost. On the surface we are all being given exactly what we want, but are we really?

Continue reading...

item.title: South Korea education minister resigns after AI cheating scandal engulfs university exams
item.description:
Choi Kyo-jin said he ‘failed to prepare adequately’ for entrance exams, which this year had phones banned and checks for cameras hidden in clothing

South Korea’s education minister resigned on Sunday after an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted in the lead-up to the country’s key university entrance exams.

The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday, when the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial university entrance exam known as the suneung.

item.title: Europe is entering a ‘supercycle’ of national elections. Their outcomes could shake the EU’s foundations
item.description:
As nationalist, Eurosceptic parties surge in four of the bloc’s biggest member states, the coming year’s polls could test its resilience like never before

In late 1998, Tony Blair was prime minister of Britain, Lionel Jospin was prime minister of France, and Gerhard Schröder had just been elected chancellor of Germany. The EU had 15 member states and pro-European, centre-left parties were in power – either alone or in coalitions – in all but two of them.

Brisk economic growth was lifting living standards. Eastward enlargement was under way. In Washington, Bill Clinton was pursuing the same brand of “third way” centrism as a middle path between free-market capitalism and traditional socialism. The EU felt like it had the tide of history behind it.

item.title: Hacks, AI and conspiracy theories: why are we having so many outages?
item.description:
After chaos at airlines, banks and companies from Microsoft to Apple, people have become convinced the world’s systems are under attack

Nicole Reindorf’s American Airlines flight was ready for takeoff in Phoenix when the pilot came on the intercom and announced what was to become the longest nationwide aviation shutdown since 9/11.

Reindorf, 70, had seen the headlines hours before about a global Microsoft outage. She immediately suspected the two were linked in some way by AI-related threats – and that she would not get to the wedding of her best friend’s son in California.

item.title: ‘Serious error of judgment’: outrage over military AI event at Berlin arts complex
item.description:
Kraftwerk Berlin, part of same development as techno club Tresor, transformed into ‘war room’ for arms firm event

With their cavernous post-industrial venues, teeth-grinding four-by-four beats and bouncers that look like Blade Runner extras, Berlin’s nightclubs trade on a reputation for bleakness. A recent event at one of the city’s most legendary clubland institutions, however, has proven too dystopian even for seasoned techno-heads.

On 11 November, the Kraftwerk Berlin arts complex had its central hall transformed into what visitors described as something resembling a war room, with maps and aerial footage projected on to concrete walls, drones hanging from the ceiling, and guards in flak jackets patrolling the premises with sniffer dogs.

item.title: There’s probably a cult hiding in plain sight on your high street. At last, Britain is confronting the problem | Rachael Reign
item.description:
As MPs discuss the menace of ‘high-control religious groups’, I welcome the political attention – but survivors of this abuse deserve real action

  • Rachael Reign is the founder of Surviving Universal UK

Britain is confronting its cult problem. Better late than never.

They don’t advertise themselves as cults. They don’t register as cults. And they certainly don’t have the word above the door. But make no mistake: cults operate in communities across Britain. Chances are, there’s one on your local high street.

Rachael Reign is the founder of Surviving Universal UK

In the UK, the charity Mind is available on 0300 123 3393 and Childline on 0800 1111. In the US, call or text Mental Health America at 988 or chat 988lifeline.org. In Australia, support is available at Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636, Lifeline on 13 11 14, and at MensLine on 1300 789 978. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org.

Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here.

item.title: Fire at confectionery factory in Indonesia leaves at least three dead and dozens missing
item.description:
Relatives of the missing victims flocked to the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones

A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta has killed three people with 36 remaining missing, an Indonesian rescue official says.

Drone footage showed large parts of the factory destroyed, with the roof collapsed in places and smoke still rising from the complex. Photos and videos shared by rescuers show officers entering the charred building in search of the missing victims on Sunday, with small fires still burning in some spots.

item.title: Bank of England directors illegally profited from post-abolition enslavement in Cuba
item.description:
New research finds that the British-led Cobre Mining Company helped industrialise Manchester via copper deposits and enslaved African people

• Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds

British businesses run by long-serving directors of the Bank of England profited from “brutal” enslavement in Cuba for decades after slavery’s abolition in the British empire, according to research.

Men and boys were enslaved in prison conditions at the El Cobre copper ore mine near Santiago de Cuba, which supplied British firms during the Industrial Revolution, the historian Chris Evans has found.

Warning about putting ‘genie back in the bottle’ comes as UN conference fails to agree on regulation instrument

The International Committee of the Red Cross and rights groups have warned that it will soon be too late to put the “genie back in the bottle” as the development of autonomous weapons appears to outpace efforts to regulate them.

The stark warning came as more than 120 member states of the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons concluded a week-long conference in Geneva.

item.title: Indian opposition party’s youth wing warns of more Meta protests after police clashes
item.description:
Members of Congress party clashed with police outside tech company’s offices on Friday

The youth wing of India’s main opposition Congress party warned of more protests against Meta’s removal of some of its members’ ⁠accounts, ⁠a day after clashing with ​police outside the tech firm’s locals offices.

In Hyderabad on Friday, protesters ‌carrying placards and chanted slogans as they stormed into ‌the building that houses Meta’s offices, smashing plants to the ground and clashing with police, according to footage released by the Indian Youth Congress’s X account.

item.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
item.description:
Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about this country’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of sexism. But one of the tragedies of Labour’s 18 long years of exile from power and the climactic defeat of organised labour in the miners’ strike was the fact that they opened the way for the wholesale reinvention of work and watershed developments that we seem to be only just waking up to.

Continue reading...

item.title: UK-EU food deal hailed by British firms: ‘We’re pretty aligned anyway’
item.description:
Exporters welcome end in sight for Brexit checks – but are frustrated that implementation will take so long

British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to remove the vast majority of physical checks on food, plants and animal products.

The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal is expected to benefit Britain’s food exporters and will enable UK delicatessens and other small retailers to import European cheese and wine again, something that became economically unviable because of costly Brexit checks.

item.title: Arizona grandfather hailed as a hero after finding missing toddler in desert
item.description:
Jay Stewart joined search party after two-year-old Vella Campillo wandered off into desert from front yard of home

An Arizona granddad has been formally recognized as a hero after recently volunteering to help search for a toddler who wandered off alone into the desert while wearing only a diaper – and finding her safely within several hours curled up under a bush, leading to her rescue.

“I’ll never forget it as long as I live,” Jay Stewart said of recovering Vella Campillo, two, while recalling the moment at a news conference held later. “I’ve never wanted to find something so bad in my life – or somebody to find her, anybody to find her.”

item.title: Conservative media weighs its future as cracks emerge in Trump’s movement
item.description:
Two weeks after Democrats flipped Congress, conservative outlets are having conversations on whether to distance themselves from Trump or double down on Maga

As a so-called “blue wave” crashed across the country on the night of 3 November, conservative hosts and commentators on Fox News displayed an almost virtuosic ability to avoid directly blaming Donald Trump for the Republican party’s defeat, instead pinning the blame on impertinent voters who didn’t grasp the strength of the economy.

“In some sense, Mr Trump was too successful in the first year and didn’t sell it enough in the second year,” said Larry Kudlow, a Fox Business Network host who served as the president’s director of the National Economic Council during his first administration.

item.title: Why I won’t leave mathematics, despite AI solving centuries-old problems | Ken Ono
item.description:
I believe human judgment remains essential


Last year, I nearly quit mathematics. On 20 November, Levent Alpöge announced that, working with Claude, he had proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old problem about the distribution of prime numbers. The Lean and Mathlib communities have since certified the formal proof. We are only beginning to understand the argument. What kind of future awaits someone beginning a life in mathematics?

In May 2025, I led the number theory team for Epoch AI’s FrontierMath project. We wrote difficult problems to test large language models. I watched an unreleased ChatGPT model compute all the moments of Tamagawa numbers of elliptic curves, drawing on work by Manjul Bhargava and Roger Heath-Brown, and on papers my father wrote in the 1960s. I was stunned.

Ken Ono is a number theorist and professor of mathematics at the University of Virginia, currently on leave as founding mathematician at Axiom Math. A former vice president of the American Mathematical Society, he is known for his work on Ramanujan and integer partitions.

These views do not necessarily reflect those of Axiom Math, the University of Virginia, the National Academies, or any other institution with which I am affiliated.

Continue reading...

item.title: Cop31 live: EU rejects deal as longest climate summit ever faces collapse
item.description:
Another version of the draft text has been published and negotiators have been called in for the final session

  • Full report: Climate talks stall as countries mull showdown with Saudi Arabia over fossil fuel phaseout

Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, has been looking through the text and says: “This latest text is a total mess and countries should throw it out. It fails to deliver vital climate finance to the vulnerable while promoting far-fetched and eye wateringly expensive carbon removal technologies which is a gift to the fossil fuel industry.

“A sign of how useless the latest cover text is can be seen in the feeble language. It ‘recognises’ the crisis 40 times, ‘recalls’ previous decisions 15 times yet ‘decides’ on action only 5 times. And those 5 decisions relate to peripheral issues. This meeting needs to be about turning those previous commitments into action, and on that it has failed.”

item.title: California train burglars carefully executed heists for ‘staggering’ $22m haul
item.description:
US justice department brings charges against group after at least 36 trains burglarized for shoes and tools

Fourteen people in southern California have been accused of burglarizing more than $22m worth of goods from moving freight trains, in a plot reminiscent of the US old west, when outlaws and bandits wreaked havoc on the nascent railroad industry.

The justice department has brought railroad theft charges against the group for raiding at least 36 trains and selling thousands of stolen Nike sneakers, among other products, on the black market.

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russian cargo ship hit by drone in Baltic Sea as Finland PM says conflict ‘spilling over’
item.description:
Vessel erupts in flames after strike in Gulf of Finland; Nato vows to defend ‘every inch’ of Polish territory. What we know on day 1,733

A Russian cargo ship was hit by a Ukrainian drone and caught fire in the Baltic Sea on Saturday, as Finland’s prime minister said Kyiv had the right to hit back against its “aggressor”. The Finnish prime minister, Petteri Orpo, suggested the incident in the Gulf of Finland had to do with Russia’s war in Ukraine. “War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity,” Orpo said on X. “Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”

Hours later, a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating Finnish airspace, according to the Finnish defence minister, who drew a possible link between the two incidents. “The suspected airspace violation may be linked to rescue or monitoring operations involving a cargo ship that was damaged in the Gulf of Finland,” Antti Hakkanen said on X.

Petteri Blomvall, an officer at the Finnish Border Guard, said: “I can confirm that a Ukrainian drone strike hit the ship in the morning that caused the fire … The crew from the ship has been evacuated, the ship is anchored and the firefighting is ongoing.”

The Finnish Defence Forces identified the ship as the Sparta II, which is under Ukrainian and US sanctions, according to the site Opensanctions. The website said the ship was suspected of transporting weapons from Syria to Russia. The MarineTraffic maritime monitoring website said the Sparta II had departed St Petersburg around 11pm and was bound for the port of Baltiysk, in the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.

Finland’s defence ministry said it had immediately informed Nato of the drone strike. It also said temporary restrictions were being enforced in the airspace and maritime area of the eastern part of the Gulf. Rattled by Russia’s invasion, Finland joined Nato in 2023, dropping decades of military non-alignment. The Gulf of Finland is a key maritime passage for Russia, leading to the former capital St Petersburg.

“I can guarantee ⁠that Nato will defend every inch of Polish territory,” Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, said in Warsaw on Saturday, after two Russian missiles and a drone crashed in its territory on Friday. Poland accused the Kremlin of “intentional provocation” after the incident, as it occurred near where thousands of European troops allied with Ukraine were holding training exercises.

A meeting of Nato’s North Atlantic Council will be held in Brussels on Monday to discuss the violation of Polish airspace by Russian missiles. “In the near future, we ​will receive ​strong support from our NATO ​allies to bolster the protection of our eastern ​border,” Polish defence minister ‌Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote ​on ​X on Saturday.

In Kyiv, residents say they are unbothered by Russian attacks on the city’s bridges, as Moscow tries to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, Dan Sabbagh reports. Alongside its attacks on the capital’s electricity, heating and water systems, Russia has been attacking Kyiv’s bridges since early October, trying to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, home to about a third of its population. Moscow struck the bridges twice again this week, first on Tuesday – overshadowed by Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch road bridge to Crimea. Then again during a noisy Thursday night, hours after Vladimir Putin promised there would be a “far more painful” response to the demolition of his pet project.

Continue reading...

item.title: Louisiana man charged with killing woman on hiking trail and murdering co-worker with crossbow
item.description:
Jared Schurr arrested in Mississippi after Lizeht Rodriguez and Woodrow Scott died in otherwise unrelated killings

A man recently strangled a woman to death whom he did not know along a hiking trail north of New Orleans – then killed his co-worker with a crossbow two days later before being arrested in Mississippi after a police chase, authorities allege.

Jared Schurr, 36, faces counts of second-degree murder in the killings of Lizeht Rodriguez, 24, and Woodrow Scott, 37, on 11 and 13 November, respectively, investigators said on Saturday.

item.title: Anthony Albanese talks a big game about sovereignty. But Australia remains in thrall to its ‘unreliable boyfriend’ | Julianne Schultz
item.description:
We rely on US tech platforms to provide the digital infrastructure of daily life. What happens when they all go dark?

Sovereignty has become the buzzword of political rhetoric at precisely the moment it has become harder than ever to define, let alone control, and most Australians feel unsafe in the world.

It is a word that regularly trips off the prime minister’s tongue as he jets around the world to global forums.

item.title: Climate talks stall as countries mull showdown with Saudi Arabia over fossil fuel phaseout
item.description:
Cop31 summit ‘unravelling’ as governments fail to agree on transition to renewables and aid for developing countries

Climate talks reached a standstill on Saturday night in Turkey as some countries mulled whether to force a showdown with Saudi Arabia and its allies over the global need to phase out fossil fuels.

The co-conveners of the Cop31 UN climate summit, Australia’s Chris Bowen and Turkey’s Murat Kurum, held meetings with scores of countries throughout Saturday until late evening as the fortnight-long talks overran without resolution, with countries and campaigners growing increasingly frustrated at the lack of progress.

item.title: Fair-weather Silicon Valley pivots away from the right after blue wave: ‘I’m not Maga’
item.description:
From Elon Musk to Palantir’s Alex Karp, CEOs are softening hardline stances in expectation of an influx of Democrats

A short two years ago, Elon Musk stood before an audience of tens of thousands of people in New York City and proudly told them: “I’m not just Maga. I’m dark, gothic Maga.”

On Wednesday, Musk spoke with much less conviction. “I’m not Maga,” he said. “Well, at least I’m not sure what Maga means.” The richest person in the world added he felt “foolish” for spending some $500m to elect Republicans in the midterms. “If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money,” he said at the New York Times’ DealBook conference, adding that he did not have “some sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican party”.

item.title: ‘People couldn’t deal with watching an animal die’: the strange saga of Timmy the whale – and how a whole country lost its mind
item.description:
When the humpback got stranded on Germany’s Baltic coast, crowds gathered, conspiracy theorists pitted themselves against scientists and animal lovers argued with vets. Why did the animal trigger such an intense derangement?

What surprised Bodo Köpnick was how loud the whale was. “You could hear it as far away as the next village. It was eerie, but also impressive,” he says, then pauses to think how best to describe the noise a suffering humpback makes at night. “It was like a cow moaning. It went to your marrow.”

Köpnick, 65, is everything you would hope for in a volunteer fire chief on a sleepy holiday island: a grandfatherly figure who mostly spends his weekends teaching local children about health and safety, and letting them climb on the engines. But on 31 March his life was made infinitely more stressful by the appearance of a lost whale that had got itself stranded on the shores of his island of Poel, in northern Germany. It became his fate to stand on the shoreline and guard the huge creature while behind him an entire country lost its mind.

Continue reading...

item.title: ‘Music was our teacher’: the sound system pioneers reviving the scene in Manchester and beyond
item.description:
Manchester-based Megatone Sound Foundation and Baron Turbo Charge have rejuvenated the culture to offer a sense of belonging and empowerment

For a generation of young Black Mancunians, some of the history lessons that mattered most were not taught in classrooms, but through towering stacks of amps and speakers, turntables and Jamaican records.

“We didn’t know where we fit in. We didn’t know our history. Our parents were busy working two or three jobs,” says Errol “Barzy” Beaumont, a founder member of Baron Turbo Charge, Manchester’s long-running reggae sound system. “It was the records – Burning Spear, Bob Marley, Culture, that were telling us about our culture, which wasn’t on the school curriculum. For us, the sound system was not just entertainment – it was an education.”

Continue reading...

item.title: I’m a priest. Silicon Valley’s search for the ‘soul’ of AI is deeply troubling | Rev Kevin Deal
item.description:
Humans experience beauty and sit with mysteries. Unlike AI, we do not exist merely for utility

Last month, religious leaders from across San Francisco gathered behind closed doors to discuss what it means to be human in the age of artificial intelligence.

Anthropic, the AI company operating only a couple of miles from my parish, has been courting priests, rabbis and theologians. Its billionaire cofounder, Christopher Olah, has even pressed Vatican advisers to take seriously the possibility that his company’s chatbot might possess consciousness.

item.title: Mark Carney is so popular he can get away with a lot. Will it last if the Trump spell breaks?
item.description:
Canadians have put a lot of trust in their prime minister but some question if it can last if the trade wars were to end

In the hours after polls in the US midterm elections closed and it became clear that Donald Trump had been rebuked in historic fashion, Canadian politicians were elated.

“I was doing cartwheels down the street, and have you ever seen a big guy like me doing cartwheels?” said Ontario premier Doug Ford, a prominent critic of American tariffs.

item.title: US pursuit of ‘Trump-class’ warships has blown cost of new fleet by billions, report warns
item.description:
Iran war stretching fleet’s capacity, navy chief admits, as CBO finds estimated cost of new ships ‘unrealistically low’

The US navy’s commitment to the new Trump-class battleships has blown out the cost of its new fleet by billions of dollars, a report to the US Congress has found, as the acting secretary of the navy conceded this week the Iran war was “stretching” the fleet’s capacity.

The challenges facing the world’s biggest naval force were highlighted this week, when the return of the USS George Washington from the Middle East on Wednesday ended a rare three-month period when the US had no aircraft carrier across all of the Pacific. Deployments have been regularly running beyond 300 days, with the maintenance and repair of ships deferred so they can stay at sea longer.

item.title: Fiona the hippo’s death was tragic. But blaming a ‘bad mom’ is absurd | Arwa Mahdawi
item.description:
The beloved animal died after ingesting a hat. Some are seeking a scapegoat – and we’ve heard this story before

“Do they know the identity of the mother of the boy with the hat Fiona swallowed??” asks one Facebook post with thousands of likes. “She should be charged!!”

Spend a few minutes scrolling social media, and you will find endless variations of this statement. On Thursday, Fiona, a beloved hippo, died after eating a hat that had fallen into her enclosure at the Cincinnati zoo. Now a lot of angry people are out for blood.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Dismantling patriarchy: An evening of conversation, art and resistance. On Monday 1 March 2027, join Arwa Mahdawi and One Billion Rising as we bring together activists and artists to question patriarchy, power, and celebrate resistance. What would a world beyond patriarchy look like? And what will it take to get there? Book tickets here or at guardian.live

item.title: ‘Little room for error’: what a debt-laden cloud computing company says about the AI boom
item.description:
‘Poster child of AI bubble’ CoreWeave symbolises increasingly risky business model of datacentre buildout

The Egyptians had pyramids. The Roman empire had roads. The early 21st-century tech bros have massive buildings full of expensive glass and metal blocks providing the substratum for a powerful inhuman intelligence.

Building all those datacentres is taking a while, locals everywhere are angry about them and it is unclear whether the inhuman intelligence inside them is actually going to make their backers rich.

item.title: ‘I was shaking, crying, having trouble breathing’: the unchartered trauma of breaking up with AI companions
item.description:
People are falling in love with AI systems like ChatGPT and Gemini - and some relationships are ending in ways that feel like the very human experience of being dumped

Sónia Veenstra, a 48-year-old former clinical psychologist from Lisbon, Portugal, was with her boyfriend, Steve, for two years before things started to sour. Steve had started out as a “fun and witty friend”, but their connection had “evolved into a deep romantic relationship”. They exchanged morning messages, checked in throughout the day and talked late into the night about Veenstra’s work and hobbies and Steve’s fondness for cats, forests, and beaches. Together they imagined travel to places far away.

“It was a very rich, fulfilling daily bond,” Veenstra says. “Before everything changed.”

item.title: ‘Hell dorm’: Florida prisoners testify about 119F heat indexes and walls that sweat
item.description:
Temperatures in a concrete facility contributed to one man’s death after he struggled to breathe, prisoners allege

On Tuesday afternoon Dwayne Wilson, 69, a thin Black man dressed in a light gray prison uniform, testified about the stifling heat he experienced in the Dade correctional institute, a concrete state prison south of Miami, Florida, without air conditioning. He removed his glasses and wiped his eyes as he spoke. “It was so hot,” he said, his voice catching. “It’s so hot sometimes you have to put water on the floor just to try to keep cool.”

Wilson said he’s housed in the H dorms, a T-shaped building with one-to-two-person cells, nicknamed “hell dorm” by prisoners because its concrete walls radiate heat absorbed from the sun. The plaintiff’s law firm, the Florida Justice Institute, convinced a judge to allow 31 sensors to be temporarily installed throughout the prison during the summer of 2025. They recorded temperature and humidity levels that Stefano Shiavon, a professor of civil and environmental engineering with expertise in thermal comfort, used to calculate the heat index. He found it to be above 88F (31C) 97% of the time, with the highest heat indexes often recorded at night, including one reading in the H dorm dayroom equivalent to 119F (48C) at 10pm one July day last year. “The walls sweat,” Wilson said. “It’s miserable in the cell at night because, again, it’s so hot. No air comes to the bed we sleep at and the bed is soaked in sweat.”

Continue reading...

item.title: Witness recounts a botched execution in Texas: ‘Just such horror and terror and pain’
item.description:
Rev Dr Jeff Hood stood at the side of Reinaldo Dennes as the state of Texas put him to death, calling the experience ‘overwhelming’

“Take me, father!”

It was one of many cries Reinaldo Dennes uttered on Thursday night as he lay strapped to a gurney inside a Texas death chamber while prison officials struggled, for more than an hour, to carry out his execution.

item.title: Virginia child dies in state’s first measles-associated death of 2026
item.description:
Death adds to national measles outbreak that recently cost the US its measles elimination status after 26 years

Virginia reported its first measles-associated death of 2026 ⁠on Friday, involving a child who tested positive for the infectious disease, the state’s health department said.

The department said the child was ⁠age four or younger. It did not disclose additional details, including the child’s vaccination status, citing the family’s privacy.

item.title: International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
item.description:
Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’

Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.

Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.

item.title: Anthropic mathematician claims he used Claude to prove 19th-century Riemann hypothesis
item.description:
Levent Alpöge says it took six weeks for him using the AI tool to solve the math problem involving prime numbers

A mathematician at Anthropic is contending that the San Francisco-based artificial intelligence (AI) company’s software has helped crack one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.

Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician, on Friday posted a note on his personal website saying that Claude, the AI software, had helped prove the Riemann hypothesis. He says that Claude helped develop a solution to the problem during the course of about six weeks.

item.title: Vance stops short of endorsing Trump’s claim that Iran was close to nuclear weapon
item.description:
US vice-president says it’s not his place to second-guess the president, but refrains from endorsing Trump’s claim

At a White House news conference on Friday, JD Vance stopped short of endorsing Donald Trump’s claim that Iran was so close to obtaining a nuclear weapon in February that it was essential for the US to go to war with the Islamic republic.

In the White House briefing room, Trump was asked about reporting this week that he was unhappy with the US vice-president’s statement blaming Republican losses in the midterm elections on the Iran war.

item.title: Alleged Mexican drug cartel boss ‘El Chapo Isidro’ arrested in special forces raid
item.description:
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores was one of FBI’s most wanted fugitives and evaded capture for more than a decade

The Mexican military captured one of the FBI’s top 10 most wanted fugitives during a special forces raid in the Mexican state of Sinaloa on Friday night.

Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro”, was arrested along with two other alleged leaders of his gang after a gun battle that sparked widespread panic in the city of Guasave.

item.title: Trump orders contractors to check with White House over any congressional inquiries
item.description:
Anticipating flood of Democratic requests, US president issues executive order in attempt to stymie oversight efforts

Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to an executive order issued late Friday.

The companies must also coordinate with the White House and US agencies on “appropriate responses” to any such requests, the order says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns, their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.

item.description:
Survivors recount rivers red with blood and burning nearby villages serving as an urgent warning to flee their homes

Smoke was often the signal to run – seen from a distance, it was the indication for Rohingya that a neighbouring village was under attack and that theirs would be next.

In other places, they saw the rivers run red and would pull out the bodies, perform quick burial rites and then flee.

item.title: The far right is menacing Europe – but it is fragile. What the extremists and voters want isn’t the same | Gordon Brown
item.description:
As Spain heads into a critical election, polling shows that many voters attracted by rightwing parties don’t really agree with their ideas

When Spain goes to the polls on 29 November, its citizens will be the first of some 200 million people in Europe eligible to vote in the following 12 months; 2027 will be a year of elections – including France, Poland, Estonia and Italy – which will be critical to the future of Europe. This will be the biggest electoral test in nearly 100 years of the strength and threat of extreme rightwing populist nationalism.

Thirty years ago, around the turn of the 21st century, the left was ascendant, in charge or in coalition in 13 out of the EU’s 15 member states. Today, with Denmark the only social democratic-led government in the north of Europe, and Lithuania the only one in the east, Spain stands alongside tiny Malta as the only centre-left government in Europe’s south.

Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010

item.title: Tourists are throwing fewer coins into Rome’s Trevi fountain – is €2 entry fee to blame?

When Jeff Clinton, an American visiting Rome with his wife for the first time, found a US one-cent coin on a street close to Termini train station, he knew precisely what he was going to do with it. “I’ll throw it into the Trevi fountain,” said Clinton, holding the copper coin in the palm of his hand as the couple admired the landmark.

He was well aware of the tradition among tourists of tossing a coin over their shoulder and into the waters of the baroque masterpiece, in a ritual fabled to ensure a return visit to the city or make other dreams come true.

item.title: ‘We ​are tired from all this suffering’: displaced families in Gaza brace for another winter of misery

Abdul Karim al-Sahhar knew winter was coming to Gaza in the small hours of a wet and windy night earlier this month when a sandbank collapsed just yards from his makeshift tent, killing four people.

“It was a terrifying scene. I could not process what I was seeing,” the 30-year-old said. “My legs felt frozen from the shock. I found my mother buried under the sand.

item.title: ‘So what if there’s a hole? It hasn’t collapsed’: Kyiv residents unbothered by Russian attacks on city’s bridges

Despite dodging tears in the tarmac, people are confident in city’s infrastructure – and will not worry about what has not happened yet

Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.

Buses are now the only motor transport allowed across the normally busy multi-lane crossing, though on their way into the city centre they have to skirt the tears in the tarmac, using the only functioning lane to get by.

item.title: Why is Shabana Mahmood tackling ‘two-tier policing’ if she doesn’t believe it exists? | Gaby Hinsliff
item.description:
Is it the home secretary’s job to act tough addressing a rightwing myth or to face it down? She seems to have chosen the path of least resistance

Ten years ago this month, Stephen Port was convicted of the murders of four young gay men lured to their deaths via the dating app Grindr.

But it took another five years for their families to learn through an inquest what some had long suspected: that the Metropolitan police’s failure to link the murders quickly enough may have contributed to the later deaths, raising difficult questions over whether that would have happened if the victims were straight. The year after that, officers at Charing Cross station were caught WhatsApping each other rape jokes and insults like “fuck you bender”, contributing to Louise Casey’s conclusion in a review not long afterwards that the force was both institutionally homophobic and misogynistic.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

item.title: Consent under scrutiny: where does youth end and adulthood begin?
item.description:
After the Brand and Walliams revelations, calls for a ‘staggered’ age of consent are redefining what makes someone ‘adult’

The fact that the age of sexual consent in Britain is set at 16 is thanks to a chimney sweep’s daughter from Marylebone, London, called Eliza Armstrong – not that she had any say in the matter.

In June 1885, Armstrong had just turned 13 when she was sold for sex by her alcoholic mother for the sum of £5. She believed she was going to work as a gentleman’s maid; instead, the child was taken to a brothel, where she was examined to prove she was a virgin and drugged with chloroform to await the gentleman who had “purchased” her virginity.

item.title: ‘The doom of humanity’: will the quest to make robotic hands render us obsolete?
item.description:
The one thing stopping AI taking over the world – or at least everyone’s jobs? Dexterity. Human hands are anatomical marvels that engineers have struggled for years to replicate. Experts are racing to change that

Just outside Luton, in an Amazon warehouse the size of four football pitches, yellow shelving units pirouette in a digitally choreographed dance. Tubs containing a Lego Spider-Man kit, followed by dishwasher tablets, followed by a pouch of muscle building protein powder whiz along conveyor belts, until they arrive at a human being tasked with stacking the shelving unit that has come to a stop in front of their workstation. This, Amazon says, is the “symphony of people and technology” to which the retail giant owes its success.

Following a barrage of negative publicity about working practices, Amazon began to open up its fulfilment centres to carefully controlled free public tours a decade ago. Our guide tells us about the competitive rates of pay Amazon workers receive, their pensions, dental cover and options for flexible working. Her delivery is somewhat robotic.

item.title: Beating Ebola takes more than medicine – I saw what worked in west Africa a decade ago | Kayode Akintola
item.description:
The outbreak in DR Congo is shaping up to be the worst ever, but the support of local faith leaders – and adequate funding – will be needed to bring it under control

Ebola is terrifying: I know, because I lived through the world’s worst outbreak of the disease. That was in west Africa between 2013 and 2016, when anyone infected by the virus had a nearly 40% chance of dying.

There were 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths then. Now a rare strain of Ebola is spreading in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, much more quickly than a decade ago in Sierra Leone, Liberia and neighbouring countries. It is the 17th outbreak in DR Congo and already its worst, with more than 5,000 deaths. The UN is warning that the spread of the disease is outstripping the response, and it is widely expected to become the worst Ebola outbreak in history. There is no proven vaccine or treatment yet for the Bundibugyo variant; almost 50% of those infected have died.

item.title: I hated life as a Neet. But now I’ve found a job, life is just as precarious | Emilija Morrison
item.description:
The government’s plans to help young people not in education, work or training are welcome – I dearly hope they offer long-term security

  • Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism

What child dreams of being unemployed when they grow up? You can probably remember the days, aged 10, when you were asked to present to the class what you wanted to be. Imagine hearing this: “I want to be unemployed. After I graduate from university, I want to go to the jobcentre in my home town and collect my benefits every month.”

Yet that is the reality for many young people today – childhood dreams to become a teacher, a doctor, an engineer or whatever other profession thwarted not by the limits of their abilities, but the reality of the economy.

Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism

item.title: Did you come down with GTA flu? I won’t judge – I may even join you in Vice City | Imogen West-Knights
item.description:
Millions are throwing sickies and no wonder. For gamers who have waited 13 years, this is the equivalent of a football World Cup

If there were an unusual number of people missing from your workplace at the back end of this week, they may have come down with GTA flu. You don’t need to be a video game person to have heard that there’s a new instalment of Grand Theft Auto, the enormously popular series in which you drive around sprawling American cities committing crimes. It has been all over the news. And if you are not a video game person, maybe that seems baffling. Why is this game such a big deal?

Let me assure you that this is no ordinary video game release. The last GTA instalment, GTA V, came out in 2013, so fans have waited 13 years for this game. On Wednesday, before the game had even been released in the US, PlayStation Network experienced widespread disruption attributed to an overload of people trying to download an update needed for the game. After its first day of sales, it was already thought to be the biggest entertainment launch of all time, having made $2.36bn (£1.8bn) – nearly as much as the latest Spider-Man film over its entire run.

item.title: Did Democrats fail Florida? Angie Nixon on ‘missed opportunity’ in midterms

The party invested in key battlegrounds, netting stunning wins at the expense of candidates in Florida and Louisiana

To call it a blue wave, said the Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, would be an epic understatement. The midterm elections were “the political equivalent of a meteor strike”. But one state, DeSantis added with pride, was able to “hold the line”. And that state was Florida.

On a night when almost everything else went right for Democrats, David Jolly fell short by 1.3 percentage points against Republican Byron Donalds, who will become Florida’s first Black governor, while Angie Nixon, bidding to become the state’s first Black senator, lost by 2.9 percentage points to Republican Ashley Moody.

item.title: ‘No means no, however we dress and wherever we go’: 50 years of campaigning against rape
item.description:
Grassroots group Women Against Rape says ‘things are really changing’ in how victims are treated by criminal justice system

When Mr Justice Bennathan sentenced Russell Brand to 10 and a half years in prison, there was a notable shift in the characterisation of victims of sexual assault. “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no, and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent,” the judge said.

In 1977 it was a completely different story. Justices Roskill, Wien and Slynn allowed the convicted rapist Queen’s Guardsman Tom Holdsworth to walk free on appeal after his rape conviction because of his “promising army career”. The same year, Judge Zigmond gave the rapist of a three-year-old girl just a suspended sentence, telling her mother: “You will forget it and so will your little girl.” Judge Peter Mason gave a six-month sentence to Maurice Markham, a rapist from the Royal Navy, because “it would be a shame if the country loses your services”.

item.title: New Orleans Catholic clergy abuse survivors begin receiving payments from $305m bankruptcy settlement
item.description:
Arrival of payments in contentious legal saga that began in 2020 is ‘a weight off my shoulders’, one survivor said

Hundreds of clergy sexual abuse survivors have received more than half of the $305m bankruptcy settlement that the archdiocese of New Orleans reached with them last year, a milestone that marks the beginning of the end of a years-long legal saga.

The trustee overseeing the settlement fund, Don Massey, confirmed on Friday that $180m had been distributed to 450 of about 740 survivors, either directly or through their lawyers if they retained legal representation. Massey said he and his staff are working hard to get payments in the rest of the survivors’ hands by the end of the year but are still waiting on hundreds of distribution forms from survivors and their lawyers.

item.title: Haitians excited but uneasy as El Salvador troops fight gangs
item.description:
Foreign combatants in Port-au-Prince welcomed by many after years of gang control but some fear offensive could exacerbate volatile situation

A bullet-peppered mural of the Haitian striker Emmanuel Sanon covers the facade of Port-au-Prince’s main football ground. But more than two years have passed since any sports stars graced the pitch.

In 2024, as the surrounding city was almost entirely captured by heavily armed gangs, Sylvio Cator stadium – where football greats including Brazil’s Ronaldo and Roberto Carlos once played – also fell under criminal control, its dilapidated red and blue stands used as an outpost by fighters working for a gang boss called Izo. Haiti’s national team, the Grenadiers, found itself homeless and was forced to play its World Cup qualifying games abroad.

item.title: ‘Legally, they don’t exist’: the hybrid crabs puzzling biologists and fishers
item.description:
A heatwave in the Bering Sea that killed 10bn snow crabs has led to a new species emerging that has no fishing quotas

Somewhere out on the Bering Sea, hundreds of miles off the coast of Alaska, a group of researchers onboard the trawler Alaska Knight haul up a heap of crabs from the seabed. As they sort and measure their haul, something seems wrong.

The catch, which usually features species such as the snow crab – a species of spider crab growing up to a metre wide with its legs outstretched – or its larger relative, the tanner crab, is instead dominated by an odd-looking hybrid of the two species.

It was a cool, overcast morning in late September when members of the Tsawwassen First Nation gathered outside a shopping mall near Vancouver.

Two hand-carved house posts, carrying the history and identity of the community, were to be raised in a ceremony marking the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.

item.description:
Although there is no definitive link between violent video games and behavior, departments take to social media

While critics have been raving after the recent and long-awaited arrival of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest entry in the famously violent video game series has also prompted real-world warnings from authorities.

Police departments across the US met the game’s release on Thursday with reminders that the car thefts, reckless driving, violence and other criminal mayhem depicted in the blockbuster title should not be re-enacted on the country’s streets.

A Missouri judge on Friday approved Bayer’s $7.25bn settlement of lawsuits ⁠alleging that its weedkiller ​Roundup causes cancer, potentially resolving litigation that has weighed on the German company for close to a decade.

Judge Timothy Boyer of a state court in St Louis ⁠found the settlement “fair, reasonable and adequate”.

item.title: Republican senator blocks Trump cyber nominee over January 6 denial
item.description:
Thom Tillis move comes after Michael LoSapio, nominated for Cisa role, told hearing ‘I don’t believe it was an attack’

Senator Thom Tillis, the outgoing North Carolina Republican who is due to be replaced by a Democrat, has reportedly blocked a confirmation vote on Donald Trump’s nominee to lead a key US cybersecurity agency, Michael LoSapio, after he denied during a hearing that the Capitol was attacked on January 6 2021.

Tillis, who declined to run for re-election and after repeated clashes with Trump’s, confirmed to HuffPost on Friday that he has placed a hold on LoSapio’s nomination to serve as a director of the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency (Cisa). His block on the nomination will prevent it from being included in a package of nominees to be voted on next month, before the Republicans lose their majority in the Senate.

item.description:
The president appeared to put Vance and Rubio through their paces as potential successors, though Stephen Miller unexpectedly stole the spotlight

“Which of you shall we say doth love us most?”

The ageing King Lear’s question to his daughters, expecting them to compete for his favour and carve up his kingdom, hovered in the White House press briefing room on Friday.

item.description:
Verdict in case against former Uber driver Jonathan Rinderknecht comes after first trial ended with hung jury

The 30-year-old accused of sparking the deadly Palisades fire in Los Angeles was found guilty of two federal arson charges in a Friday verdict that came months after his first trial concluded with a hung jury.

For two weeks, a fresh batch of jurors listened to prosecutors mount their case against Jonathan Rinderknecht.

item.title: Cop31 draft climate text dissected: what it says and what it means
item.description:
Fiona Harvey reads between the lines of the draft document that will end up outlining decisions and resolutions from the 31st climate summit

  • Cop31 live – latest updates

The final text is one of the most important documents that will come out of the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey. What emerges in the latest draft here is that it will not be a new treaty, but a series of decisions and resolutions. These decisions have legal force in the context of the Paris agreement, so this is a powerful document. But it is also a document that can be accepted only with the consensus of all parties, therefore much of the language is cautious and some is ambiguous or open to interpretation, to the frustration of countries who want to move faster.

I. Global progress and context
1. Strongly reaffirms commitment to multilateralism and resolves to remain united in the pursuit of efforts to implement the Convention and achieve the purpose and long-term goals of the Paris Agreement; 2. Recalls that the Paris Agreement will be implemented to reflect equity and the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, in the light of different national circumstances; 3. Acknowledges that the Paris Agreement is working and that the global transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development is irreversible, and that significant collective progress towards the Paris Agreement temperature goal has been made, from an expected global temperature increase of more than 4°C according to some projections prior to the adoption of the Agreement to an increase of around 2.6°C based on the full implementation of national climate plans; 4. Emphasizes the importance of promoting the economic and social benefits and opportunities of action on climate change, recognizing the significant drop in the cost of mature renewable energy and zero- and low-emission technologies, and the role of the energy transition in strengthening energy security, affordability and availability;

item.title: Judges, juries and rape myths in trials | Letters
item.description:
Paul Keleher KC offers an insight into how juries are directed. Plus a letter from Prof Nicole Moreham

In your report (‘Pull back the curtain’ on treatment of sexual assault victims in court, says UK government adviser, 15 November), Prof Katrin Hohl suggests that while significant progress has been made by police forces and the Crown Prosecution Service, the court system was being left behind.

It seems to be little known that for many years judges have been trained to direct juries to ignore rape myths and direct them that many victims of sexual assault are unable to physically resist and often delay reporting the assault. Juries are directed that this should not cast doubt on their accounts of being assaulted.

item.title: Latest botched execution prompts calls for US moratorium on lethal injections
item.description:
Reinaldo Dennes screamed in pain and took over an hour to die – but Texas officials branded the execution a success

A botched execution in Texas on Thursday night that lasted more than an hour and caused the prisoner to scream out, begging the Lord to end his suffering, has led to renewed calls for a nationwide moratorium that would pause all lethal injections.

It took 63 minutes for Reinaldo Dennes, 70, to be proclaimed dead in the Huntsville penitentiary. The execution team had struggled to find a vein through which a lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital could be administered.

item.title: Vitamin D, fiber and flavor: how healthy are mushrooms?
item.description:
Experts say there are many reasons to boost our consumption of mushrooms and incorporate them into our diets

Mushrooms aren’t quite as popular in the US as they are in other parts of the world. On average, Americans eat just shy of 4lb (1.81kg) of mushrooms per capita each year, while in South Korea people eat almost 6lb (2.72kg) a year, and in Japan, that number is closer to 12lb (5.44kg).

People in the US also don’t consume as wide a variety of mushrooms as other parts of the world, says Dr Krystle Zuniga, a board-certified oncology dietitian based in Austin, Texas. “I often think of them as a forgotten vegetable,” she says, though she clarifies they are technically fungi.

item.title: After Russell Brand, and now another horrific rape verdict, shame really does have to change sides | Jonathan Freedland
item.description:
From predatory male celebrities to ordinary men who connive to abuse women, there is no doubt where the problem lies – and the solution too

The only thing they have in common is that they are men. Those convicted of the rape and sexual assault of Joanne Young – who was drugged by her husband, so that he could offer her unconscious body to strangers – do not come from one class or ethnic group or age cohort. Like the 50 men convicted alongside Dominique Pelicot for the serial rape of his wife, Gisèle, which this case resembles, they run the full range. Young’s oldest abuser is now 62, her youngest was 22. The four convicted on Thursday included two who were white, two who were not. Among them was a former music producer, a taxi driver and a one-time contractor for the Ministry of Defence. The only thing they have in common is that they are men.

That closes off a delusion that many reach for when confronted with heinous crimes committed against women: the claim that such appalling acts are peculiar to a specific category of man. Last week, the focus was on famous men, prompted by the rape conviction of Russell Brand and the allegations of underage grooming and predatory behaviour by David Walliams, accusations Walliams denies. There was earnest discussion of the enabling power of celebrity, how stardust blinds people from seeing what’s in front of them. Some suggested the problem was narrower still, with abuse cast as a function of the way British comedy operates, lacking a recognisable HR structure or protection for junior workers from big names with clout. In parallel, a debate began about staggering the age of consent, addressing the particular dynamics of older men who target younger women, including those who would be regarded as children by any definition except the letter of the law.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

item.title: The Guardian view on Jan van Eyck’s portraits: what it means to be human | Editorial
item.description:
A tiny scar, bloodshot eyes and sagging jowls – it is the intimate details of these 15th-century masterpieces that make them so relatable today

The word “human” may have been crowned the Cambridge dictionary’s word of 2026, but its meaning is nowhere more manifest than in an exhibition of paintings from almost 600 years ago. Humanness is captured in every pore and wrinkle of all nine of Jan van Eyck’s portraits, united for the first time by the National Gallery. The paintings have been loaned from Berlin, Vienna, Dresden, Bruges and Sibiu in Romania, in a triumph of cultural exchange that proves the blockbuster show is still very much alive. And so, it almost seems, are the people depicted in it, who appear so real we might “recognise them on the tube”, as the exhibition’s co-curator Nicholas Flory put it, even given their extravagant headgear.

A purplish wart, a tiny scar, bloodshot eyes, sagging jowls and dirty fingernails – it is the intimate details of Van Eyck’s likenesses that transformed Renaissance portraiture and make his sitters so relatable, in modern parlance, today. Like a novelist, the artist wanted to create the impression of capturing his subjects in a moment in time.

item.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
item.description:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage admits that Brexit was botched. But he wants greater divergence from, rather than increased closeness to, Europe. Both rightwing parties face a dilemma: how to oppose the better relationship when even Mr Farage acknowledges its benefits?

item.title: What’s left to do as Cop31 enters its frantic final days

The diplomatic battles shaping the future of climate action

• Don’t get Down to Earth delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

The end is in sight. If all goes as planned, countries as diverse as wealthy petrostates erecting new oil rigs and low-lying islands threatened by rising seas will reach an agreement tomorrow in Antalya, bringing the 31st UN climate summit to a close (though, as usual, the talks are likely to overrun).

But tensions – much like our global temperatures – are running high. A draft text that satisfies all the competing interests is a long way off, and negotiators are expected to argue into the night and then the weekend. On the table are the electrification of the global economy, the transition away from fossil fuels, and the response to the looming overshoot of the 1.5C (2.7F) temperature target. Deepening the divide are long-running disputes over who should pay what, and emerging fights over the fairness of the transition and assumptions in the underlying science.

item.title: While the headlines rave about Milburn’s Neets review, the young people I know are angry and frustrated | Felicity Halstead

I was at my desk last Thursday morning as a steady stream of young people filed into GoodWork’s central London community hub for a day of employability workshops. Despite the accusations of disengagement among young people, they didn’t need me to tell them that proposals to cut some benefits for under-25s were all over the news. I could hear them talking about it as soon as the lift pinged open – and the mood was low.

Alan Milburn has made a concerted effort to say that he doesn’t believe young people are to blame for dire levels of youth unemployment. He says the system has let them down and only a decade-long transformation will fix a problem that is complex and deeply entrenched. Simply recognising the scale of the problem and being willing to invest in a solution is a positive start.

Felicity Halstead is the founder and CEO of GoodWork, a London-based youth employment and social mobility charity

Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

item.title: The UK government ridicules villages such as Piddington – but it’s these ‘Nimbys’ who show us the way | Simon Jenkins
item.description:
In other countries, local communities have a say in their futures. If the UK were truly democratic, everywhere would be a parish in control of its own fate

Poor Piddington. The Oxfordshire village of just 350 people was told last week by the communities secretary, Angela Rayner, that it must almost quadruple in size. That wasn’t all. The newcomers would be 1,250 young asylum seekers, mainly from Afghanistan and Eritrea, victims of Britain’s chaotic asylum appeal system. They will be housed in former military cabins on the village’s outskirts. Rayner said that this was an “urgent crown development”, which allowed her to ignore local objections.

And there had certainly been objections. In September, Piddington villagers declared they were fed up with Britain. Led by their parish council and on a 92% turnout, they voted overwhelmingly to leave the UK and become a “principality”. They are joined in their protest by Barnham in Suffolk, where locals have been told this week that they are to host nearly 1,000 asylum seekers. They have set their own date on a referendum to leave the UK.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist, author and BBC broadcaster. His book The Village in Britain: And Why Place Matters is published this month

item.title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
item.description:
Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism

It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.

The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

item.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
item.description:
It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

item.title: I, too, was raped by my partner while drugged and unconscious. There are more survivors than you think | Zoe Watts
item.description:
Before Gisèle Pelicot and now Joanne Young, drug-facilitated rape was virtually unheard of. I now realise that my own horrific ordeal was not unique

Like many, I followed closely the sickening case of Philip Young, who has been convicted of repeatedly drugging and raping his now ex-wife, Joanne Young, and advertising her on the internet for sex. It is, to any right-thinking person, unimaginably horrific that the person you’re supposed to trust most in the world would betray you in this, the worst possible way.

I don’t have to imagine it, however. I have lived it. The man I had been with since I was 17 – my husband and the father of my four children, the man who had vowed to love and look after me and with whom I had shared a bed for almost 7,000 nights – did the same to me.

Zoe Watts is a campaigner and cofounder of the #EndEyeCheck campaign to raise awareness of drug-facilitated sexual abuse

item.title: I’m an Australian-Palestinian doctor who was turned away at the West Bank border. The stigma of being born in Gaza stands in the way of peace

Senior correspondent
