Senior diplomats had already confirmed this week that the EU would defer the deal on the level of tuition fees for another six months, a move designed to give the UK leverage in parallel negotiations to have the UK included in Made in Europe legislation designed to protect EU supply chains against China.

But the move to make the food and drink deal also contingent on a tuition fees deal effectively seeks to neutralise the leverage the UK gets today.

This is a serious chess game and shows the EU, again, is willing to speak very warmly about the UK but will play absolute hard ball when it comes to conceding any points to a former member state.

It was the same point France was making last night insisting the UK could not have voting rights on legislation in relation to food and drink.

item.title: Why I take this posh salt scandal with a pinch of you know what | Thea Everett
item.description:
The revelation that German rock salt is used in Maldon’s Essex-made product is causing a stir – but, however you sprinkle it, it’s all just salt

This week, a report by the Observer found that the king of flaky salt, Maldon, was using imported German rock salt in its Essex production plant. It has since followed that Cornish Sea Salt (another industry leader) is also importing European salt in its production. There has been a food media outcry, with a tone that has felt very “I’m not angry, I’m just disappointed”. According to the Observer report, “tonnes of mined rock salt are being poured into the production line” at Maldon. The scandal is that these brands call themselves sea salt (made by evaporating seawater), but rock salt is mined from dried-up underground seabeds (that were once also seas). Salt companies combine one type of salt with another to ultimately produce … salt. As food manufacturing goes, I don’t find it the most shocking transgression.

“Posh salt”, once marketed only to the upper classes in Harrods and Fortnums, has been gaining popularity over the last half century. In the early 00s, the major supermarkets started selling Maldon sea salt, and over the last 20 years, with the chef-ification of home cookery, flaky salt has reached never-before-seen heights.

Thea Everett is a London-based food writer who runs a recipe Substack called What’s That You’re Cooking, Thea?

item.title: Academic integrity matters, but students shouldn’t be penalised for using AI | Letter
item.description:

Is this really the best we can do: draconically penalise the young for making use of the latest cognitive resources and tools available to them (Ofqual urges ‘life-altering’ penalties for students who use tech to cheat, 18 November)? Our generation has allowed the introduction of “life-altering” new technologies into every walk of life without much democratic debate, public scrutiny or governmental oversight. And now our education leaders are threatening to jeopardise young people’s career prospects for deploying these technologies within an education system that can’t cope and struggles to adapt?

We all know that AI is here to stay. And importantly, it is so much more than just a cheap cheating device. Within an incredibly short space of time, it has transformed how we work, communicate, solve problems, research and learn. Surely the pedagogical response cannot simply be to devise ever more elaborate ways of preventing students from using it?

item.title: The Guardian view on Grand Theft Auto VI: a game that makes players think twice | Editorial
item.description:
For almost 30 years, Grand Theft Auto has revelled in America’s vices. Its latest instalment may find room for empathy amid the mayhem

The biggest global cultural event of the year may not be something that millions of people watch together but somewhere that millions of people venture separately. In the video game Grand Theft Auto VI, players inhabit a fictionalised America through the eyes of two lovers turned cons in a rags-to-riches crime epic. On Thursday, when the game was released, workers called in sick and students skipped lectures to play at home. Such is GTA VI’s appeal that it is forecast to rake in billions of dollars within months.

The game has been billed as a satire of American capitalism, and it is undoubtedly a landmark in interactive storytelling and art. The commercial success of its previous titles has rivalled that of Hollywood blockbusters. Playing GTA VI, as the Guardian’s video games editor observes, is like losing yourself in a doorstop novel, with hours of solitary immersion in a vividly conjured place – not a facsimile of modern Miami, but an interpretation, almost the size of Manchester, rendered with astonishing precision by the artists who designed, wrote, coded and soundtracked its virtual world.

item.title: The Guardian view on the international court of justice: the ruling against Myanmar should be only the start for the Rohingya | Editorial
item.description:
A landmark finding of genocide marked a good day for international law. But both the court and the Rohingya minority now need sustained support

The finding of the world’s highest court that Myanmar committed genocide is a landmark in international law. But at the heart of this case are “real people, real stories and a real group of human beings”, as Dawda Jallow, the Gambian justice minister, stressed in bringing it. This was one test of how the world has responded to the persecution of the mostly Muslim Rohingya minority in Rakhine state. The international community’s response to the majority judgment will be another.

This is the first time that the international court of justice (ICJ) has found a state guilty of genocide. Around 10,000 Rohingya were killed in the 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military, in many cases gunned down as they fled, with another 700,000 escaping to Bangladesh. The judges found that the aim was to destroy “a substantial part” of the Rohingya people, with the murder of infants, widespread sexual violence and razing of villages not accounted for simply by military objectives.

item.title: It’s unfashionable to say it, but class still matters – and young people know that | Polly Toynbee
item.description:
From inheritance to nepotism in the workplace, social inequality is now a daily experience for many young people

This should come as no great surprise: young people are more keenly aware of the significance of social class than those who came before them. The yawning gap in life chances at birth is something they know better than complacent older generations. Class may be unfashionable in the language of politics – long damned by the right as the politics of envy, avoided by many on the left for fear of sounding chip-on-the-shoulder – yet it’s part of the daily experience for young people.

Nearly half of 16- to 34-year-olds in the UK now say class is important to their identity – and not in a good way – according to a new Ipsos poll. That’s nearly twice as many as among the over-55s. Maybe that’s because more young people are better educated at each level, so they know more, with a grounding in reasoned thinking.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

item.title: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras
item.description:
We can’t make AI safe for humanity if tech bosses are allowed to run their companies like autocracies

Over the past two years, a troubling pattern has emerged across the world’s leading AI laboratories. Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for OpenAI’s product releases said he was quitting the ChatGPT creator because the company’s culture was “broken” and the entire AI industry was too careless in developing the technology. The previous month it was a researcher at OpenAI’s rival Anthropic who quit, warning that he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.

As a society we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle – and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal: as the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice.

Isabelle Ferreras is accelerator fellow at the University of Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI, FNRS research director at the University of Louvain, Belgium and co-founder of DemocraticIntelligence.org

item.title: Mentors, colleagues and friends: tributes paid to the ‘Eritrea 16’ who disappeared 25 years ago
item.description:
Families of journalists who vanished into state prisons on ‘Black Tuesday’ in 2001 do not know whether they are even still alive

The Eritrean writer’s personal tribute to Amanuel Asrat, a poet, writer, and founder of Zemen newspaper, was not merely about an abstract human rights case but about her mentor, former colleague and friend whose life had in effect been erased by the authoritarian state of Eritrea.

item.title: This year, the Greens have reshaped British politics. Now we need party systems to match that influence | Caroline Lucas
item.description:
Without Zack Polanski and Hannah Spencer, we might still be stuck with Keir Starmer. But after some difficult weeks, our party needs an overhaul

One that will hold other parties to account for their delivery on social and environmental justice and that will put issues on the political agenda that other parties won’t.

From Rosebank to wealth taxes and ending arms sales to Israel, Greens are stretching the Overton window so that the gap narrows between what’s necessary and what’s currently deemed politically acceptable. As we increasingly win more council seats, assembly members, mayors and MPs, we are able, at all levels of government, to help restore the natural world, tackle climate breakdown and challenge the economic framework of neoliberalism that has governed us for too long.

Caroline Lucas is co-chair of the cross-party campaign group Compass and a former Green MP

item.title: ‘It’s a biohazard’: Native communities in US south-west try to recover after flooding intensified by El Niño
item.description:
Residents and local groups band together after severe flooding submerged a New Mexico town in toxic water

On the night of 23 October, Jimmie Goodman was trying to get some rest when his sister, who was recovering from back surgery and having trouble sleeping, woke him. Authorities in their home town of Shiprock, New Mexico, had warned that the nearby San Juan River was at risk of flooding as unprecedented rain fell across the Four Corners region of the south-west US – and so Goodman peeked outside.

item.title: Cringe comedy makes my skin crawl but I will watch You Can See Everything – for the culture | Rebecca Shaw
item.description:
I love that Nathan Fielder exists, and I understand the scope of what he is doing. But watching people be embarrassed causes me psychic damage

I realise it’s only the most annoying people on Earth who say this sort of thing, but I’m going to bravely say it anyway: I am an empath. I have always felt in tune with other people’s emotions and can easily take them on. The emotion I am most intensely attuned to, the one that takes the strongest hold of my body when I see someone going through it? Embarrassment.

There is nothing I hate more than seeing a person embarrassed, even if it’s a person I don’t like. I have always been like this. I remember sitting in the cinema watching There’s Something About Mary, all of my friends dying over a scene where Ben Stiller gets his testicular skin stuck in his zipper in front of his crush. They were rolling in their seats while my insides were rolling around. I felt physically ill. I knew logically it was a funny scene, that a normal person would laugh at the plight of this poor boy and his ball skin, but my humour bone was being crushed in a vice grip, as it always is when embarrassment abounds.

Continue reading...

item.title: ‘Everyone struggled for this justice’: tears in court as Rohingya vindicated in Myanmar genocide ruling
item.description:
Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the world

There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.

item.title: The moral panic over Neets needs to stop. The problem is bad jobs, not young people | Aditya Chakrabortty
item.description:
Milburn’s review doesn’t ask what kind of work young people will be going into: zero hours, minimum wage, mind-numbing. Do we have the guts to solve that?

One big number has been repeated over and over this week: 1 million. As ministers and journalists keep telling us, about 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds are not in education, employment or training (Neet). They’re the subject of Alan Milburn’s review, which, although not commissioned by Andy Burnham, has become the first big policy of his new government.

Rather than launch into my conclusions, let me give you three more numbers by which to judge Milburn for yourself. These figures have not appeared in any of this week’s coverage, but to understand the review’s context and its chances of success they are vital.

Aditya Chakrabortty is a Guardian columnist

Colonoscopy, ultrasound, Vibration plate and patience deployed 11 days after beloved beast ingested knitted hat

item.title: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel

The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states.

In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent.

item.title: Hakeem Jeffries on brink of House history as he tells Democrats to ‘fight Maga, not each other’ – US politics live
item.description:
Democrats resoundingly nominated Jeffries to serve as speaker of the House when the new Congress is sworn in next year

  • Sign up for the Breaking News US email

The National Security Agency is seeing a third day of disruptions to its internal network, NSA Net, which allows staff to share highly classified information with each other, according to the New York Times.

The Times reports that employees at the NSA’s Maryland headquarters are under “code orange” for Thursday day shift, which requires non-essential workers are to stay home unless contacted by their supervisors.

A secret, closed-door election: Unlike the public speaker of the House vote, where lawmakers cast ballots on the chamber floor, the Senate leadership contest takes place behind closed doors. Senators vote by secret ballot, and individual votes are not disclosed.

The winner only needs a caucus majority: The Democratic leadership race is decided solely by members of the party’s Senate caucus. Now that Democrats are set to have 56 seats in the new year, the winner will need secure 29 votes for the top role.

The vote is scheduled for next month: As things stand, the election is set for 1 December. Both incumbent senators and incoming Democratic members will participate, while retiring and outgoing senators will not vote, despite many having publicly weighed in on the race.

Republicans choose their leaders separately: Republicans hold their own closed-door leadership elections in both chambers. Earlier this month, House Republicans selected hardliner Jim Jordan as their leader after Mike Johnson opted not to run for minority leader. In the Senate, Republicans unanimously backed John Thune to continue leading the conference.

item.title: How to start eating plant-based, without missing out on nutrients or foods you enjoy
item.description:
Experts agree that if you’re thinking of changing your diet, start small and keep your goals in mind

At this point, the environmental effects of the meat industry have been well-established: one 2021 study found that meat accounts for nearly 60% of all greenhouse gases from food production, and a 2025 report estimated that animal agriculture was responsible for 12%-19% of total human-caused greenhouse gases.

According to the United Nations, one of the best things people can do to reduce their personal carbon footprint is shift from a diet heavy in meat to one that is more plant-based. Many of us know this, but in the US and UK, fewer than 5% of adults identify as vegetarian or vegan. One of the biggest obstacles, according to experts? People think it’s too hard.

item.title: Cameron Bancroft’s excruciating depiction of being the sandpaper scapegoat means that Cricket Australia’s ordeal is far from over | Gideon Haigh
item.description:
It’s the silence of self-protection and the clamour for a patsy that are the most humiliating details of Bancroft’s screed, and point not just to a poor culture but a malign one, writes Gideon Haigh

  • Cameron Bancroft breaks his silence on sandpapergate: who will be next? – Full Story podcast

Australia chose the right day to lose a home series to England. By the time many tuned in on Wednesday, the last Aussie pair were batting in a largely empty Bellerive Oval, Harry Brook was bowling his filth, the commentators were talking about how Jonathan Trott used to take centre, and nobody was paying the remotest attention. The whole affair seemed utterly beside an overpowering point.

Meanwhile, somewhere in Perth, Cameron Bancroft was beginning a few days’ quiet contemplation, having got a very great weight off his mind, and dropped it on the Australian cricket team. Not only does his statement imply that Pat Cummins’s press conference last Friday was an exercise in misdirection, but it goes considerably beyond what Usman Khawaja offered in Sabr, and Chadd Sayers added at the weekend. Did even they not grasp the extent of what was going on? We knew the Australian dressing room in 2017-18 was a toxic place, but was it this … confused?

item.title: Andy Burnham is in danger of over-selling his big Brussels summit. What happens if he under-delivers? | Joël Reland
item.description:
In laying a trap for himself, the PM could derail his longer-term ambition of revisiting Brexit

This week’s UK-EU summit may, one day, be seen as the start of the UK’s long march back towards the EU. Andy Burnham’s much-anticipated first meeting with EU chiefs in Brussels on Friday will be used to unveil a suite of detailed agreements to improve trade and economic cooperation, before the Prime Minister kickstarts his longer term “national conversation” about a much closer form of political and economic relationship with the EU. This, as Burnham signalled in a speech on Monday night, could well culminate in Labour’s next election manifesto abandoning the party’s famous red lines, and proposing an application for EU membership.

For pro-Europeans, this must read like a fever dream. Just four months ago, when Burnham took office, such a bold offer on Europe from the Labour party seemed implausible. But while Burnham has certainly reinvigorated the Brexit debate, he will have to move carefully to avoid storing up trouble for himself down the road. There is a risk that Burnham will come to be seen as someone who over-promises and under-delivers on Europe – and, in doing so, halts the growing momentum around revisiting the troublesome Brexit question.

Joël Reland is senior researcher at the UK in a Changing Europe thinktank

Continue reading...

item.title: Weight-loss drugs used in nearly one in 10 homes in Great Britain, study finds
item.description:

item.title: Nothing but highlights: is Power Slap the sport we deserve?
item.description:
Slap fighting is the world’s newest combat sport. Built for short attention spans and super-viral moments, it’s aiming for global dominance. No flinching

In the days before Power Slap 22, in Belgrade, Serbia, in late July, the organisers of the world’s newest combat sport were taking no chances. At the Crowne Plaza hotel, where competitors were booked to stay, those facing off had been separated by floor, lest any unauthorised violence took place.

It turned out there was little need. The night before the main event, contestants mingled amiably in the lobby and bar. The atmosphere was more specialist sales conference than brewing barroom brawl. In the lobby, I joined Louis “Razor” Robinson, and Ryan “the Punisher” Kenny. “We’re all friends in slap,” Robinson said, earnestly, by way of a greeting. Robinson, a Brit from Stalybridge, Greater Manchester, is 30, stout, intense. Kenny, a Canadian, is 34, lofty, laid back.

item.title: Meet Phil, the bar-tailed godwit tracked on a 6,800-mile round trip to Siberia
item.description:
Scientists use lightweight tracker to map wading bird’s extraordinary migration from Norfolk to the Arctic and back

A bar-tailed godwit called Phil has completed a 6,800-mile journey from Norfolk to Siberia and back again, in the first mapping of the endurance feats of this long-distance migrant.

A wading bird not much larger than a pigeon, the bar-tailed godwit is known for making the longest recorded non-stop migratory flight of any bird, with populations that visit Britain spending summers breeding in the Arctic Circle before retreating to the unfrozen wetlands of Britain in winter.

item.title: Ram through datacentres no one wants and hope the AI bubble never bursts: that’s the UK’s growth plan | George Monbiot
item.description:
The government doesn’t know what they are going to be used for, but that’s beside the point. Their real purpose is to sustain the share price of big tech

It should have the status of an economic law: the sectors a government does most to promote in the name of growth are the sectors most likely to tank the economy. In the UK and the US, deregulation was meant to turn the financial sector into a never-ending growth machine. We have not yet fully recovered from the crash it helped cause in 2008. Fossil fuels are the most heavily subsidised sector on Earth. All that public money makes us highly vulnerable to oil price shocks, the whims of autocrats and societal collapse caused by climate breakdown. As for the great growth priority of our time – AI and datacentres – well, don’t take it from me. As Anthropic’s IPO prospectus warns, advanced AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”.

One thing we learned from the US midterm elections is that the drive to build datacentres is less a function of real commercial demand than of the need to sustain the share price of the big tech companies. After citizens across the US voted for moratoria on new datacentres, tech stocks, which have become dangerously dominant, plummeted, triggering fears of wider contagion. Whether new datacentres are required or not, we must keep building them, because confidence depends on them, and without that confidence the bubble will pop. The more you build, and the more this value dependency grows, the bigger the bubble becomes.

George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

item.title: Teachers want to prepare pupils for post-16 life. This is why it’s so difficult | Lola Okolosie
item.description:
I welcome Alan Milburn’s call for schools to focus more on students’ potential beyond exams. Yet I must ask: where is the money?

At 16, life should feel like a path leading to endless opportunities. That is at least the carrot dangled in front of young people to motivate them through the gruelling years of exam preparation. “Your life starts now,” their teachers all but tell them. And though for the vast majority that is true, there is a cohort who are forced to accept that the bright futures they were promised are beyond their reach. They are the nearly one million young people aged between 16 and 24 who are not in education, employment or training (Neets).

Alan Milburn’s second report on the nation’s Neets places schools at the heart of the solution. It proposes that schools should be judged not only on grades but also whether pupils continue their post-16 journey into further education or work. Technical education, it also argues, must be regarded with the same gravitas as the academic. Most people working in education won’t argue with this rationale. As ever, the sticking point is how it is to be funded.

Lola Okolosie is an English teacher and writer

A review by the Guardian found that Children’s Health Defense (CHD) has reopened or opened six accounts on Facebook and Instagram from May through September this year. The group is using its accounts to share false and misleading information about topics including vaccines and deadly measles outbreaks at a time when measles has come roaring back. Health officials have reported 10 measles-associated deaths in the United States this year, and the country this week lost its measles elimination status in an official recognition that it is again endemic in the US after being eliminated for 26 years.

item.description:

Anthropic set the share price for its debut on the US stock market at $83 on Wednesday, positioning the artificial intelligence company for one of the biggest initial public offerings in history. The firm is slated to begin trading on Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT, with CEO Dario Amodei and other co-founders ringing the bell to open the Nasdaq exchange.

The pricing is above Anthropic’s earlier estimates. Last week, the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, set its preliminary share price at $70 to $78. With all shares counted, those prices put Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) from $1.26tn to $1.41tn. Elon Musk’s SpaceX debuted on Wall Street in June with the biggest market offering ever at $1.77tn. With Anthropic setting its share price at $83, it could now surpass SpaceX.

item.title: Australia has a reputation for being the most secretive democracy in the world. New laws could make it worse | Tom Sulston
item.description:
A defence bill being rushed through parliament could expand the definition of ‘defence official’ and see AI datacentres deemed ‘defence security zones’

In 2019, the New York Times described Australia as “the world’s most secretive democracy”. Since then, a succession of defence, anti-terror and surveillance bills over consecutive governments have stripped away parliamentary power in favour of executive power

In this tradition, the government has been quiet about the accelerating capability and protecting bases bill that’s currently being rushed through parliament. This bill would allow the minister to grant exemptions from Australian laws to defence officials, the definition of which is to be expanded to include third-party contractors.

item.title: Waymo pulls driverless taxis from freeways across the US after California ban

Waymo had allowed riders to hail its robotaxis for freeway rides in the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Miami and Austin. The California-based company offers rides on city streets in many other areas, including Las Vegas, Dallas and Denver. Those rides remain unaffected by suspended freeway service.

item.title: ‘My family would kill me if they saw it’: the ‘harmless’ images that can be deadly for women in Pakistan
item.description:

It was just a photo of a smiling girl in jeans and a vest top, the kind of outfit any young woman might wear in any country. But for Maniza*, a teenager from a conservative town in Pakistan who never leaves the house without her hijab, the selfie she took at home put her at very real risk of an “honour” killing.

“My family are really strict and I always wore a hijab. My father didn’t want me to stay in school but my mum pushed him. He said if I got into trouble, he would kill me. It wasn’t just words, he meant it,” she says.

item.title: After 49 years, Nasa’s Voyager 1 is one light-day away from us. Can we save this ‘pale blue dot’? | Kim Heacox
item.description:
Since the spacecraft’s 1977 launch, our wonderful and terrible species has done great damage to our planet. Voyager has offered us a clear view of ourselves

Imagine traveling nonstop for 49 years, alone in the dark with no destination in sight, powered by curiosity and engineering.

Further imagine making that journey not at bullet train or jet plane speed, but much faster: at 37,800 miles per hour, free from friction in a vast sea of cold, soundless space, bombarded by radiation and cosmic rays yet still able to communicate with folks back home.

item.title: We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match | Nestor Uriarte
item.description:
After the release of Grand Theft Auto VI this week, Rockstar employees like me can make history again. We need union recognition to safeguard our jobs

When I first got the call offering me a job at Rockstar, I was thrilled. I thought back to being a child and sneaking into my brother’s room to grab the PlayStation Portable so I could secretly play Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories. The same kid who fell in love with Rockstar’s games back then now gets to spend every day helping to create those worlds as an animation programmer at the studio in Edinburgh. This week, we will celebrate the culmination of more than a decade of effort: the release of the most anticipated game of all time, Grand Theft Auto VI.

But our team has the opportunity to make history a second time this month. Right now, the ballot is open for Rockstar employees to decide whether we want the union we have built with our colleagues to get recognition. As someone who cares deeply about our team, cares about what we do, and wants us to be able to keep delivering world-class games into the future, I’m voting yes.

item.title: Am I Caribbean, or am I a tourist? How art helped me find the answer
item.description:
During my visit to the Fuze Caribbean art fair in the Bahamas, I marvelled at how creators captured the complex nature of Caribbeanness

  • Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

When I tell people I’m travelling to the Bahamas to report on Fuze Caribbean art fair, no one believes I’m really going for work. There are smirks and jokes about it being a tough life, about drinking from coconuts on the beach. The tourist gaze pervades global perceptions of the Caribbean. This week, I speak to the region’s artists about how they use images to speak back.

I have Antiguan and Jamaican heritage, so I’m familiar with the fantasies the Caribbean sparks, which Antiguan-American writer Jamaica Kincaid described as so beautiful that its fluffy white clouds, blue spectral waters and “bottomless” black nights seemed “unreal”. Images have done much to flatten the Caribbean in the global imagination – so why shouldn’t Caribbean people use images to speak back?

item.title: In rare good news, wages have risen strongly. But Australian workers are still falling behind | Greg Jericho
item.description:
Despite the highest wage growth in years, we wait for signs of workers getting ahead of inflation – or of the supposed benefits of the AI boom

  • Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

It’s rare of late to get good economic news, but on Wednesday the wage figures from the Bureau of Statistics showed a nice bump in wages. Private sector wages rose 1.0% in the September quarter for an annual growth of 3.4%, the highest in two years. But even with these good numbers, real wages went backwards, showing just how though things are for workers.

Each year the September quarter is the big time for a wage increase. This isn’t because your boss is feeling romantic and likes to remember when “grass was green and grain was yellow”. No, it’s because it is the first quarter of the new financial year and also the quarter where workers on the minimum/award wage get a pay rise via the Fair Work Commission:

item.title: ‘Huge experiment in biogeography’: US offshore windfarms are creating artificial reefs
item.description:
Scientists and fishers study how these ‘reefs’ and the creatures living on them are transforming the ocean floor – and what it means for the fishing industry

A few years ago, Tony DiLernia, a New York-based charter boat captain, heard rumors of prime fishing near the Block Island windfarm, off the tip of Long Island. So he went with his family to see for himself. Almost immediately after motoring up to one of the project’s five turbines, black sea bass and summer flounder started nibbling at his rod and reel.

DiLernia, who has fished for 50 years, wasn’t surprised: he knew about the reef effect, where certain species cluster around structures like the turbines. “It’s what we call ‘stupid fishing’,” he joked. “You’ve got this thousand-foot [signpost] sticking up out of the water saying: ‘Fish here.’”

item.title: Israel delays building contracts for West Bank settlement after UK sanctions
item.description:
Attorney general says E1 settlement decision should not be taken by caretaker government led by Netanyahu

Israel has postponed issuing contracts for the construction of a large settlement on the West Bank seen as likely to render a two-state solution unviable, days after the UK imposed sanctions against building firms operating in the area.

Israeli diplomats insisted the move was not in response to the measures from Downing Street. Gali Baharav-Miara, the attorney general, said any decision on settlement expansion should not be taken by the caretaker government led by Benjamin Netanyahu but by whatever new administration was formed.

item.title: EU proposes €45bn loan for Ukraine to avert cash crisis and boost defences

Announcing the plan to lend Kyiv the money in 2027, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said: “We think this is the best way to give Ukraine a strong hand at the negotiating table. And Ukraine only needs to repay once Russia pays for the damage it has caused in Ukraine.”

item.title: Officials seek dismissal of lawsuit over stabbing of Ukrainian refugee on train in Charlotte

item.title: The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets? | Emma Brockes
item.description:
He seemed like the thinking person’s tech titan. But then came the affairs, the share collapse – and of course, the sorry items in his wardrobe

A few years ago, I attended a small dinner at a friend’s house in the US at which a tech billionaire was the guest of honour. He wasn’t one of the most famous tech billionaires – I’d never heard of him, although I used his communications platform every day. Nonetheless, it was exciting to get up close to someone that staggeringly rich to see if he was different from the rest of us.

And he was different, sort of. Leaning back in his chair, he seemed to suggest, in a bored kind of way, that in the event of a US standoff with Russia, Putin nuking London would be the sort of collateral damage Washington could tolerate. A bit of an odd thing to say to a stranger. He didn’t observe the usual rules of conversation but rather, like a Roman emperor waiting to be entertained, remained belligerently aloof.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

item.title: Who speaks for Europe abroad? Not its top diplomat
item.description:

item.title: Instant gratification is ruining our lives – and for me it started with my CD player’s shuffle button | Adrian Chiles
item.description:
Not even a compelling TV drama can stop me from staring at my phone. But this urge started 40 years ago, with what was at first presented as a useful feature

I blame the shuffle button. That’s what started me on the long road to a thoroughly scattered mind – generally unable to focus on anything for more than a few minutes or even seconds. I was always a bit like this, hence an ADHD diagnosis in later life. But back in the day I still managed to read a lot of books, watch long films and listen to whole records at one sitting. Now? Not so much. Actually, hardly ever.

Even something on television that I’m really engaged in – a drama or a football match – can hold me for only a few minutes before I find myself scrolling on my phone looking for I know not what. I don’t know whether it’s because I’m drawn to the small phone screen, or rather that I find absorption with whatever I’m watching on the big flatscreen just too much to bear.

item.title: Blaming Ofsted inspectors for the system is unfair | Letters
item.description:
Inspectors and educators alike have been placed under even greater pressure year after year, says Helen Kenny

As national officer for the FDA, the union representing a large number of His Majesty’s Inspectors (HMIs), I read Simon Jenkins’ piece with great interest (Ofsted’s menacing inspections are still disastrous. Schools should answer to the communities they serve, 13 November). Jenkins dismisses the work of HMIs as merely a “sniff” of the air and a stroll back to Whitehall, showing a lack of knowledge about their role. HMIs are former school leaders, with a deep knowledge and dedication to educating children and young people. They are as far from the typical civil servant (if there is such a thing) that it is possible to get, and in any case are not based in Whitehall.

Jenkins does at least suggest an alternative approach, unlike some who are calling for the abolition of Ofsted, but I really question whether he has thought it through. Parents value the provision of inspection, and most educators agree that assessments are fair – independent YouGov polling showed that 74% of educators believed their most recent inspection was accurate.

The Nvidia scandal. Plus: A tale of two rape trials

item.title: The Guardian view on ‘two-tier policing’: tackle the myth, don’t pander to it | Editorial
item.description:
Confidence in the system is being corroded by cynical campaigns and far-right propaganda – that is the challenge to be confronted

There are many areas of policy where public opinion diverges from evidence. Voters overestimate rates of crime, for example. Many will be sceptical of politicians who say today’s streets are safer than they used to be, although that is the reality. The challenge is to find methods of persuasion that don’t belittle the experiences of people who are afraid, and don’t like to be told their fears are unfounded.

But there is a different challenge that arises when the cause of public concern is a problem that doesn’t really exist. Many people are angry about “two-tier policing” in Britain, supposedly characterised by disproportionately severe enforcement against white people and leniency towards minorities. There is no evidence to support a systemic bias of that kind. By contrast, the data suggests an imbalance of fair treatment goes the other way. People of colour are underrepresented in the police, disproportionately targeted with stop-and-search policies and, if arrested, likelier to have force used against them.

item.title: The Guardian view on the Trump, Xi and Putin meeting: it may be a first, but it’s not progress | Editorial
item.description:
A trilateral gathering is good news for China and Russia, but bad for the US – and its traditional allies

“Historic” is a neutral descriptor, not a favourable one. Things can be unprecedented for good reason. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Thursday will be the first time that the leaders of the US, China and Russia have gathered for talks as a trio. The trilateral on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is striking, but it is not an achievement.

The lack of a clear agenda is telling: the spectacle really is the substance. Mr Trump sees international affairs in terms of spheres of influence. This meeting reinforces the obvious conclusion for the rest of the world – that they don’t get to sit at the table, only to be on the plate. Mr Xi promotes the notion of a multipolar world. Others would be more sympathetic if all three governments were not determinedly undermining multilateralism.

item.title: There is no public interest in watching Isaac Heeney or Pat Cummins argue with their partners. We should look away | Megan Maurice
item.description:
Not every aspect of the human experience needs to be recorded, distributed and discussed – even if those in question are public figures

This week the Sydney Swans player Isaac Heeney and his partner were followed and filmed arguing in a local park in the wake of investigations into an incident at a Melbourne hotel in August that led to his suspension. Last week it was the Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins and wife Becky who were filmed in a heated discussion outside their Sydney home after Usman Khawaja made new claims about the infamous “sandpapergate” incident.

While both men have had questions swirling around them that have thrust them squarely into public discussion, this ogling of their personal lives during harrowing moments has raised questions. Most notably about who deserves privacy in a time when the public has become so accustomed to the sharing of private information that they feel entitled to know the details of the personal lives of every public figure.

Megan Maurice is a Sydney-based writer with a passion for diversity and inclusion in sport

item.description:
Masculinity isn’t set in stone or written in our DNA. It’s made between us, at the dinner table, at the pub, in the office

Over the past decade I’ve been invited into a lot of rooms: boardrooms, school halls, clinics, conference centres. I’ve even been cornered at a Sunday barbecue, where I’d wrongly assumed I was off the clock. On Wednesday, it was the National Press Club.

The brief in all these settings is the same.

In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. In the US, the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline is 1-800-273-8255. In the UK, Samaritans can be contacted on 116 123. Other international suicide helplines can be found at befrienders.org

item.title: Trump, Xi and Putin have a shared vision of global power – with no place for Europe | Rafael Behr
item.description:
In a world carved into continental blocs by authoritarians, Britain has to make common cause with its neighbours

In the chronicles of 21st-century diplomacy few statements have caused as much offence with as few words as Barack Obama’s 2014 description of Russia as a “regional power”.

Vladimir Putin’s politics were defined then, as now, by vengeful resentment of his country’s relegation from superpower status after the cold war. His worldview is warped by a paranoid conviction that Nato never stopped striving to deepen that humiliation, even after the USSR had unravelled. From his Kremlin throne, the Russian president expects to be treated as a colossus of world history. It is hard to overstate how bitterly he hated being dismissed by Obama as a geopolitical B-lister.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

item.title: ‘They want silence’: how the film NAZA is shaking Israel
item.description:
The documentary has triggered fierce backlash, but by exposing the army’s conduct in Gaza it’s proved impossible to ignore

It was on Yom Kippur this year that Nadav Weiman first sensed the documentary NAZA was having a significant impact in Israel – despite the fact that back in September, when the Jewish festival fell, barely a handful of Israelis had seen the film.

NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and will stream for free on its website in early December, depicts 24 army intelligence officers interviewed anonymously on rooftops across Tel Aviv. They talk about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza over the past three years, and the secret signoff system employed by Israel’s military. item.title: Childhood neglect, unmet needs, mental health struggles: this is the making of a Neet | Mark Mon-Williams
item.description:
As a researcher for the Milburn review, I’ve seen how we’ve failed a generation – then castigated them. Britain must break this vicious cycle

  • Mark Mon-Williams is chair in cognitive psychology at the University of Leeds and professor of psychology at Bradford Institute of Health Research

Alan Milburn and Peter Fonagy have, between them, expertly diagnosed the UK’s illness. Their reviews show we don’t just have a Neet crisis. Or a school absence crisis. Or a Send crisis. We have a neglected childhood crisis that will wreck the country’s long-term prosperity if we just keep patching over these symptoms.

The solution to any problem starts with understanding its causes, and Milburn and Fonagy provide a thoughtful analysis. I have worked closely with both of them, being a topic group member for Fonagy’s independent review into mental health conditions, ADHD and autism, and supporting Milburn with data analytics. Their reviews have followed the evidence, all of which shows a system neglecting children at scale. We have decreased benefits and slashed the support provided to children: today 4.5 million children are living in poverty. When these children grow up and are diagnosed with anxiety and depression, impeding their ability to work, they are often castigated as feckless snowflakes. It is easier to do this than admit that we have failed a generation, and that this is the predictable consequence of political decisions.

Mark Mon-Williams chair in cognitive psychology at the University of Leeds and professor of psychology at Bradford Institute of Health Research

item.title: I got scammed on Instagram – and it led to a truly disgusting dinner | Zoe Williams
item.description:
Intrigued by an unusual recipe for spinach tacos, I followed the instructions, but was left with a soggy, inedible mess. It turns out there are a lot of made-up meals out there

I can’t tell you when my Instagram algorithm changed, from – this is embarrassing, but what the hell – buff guys trying to exercise and being interrupted by a Staffordshire bull terrier who wants to help them exercise, to cooking videos, but it has. I now get endless food content, following the same format: a millennial has 20 minutes to make dinner for his or her beloved (it’s very gender neutral), and launches into some unlikely techniques. He might shove a load of chicken into a cake tin, sprinkle mismatched spices all over, bake it, then slice it, as if it were a cake. Or she might cook tagliatelle in a pan of milk and salmon. This is not how it’s done, I think, as I watch all the way to the end, and then am astonished to be fed yet more weird food content.

Drawn with an almost zombified lack of free will, I got the yen to try it for myself. What would happen if you boiled a white cabbage whole, then roasted it in honey and miso? Well, I can tell you: the cabbage is very soft on the outside, and still uncooked on the inside, and this is why cooks, since time began, have been slicing a cabbage before they try to cook it.

item.title: Let’s take over the ossified Democratic party and deliver a modern New Deal
item.description:
America’s future depends on progressive, anti-establishment fighters

Welcome back to How We Win, a Guardian opinion series with leading thinkers, offering bold ideas for America’s political future. Last week, Naomi Klein, Guardian US columnist, argued for taking on the billionaire class. Today’s edition was written by Wajahat Ali, editor of The Left Hook and co-host of The Democracy-ish Podcast.

Change is slow, and then, once in a while, all of a sudden.

The future of America depends on progressive, anti-establishment fighters to champion a politics of transformation.

Tax billionaires.

Medicare for All.

Abolish ICE and put forth an immigration reform policy that centers both humanity and security.

Call out Israel’s genocide and withhold money and weapons from foreign countries that commit war crimes with our resources.

A living wage.

Reject corporate Pac money and deliver campaign finance reform.

Combat climate change and move away from fossil fuels.

Expand and aggressively reform the supreme court, because without that, we get nothing.

item.title: Where do people want to see Britain’s climate action plan working? On their own doorstep | Miatta Fahnbulleh
item.description:
I am at Cop31 – concerned about the crisis around the world, but mindful that voters want jobs, warmer homes and cheaper prices

  • Miatta Fahnbulleh is the UK secretary of state for energy security and net zero

In this cold weather, it is easy to forget that Britain has just been through its hottest summer on record, part of our new reality as the climate crisis reaches our doorstep. For millions around the world, the consequences have already been more devastating for the communities that did the least to cause this crisis.

That is the backdrop to Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, where I arrive on Tuesday as the UK’s chief negotiator. As I have prepared for these negotiations, I’ve been reflecting on the gap between the science and the political debate in Britain. Early predictions by the Met Office indicate that 2027 will surpass 2024 as the hottest year on record globally as El Niño rips through the Pacific. This is a sobering reality. And yet, the Conservatives and Reform UK want to bury their heads in the sand and break the consensus on delivering net zero. But we know sustained climate action can work.

item.description:

There was a time, within living memory, when Australian Christianity had a definable and active left wing: Palm Sunday peace marches, guitar masses, priests coming home from far-flung missions with stories of liberation theology and, in the early 2000s, powerful and sustained activism against government policies of mandatory detention.

The stoppage was seemingly caused by the transition from copper telecommunication lines

During an interview on Fox News on Monday, host Laura Ingraham pressed Vance on why his fellow Republicans had not been able to fix issues with air traffic control even though they had controlled the White House and Congress for the last two years.

item.title: Hundreds protest against ex-border patrol chief Greg Bovino at Rutgers University talk
item.description:
New Jersey university’s Republicans club invited Bovino, who oversaw Trump’s ICE surges, to speak on campus

Hundreds protested outside a Rutgers University campus building on Monday night, jeering the former border patrol commander Greg Bovino, who was inside addressing a crowd of about 25 people.

The university’s Republicans club had invited Bovino to speak, calling him the “Great Commander” and the “GOAT” in social posts promoting the event at the New Brunswick, New Jersey, campus. During the two-hour talk, the room never quite filled up, occupied mostly by journalists, club members and other students criticizing the former border patrol chief.

item.title: Should JD Vance run for president? I say go for it, habibi! | Arwa Mahdawi
item.description:
Now the vice-president’s luck is turning, he seems reluctant to commit himself to the next presidential race – and I, for one, hate to see it

How do you think history will remember JD Vance? As the first vice-president to spark a vigorous debate about their eyeliner routine? As one of the last public figures to see Pope Francis alive? As the only politician in US history to have been the subject of a rumour about sexual relations with a couch (even though it was unfounded)?

I have no idea. But it seems increasingly unlikely he will be remembered as the 48th president of the US. After Maga’s midterm thrashing, Vance’s political future doesn’t look as bright as it used to. So much so that there has been a flurry of recent headlines debating whether or not Vance, once considered Donald Trump’s heir apparent, may slink away from a presidential run altogether.

Continue reading...

item.title: Hoping for Britain to rejoin the EU with Andy Burnham? You may be waiting a long time | Timothy Garton Ash
item.description:
The PM’s first big speech on the UK and Europe was cautious and disappointing. Don’t expect any great leaps towards a new deal

Ever since Andy Burnham became the British prime minister this summer, people all over Europe have been asking me one question: “Will the UK rejoin the EU?” Sometimes they add: “And if so, when?” None of the intermediate options between the current hard Brexit and Brejoin are of any interest at all to most other Europeans.

Measured against these great expectations, Burnham’s first big speech on Britain and Europe, delivered on Monday evening amid all the pomp and circumstance the City of London could furnish, must be considered a disappointment. It was both a cautious and a curiously old-fashioned speech.

Continue reading...

item.title: Trump claims US is ‘looking into’ Iranian bomb plot in Washington despite ‘no credible threats’
item.description:
US officials ‘debate whether Iran can or will attempt to execute’ plot to detonate a ‘dirty bomb’, report says

Donald Trump has claimed the US is “looking into” whether Iran is developing plans to detonate a so-called “dirty bomb” in Washington, even as the White House said there were “no credible threats” at this time.

Trump said his administration takes the idea “very seriously”

Continue reading...

item.title: US loses measles elimination status amid worst outbreak since 1991
item.description:
Infectious disease is now continually spreading after being eliminated for 26 years, with more than 5,400 US cases

The US lost its measles elimination status, global health authorities announced, an official recognition that the infectious disease is endemic in the US after being eliminated for 26 years.

The announcement comes as the US endures the worst measles outbreak since 1991, with more than 5,400 cases and eight deaths in 2026.

item.title: ‘They were keeping it for a rainy day’: Ukraine’s Kerch bridge attack is proof Kyiv still has cards to play
item.description:
Partial demolition of bridge linking Russia and occupied Crimea is obvious embarrassment to Putin days before meeting with Xi and Trump

  • Europe live – latest updates

Ukraine’s attack on the Kerch road bridge overnight is the culmination of weeks, and perhaps months, of military operations plus years of industrial development, during which Kyiv has developed its own cruise missiles and long-range drones.

The demolition is not quite total, because the rail bridge is still standing, one line in operation – but the attack is an obvious embarrassment to Russia two days before Vladimir Putin is due to meet Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.

Continue reading...

item.title: California DAs sue Gavin Newsom to stop death sentence commutations
item.description:
Thirty district attorneys challenged governor’s mass clemency, on behalf of victims’ families and advocates

California prosecutors and victims’ advocates have sued the state’s governor, Gavin Newsom, to stop him from commuting the death sentences of all 548 people facing execution in the state.

The district attorneys from 30 of California’s 58 counties filed the lawsuit on Monday, challenging the Democratic governor’s mass clemency action announced earlier this month, which would be the largest clearing of any death row in modern US history. Other state prosecutors have supported Newsom’s announcement and are due to speak in favor of the commutations in a press briefing on Tuesday.

Continue reading...

item.title: Climate crisis more visible in film and TV but solutions remain rare, study finds
item.description:
A report analyzing more than 35,000 scripts finds that storylines address its causes, but individual actions remain more prominent than systemic solutions

Climate change and its causes are appearing more frequently in film and television, but entertainment continues to focus more on the consequences of the crisis and individual actions than large-scale solutions, according to a new report.

Released Tuesday and just weeks after Digger, the latest high-profile climate movie that features Tom Cruise as an oil tycoon, the report from the USC Annenberg School for Communications and Journalism and Good Energy, a nonprofit story consultancy, examines climate change in scripted entertainment. The report analyzes 35,120 scripts from 2021 to 2024, building on a 2022 report that found climate-related keywords in just 2.8% of scripts.

Continue reading...

item.title: Costa Rican journalist shot dead in first such killing in 25 years
item.description:
Camilo Rodriguez’s death comes as the country grapples with a surge in drug violence

The Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodríguez, who gained prominence for publishing allegations against ⁠suspected drug traffickers and politicians, was shot dead on Monday, authorities said.

The first known killing of a journalist ⁠in Costa Rica in ⁠25 years, ​Rodriguez’s death comes as the country grapples with a surge in drug violence driven by international trafficking groups, despite long ⁠being regarded as one of Central America’s most peaceful and stable democracies.

Continue reading...

item.title: How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule
item.description:
With the SpaceX satellite system faltering, Ukraine’s military launched a surprise, multi-pronged attack to take down vital bridge to Crimea

At 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south.

Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions.

Continue reading...

item.title: Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ to return to Nvidia as CEO
item.description:
Huang resigned last week over affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and multiple employees who reported to him

Jensen Huang said he would be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO in his first remarks since resigning from the company Thursday.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote in a statement published in the Wall Street Journal and CNBC.

Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.

Continue reading...

item.title: Anti-Arab hate speech surged on social media during Israel’s election, report finds
item.description:
Digital monitors recorded 400% rise in posts attacking Arab Israelis, including Netanyahu’s disproven fraud allegations

Anti-Arab hate speech surged on social media in Israel around the country’s general election last month, digital monitors have said, as politicians including Benjamin Netanyahu levelled disproven allegations against Arab Israeli parties of election fraud.

A new report by the Israel-based Brandeis Institute and FakeReporter recorded a deluge of anti-Arab discourse across social media platforms such as X, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok in the days surrounding Israel’s 27 October election.

Continue reading...

item.title: Jensen Huang to testify before Congress on ‘potential breach of national security’
item.description:
High-stakes hearing comes in wake of resignation from Nvidia after alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy

Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang will testify before several congressional committees on 1 December, setting the stage for a high-stakes hearing in the wake of his resignation following an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, has also agreed to appear for a closed-door transcribed interview the following day, 2 December.

Continue reading...

item.title: UK backs idea of new levies on polluting sectors to pay for climate action costs
item.description:
Britain joins other signatories to statement urging introduction of targeted taxes on heavy emitters

The UK has signed a statement that backs levies on polluting sectors to pay for the impacts of the climate crisis, in a strong political signal that could pave the way for frequent flyer and crypto taxes.

Signing the statement at the UN climate summit means the UK joins a group of governments urging Cop31 to look at “the potential of targeted, small levies to ensure a contribution to the costs of climate action from polluting sectors”. The other signatories so far are Kenya, South Sudan, Spain, Timor Leste, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.

Continue reading...

item.title: Joy, hope and anger as Serbia student movement’s political novices enter parliament
item.description:
Celebrating supporters say they feel vindicated by arrival of Student List candidates in national assembly

The paved plateau in front of Serbia’s national assembly became an impromptu dancefloor, as people of all ages joyfully whirled in a kolo. Drivers passing by sounded their horns, while hundreds of people waved flags, blew whistles and cheered. Every now and again, the crowd parted, allowing smartly dressed men and women to walk up the steps and into the building.

These were the candidates from the Student List, on their way to being sworn in as members of parliament after their stunning victory in last month’s parliamentary elections. Those who had come to cheer them on displayed their feelings on badges, flags and placards.

Continue reading...

item.title: Joe Biden criticizes Zelenskyy as ‘moody’ and ‘not as grateful’ in new memoir
item.description:
Promise Me, America was published just before the former US president’s 84th birthday as he battles advanced cancer

In a new memoir, Joe Biden offers harsh criticism of Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has led Ukraine through four-and-a-half years of war against Russia. According to Biden, the Ukrainian president was “difficult to work with”, “moody and stubborn in our private conversations”, and “not as grateful as I expected” for US diplomatic support and military aid.

Biden’s memoir, Promise Me, America, was published on Tuesday, shortly before his 84th birthday and as he battles advanced prostate cancer. Largely a trumpeting of achievements in office, with scant admission of failings ultimately crowned by his own party deeming him unfit for office and forcing his withdrawal from the 2024 campaign against Donald Trump, the book has not been well reviewed.

Continue reading...

item.title: Is Cop worth it? Fiona Harvey and Ajit Niranjan answered your climate talks questions
item.description:
The Guardian’s environment editor Fiona Harvey and Europe environment correspondent Ajit Niranjan tackled your questions on Cop31, the draft deal on fossil fuels, the fight over climate finance and what overshooting 1.5C means for the world.

Tim asks by email: I heard it was the first zero waste Cop. What positive outcomes have happened at Cop31 for zero waste agenda and how is it related to climate?

Fiona: The waste agenda is one that has been proposed by Turkey, whose first lady is a keen advocate of cutting waste and creating a “circular economy”. There is a zero waste centre here within the blue zone, and other zero waste pavilions within the green zone, with displays and practical demonstrations of how a circular economy can work in practice. The green zone is the bit you don’t need a UN-supervised pass to get into, where companies and governments show off their wares – it’s proving to be a lovely day out for lots of local people!

Continue reading...

item.title: National Security Agency network for internal communications goes down
item.description:
NSA issues ‘code yellow’ as NSANet, used by staff to share classified material, including top-secret intelligence, fails

The National Security Agency’s classified internal communications network went down on Tuesday, disrupting work at the US signals intelligence agency, according to several US media reports.

The network, known as NSANet, is used by NSA staff to share classified material, including top-secret intelligence. The New York Times and CNN reported that the agency had told staff at its Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters to arrive in staggered shifts while it assessed the problem. The Wall Street Journal also reported the outage, citing one person familiar with the situation, who said it stemmed from a software update to patch the system and that it would only be down temporarily.

Continue reading...

item.title: The Guardian view on climate debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31 | Editorial
item.description:
Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability

The catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has earmarked just $20m for Nepal – less than 5% of the $482m that Kathmandu must pay its external public creditors this year.

“The scale of resources needs to increase,” Nepal’s delegation to this year’s UN climate conference drily observed. They are not the only ones agitating for change at Cop31. In its September report, Debt Fuels the Climate Crisis, ActionAid noted that the global south’s external borrowing is 100 times more than the climate finance it received. Poor nations end up trapped in debt dependency because they export cheap raw materials, but import expensive food, fuel and manufactured goods, invariably priced in dollars. The charity warned that climate-vulnerable countries are now expected to fund decarbonisation while servicing dollar loans that often pressure them to export fossil fuels rather than invest in green industrialisation.

Continue reading...

item.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
item.description:
This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust

The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate.

Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work, he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit.

Continue reading...

item.title: Fossil-fuel industry accused of violating Colorado law over not disclosing drilling chemicals
item.description:
Non-profit FracTracker Alliance alleges regulators have exempted compounds used in drilling despite 2022 law

The fossil-fuel industry is violating Colorado law by not disclosing which chemicals it uses in drilling, a new analysis by the FracTracker Alliance non-profit alleges, and state records show it has used illegal or dangerous compounds while fracking.

Drilling chemicals can include xylene, toluene, benzene, Pfas and other dangerous toxicants, industry records and literature from other regions show. A first-in-the-nation 2022 Colorado law requires fossil-fuel operators and their suppliers to make public all chemicals used in “downhole oil and gas production”. But regulators have exempted compounds used in drilling, claiming that drilling is not part of production.

Continue reading...

item.title: NSA claims temporary internal network outage caused by ‘scheduled routine maintenance’ – live
item.description:
Sources told CNN there was no evidence of cyberattack against NSA Net, the network that allows the agency’s employees to send classified information internally

  • Sign up for US Breaking News email

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic-Senator elect from Michigan, said today that he would be happy to work with the Trump administration to pass one of his tentpole policy agenda items – Medicare For All.

“Everybody’s like, ‘ah well, you’d work with Donald Trump to get Medicare For All?’. I’m like hell yeah, because the point for me is Medicare For All. I don’t care who puts their name on it. I need to go back and talk to Michiganders, and I need to know that our service made their lives easier,” he said at the Atlantic Summit in Washington DC.

item.title: Dolores Huerta honored in ceremony at California state capitol
item.description:
Labor leader was remembered for her advocacy and co-founding union that would become United Farm Workers

California officials paid tribute to Dolores Huerta, one of the nation’s most influential labor leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists, at a memorial ceremony Monday at the state capitol.

They remembered her as a relentless advocate for a more just and fair world. Huerta co-founded a union that became the United Farm Workers with César Chávez and made famous her rallying cry, “Sí, se puede!” – which translates to “Yes, it can be done!”

item.title: ‘Nothing they said made sense’: down the rabbit hole with Britain’s sovereign citizens
item.description:
It is an anti-government ideology that began in the US and has spread across the world – wasting public resources and ruining lives. But why have the wild ideas of this movement become so appealing?

In the early morning of 20 June 2023, 13 police officers raided a five-bed barn conversion in rural Hampshire. The occupant, a 57-year-old man named Iain Clifford Stamp, was rudely awoken. The police informed him that they were executing a warrant on behalf of the Financial Conduct Authority, the body that regulates financial services in the UK. FCA raids are rare. They are only permitted when the regulator can persuade a judge that there are reasonable grounds for believing the person or firm that they are investigating will not cooperate. In this case, it seems, there was good reason to believe that Iain Clifford Stamp might cause trouble.

Stamp’s frosty relationship with financial authorities dated back to 2008, when his first company, a financial product provider called Integrity, imploded and was left facing claims from clients of up to an estimated £80m. Back then, Integrity had been publicly censured by the Financial Services Authority for not fairly communicating to customers the risks in the products it was selling. This time was more serious. Stamp was arrested for suspected breaches of the Financial Services and Markets Act: the FCA believed it had evidence he was offering financial services, such as debt and investment advice, without a licence. The day he was arrested, police also raided an industrial estate in Chessington, south-west London, where Stamp’s company had its offices, and seized dozens of computers and files.

Continue reading...

item.title: Serbia’s Student List candidates sworn in as MPs after election triumph
item.description:
Inaugural parliamentary session comes as ousted populist Aleksandar Vučić threatens mass protests of his own

Candidates for Serbia’s Student List, the grassroots movement of political outsiders that pulled off a spectacular victory in last month’s elections over the party of the populist leader Aleksandar Vučić, are to be sworn in as MPs as they begin the process of forming a government.

The 140 candidates – among them academics, lawyers, scientists and the odd actor – will be sworn in on Tuesday during the inaugural session of the new parliament, bringing 14 years of rule by Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) to an end.

Continue reading...

item.title: ‘I’m not ready to go to jail’: co-founder of Egypt’s last independent media outlet faces prison
item.description:
Mada Masr, the news site co-founded by Lina Attalah just before the 2013 military coup, is fighting for its life after being shut down, but its journalists have not given up hope

Facing a year in prison for running Egypt’s leading independent news outlet Mada Masr, Lina Attalah is trying to focus on the everyday: waking at dawn to hear the birds sing before Cairo’s streets come alive and visiting Mada Masr’s shuttered offices with her reporters to water the plants and feed their four cats.

Attalah is the reluctant face of Egypt’s embattled independent press at a moment of crisis. In the last six weeks, Egyptian authorities have waged a renewed crackdown on the few remaining independent media outlets left in the country, beginning with the arrest of the entire newsroom of the factchecking website Matsadaash.

Continue reading...

item.title: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia named as biggest CO2 exporters in history
item.description:
Analysis of fossil fuel exports since 1850 differs from most assessments – which look at countries where CO2 is released

Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are the three biggest exporters of carbon dioxide in history, according to analysis of fossil fuels since 1850.

Russia tops the list of global exporters of fossil fuels, with its vast coal, oil and gas deposits. Accounting for the CO2 produced by burning these exports, Russia has been responsible for more than 70 gigatonnes, up to the end of 2025.

Continue reading...

item.title: European-made pesticides named in 1,605 poisoning reports in Brazil last year
item.description:
About a third of cases involved chemicals banned for use on EU farms, according to investigation by Unearthed and Public Eye

Pesticides sold by European chemical companies were named in more than 1,600 poisoning reports in Brazil last year, an investigation has found.

About a third of the cases involved chemicals banned from use on farms in the EU because of the risks they pose to people and the environment. But European companies are not banned from manufacturing these chemicals, as long as they export them overseas to countries where they are legally allowed to be used.

item.title: Don’t wait for a change in the age of consent. Adults can act to stop age-gap abuse | Gaby Hinsliff
item.description:
The law is important, but so is the fact that people know when associates embark on inappropriate relationships. They bear responsibility too

Mia Latter was 16 and out clothes-shopping when Russell Brand stopped her on the street. He riffled through her bags to choose a dress he told her she should wear for the date he’d be taking her on. And so began a short relationship – if that’s the right word, given she was still at school and he was a 30-year-old MTV presenter, who she says publicly referred to her as “the child”. Towards the end, she claims, Brand orally raped her.

Lilly Creightmore was 18 when she says the then 32-year-old celebrity David Walliams asked her to dinner and then began pestering her for sex. There’s a hauntingly awkward photograph of her with him at a celebrity bash. Another time, at a house party, a fellow guest remembers her sitting on the floor alone, like a bored child. She now feels his behaviour was an abuse of power over someone vulnerable. Walliams’s lawyers say he denies grooming her or behaving inappropriately.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

Continue reading...

item.title: David Jones: what went wrong and what happens next? Five takeaways from first creditors meeting
item.description:
Upmarket retailer, which recorded a net loss of $228m last financial year, has total debt over $400m including $11m owed to staff

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Upmarket retailer David Jones owed hundreds of millions of dollars when it collapsed into administration, after accelerating financial losses and reputational damage threatened its ability to stock shelves for Christmas.

About 500 creditors attended its first meeting on Tuesday, where administrators McGrathNicol started to break down who is owed what, when those left out of pocket will know where they stand, and what ultimately went wrong.

item.title: Hundreds arrested in anti-Trump protests in Philippines amid anger over Iran war and AI pact
item.description:
Organisers say up to 10,000 people could join the next round of demonstrations ahead of the US president’s arrival in Manila for the Asean summit

  • Asean and Apec summits – live updates

Hundreds of people have been arrested in heated demonstrations against Donald Trump in Manila, as authorities braced for more protests ahead of the US president’s arrival in the city for a leaders’ summit.

Organisers claim as many as 10,000 people will join protests against Trump in the Philippine capital on Tuesday, when he will attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit. The crowds are expected to try to walk to the summit site.

item.title: Millionaire factory: Anthropic IPO set to fuel AI gold rush in London’s high-end property market
item.description:
New tech wealth, amassed with remarkable speed, is now washing up on British shores

Sporting hoodies and white trainers rather than the gilets of London’s banker and lawyer class, tech bros can struggle to be taken seriously by the capital’s luxury property agents. “We worked with a young tech entrepreneur with a substantial budget, who agents assumed was looking to rent a one-bedroom flat,” says Jo Eccles, a buying agent who sources off-market properties for ultra-wealthy clients.

But this week’s float by Anthropic, the AI developer behind the chatbot Claude, promises to bring even more credibility for the growing cohort of tech millionaires, which could breathe life into London’s ailing high-end property market. Its IPO on Thursday, expected to value the company at $1.4tn (£1.1tn), is likely to turn more than 4,000 of its staff into millionaires as their stock options vest. SaaStr, a California research firm, has estimated that the minimum value generated for staff at the AI lab will be $20m each.
